candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures claims about AP/IB/honors/early-college/dual-credit offerings, built-in tutoring/mentoring, and concrete college admissions or scholarship outcomes — e.g., many square reviews name AP/IB/Early College, before/after-school math tutoring, Presidential Scholars, and alumni accepted to selective universities, while circle reviews repeatedly note a lack of AP/honors and poor college preparation.
candidate_defs.square entries report a broader, higher-: This groups descriptions of many clubs, outstanding band/music/theatre programs, vocational pathways, ROTC/magnet arts, signature events and strong school spirit — e.g., square reviewers cite '100+ clubs,' award-winning band/ensembles, magnet/culinary/media facilities and community turnout for athletics; circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth or traditions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers firsthand accounts of ongoing bullying (including racially motivated or targeted harassment), daily fights, vaping/drugs/smoking, sexual-assault allegations, bus-related disruptions, and reviewers’ reports that staff/administration ignored or covered up incidents — circle entries generally lack these severe safety claims or report less persistent/less severe behavior problems.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This captures allegations of layoffs and inexperienced hires, opaque fundraising and budget cuts, administrators protecting staff or covering incidents, systemic favoritism (especially toward athletes/affluent families), poor inter-department communication, and politicized decision‑making (superintendent-as-CEO narratives), whereas circle reviews contain fewer of these governance/resource complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This groups concrete, physical-plant and ops issues such as multiple lunch shifts, classes with >40 students or no desks, lack of lockers, chaotic scheduling/arena-registration failures, long traffic/parking delays, mismatch between teams and facilities (swim team/no pool), and inconsistent technology deployments; circle reviews rarely cite these kinds of capacity or day-to-day operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report substantially wors: These reviews describe concrete campus-safety failures at square schools: frequent fights, pervasive bullying (including incidents that forced students to leave), drug/alcohol/vaping epidemics, weapons threats/lockdowns, sexual-assault reports, and slow or ineffective security responses (e.g., pepper‑spray use, security taking long to break up fights). Example evidence: 'we had to take her out of the school due to her being excessively bullied,' 'rampant drug use on campus,' 'students are choked out while staff did little to stop it,' and 'security is not all that strict... it takes a long time for them to get there.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and more: Many square reviews list concrete program breadth and college-prep pathways—multiple AP/IB/honors options, dual-enrollment partnerships, vocational/CTE shops and high‑tech labs, required senior internships, and named elite-college matriculations—while circle reviews lack comparable program detail. Example evidence: 'many AP, IB classes,' 'dual enrollment with Virginia Western,' 'laser engraving and CNC machines... Project Lead the Way,' 'required senior internship: 80+ hours,' and named outcomes like Harvard/Yale matriculation or large transferable college credit totals.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent teac: These reviews document staff-level failures at square schools: teachers or counselors ignoring IEPs/504s, refusing interventions, losing submitted work, poor college advising, unprofessional/abusive teacher behavior, or conversely a few highly supportive staff amid broad inconsistency. Example evidence: 'her IEP was ignored by nearly all her teachers,' 'WE BEGGED THE SCHOOL... NO CONCERN,' 'counselors unwilling to help... missed National Merit opportunities,' and 'teachers that routinely scream at them and call them idiots' (versus isolated reports of helpful teachers).
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize physical facili: Square reviews frequently catalog facility upgrades, large athletic investments, strong band/music programs, wide extracurricular/club/CTE offerings and also criticize resource allocation that prioritizes athletics over classroom materials. Example evidence: 'new stadium and an Olympic sized pool,' '140+ member award-winning marching band,' 'Trades … Welding, Automotive Tech,' and complaints like 'spent 5 MILLION on a SPORTS facility when education department is lacking.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These items describe systemic administrative failures or governance choices at square schools: poor record transfers/registration delays and refund problems, opaque/defensive leadership or cover‑ups, favoritism (especially toward athletes or well‑connected families), discriminatory discipline, contentious transfer/admissions or graduation-ticket policies, and litigation concerns. Example evidence: 'gave our son's new school a hard time when they requested his school records,' 'The Principal and Assistant Principal cover up...,' 'accepts practically all interdistrict transfers... lowered standards,' and 'graduation is now regulated by ticket number'.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, broader: This bucket groups items where square reviews name many AP/IB/dual‑enrollment courses, industry credentials, and concrete college placements or credit (e.g., '25 AP courses', IB diplomas, dual credit, CNA/EMT/FAA certifications, students accepted to Ivy/major universities and large scholarship totals), whereas circle reviews do not provide comparable, documented advanced‑course breadth or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This cluster covers safety and student‑behavior evidence: square reviews repeatedly describe drugs/vaping triggering fire alarms, consistent fights, assaults and theft, sexual/assault incidents and alleged law‑enforcement misbehavior, and claims that bullied students were suspended or investigations mishandled — complaints that circle reviews largely omit or counter with statements of students being safe and bullying handled.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Included are concrete governance and discipline issues in square writeups — mass staff exits and frequent principal turnover, alleged misuse/diversion of funds (stadiums over air‑conditioning), district policies to inflate grades, suspending victims, alumni‑dominated hiring, and favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families — whereas circle reviews do not document the same systemic administrative dysfunction or entrenched favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive, hi: Square reviews frequently name outstanding band/choir/theatre programs, award‑winning music directors, successful athletic teams, JROTC/AFJROTC, and high extracurricular participation, while also noting that sports sometimes receive preferential treatment or funding over other programs; circle reviews rarely document comparable arts/athletics breadth or high‑level extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries discuss facility, operati: This bucket covers physical and operational evidence: square reviews cite overcrowding, unsanitary bathrooms, missing supplies, contested parking fees, and underfunding alongside concrete upgrades or initiatives (campus makeovers, renovated pools, 1:1 laptop programs and reported tech distribution), whereas circle reviews generally lack such detailed accounts of facilities, maintenance, or specific capital/technology actions.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews report concrete program breadth and outcomes in square schools (AP/IB/Honors, tracked pathways, early‑college/AP credit, high college matriculation and National Merit mentions) while circle reviews rarely name or document comparable advanced-course access or elite college placement (examples: multiple square notes of “AP program is the best…accepted to Georgia Tech/Princeton,” IB/AP lists, early‑college associates programs vs. circle’s lack of program detail).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews repeatedly describe fights, gang/drug activity, sexual harassment, suicides/mental‑health crises, and visible security/police interventions (e.g., 'many fights weekly', 'heroin use…epidemic', sexual assault with no staff support), whereas circle reviews rarely document violence at that severity and often describe a safer peer climate.
candidate_defs.square entries document larger, better‑o: Square reviewers cite robust extracurricular ecosystems—award‑winning bands, extensive clubs, strong theater and vocational programs, well‑attended athletic events and active booster/foundation fundraising, even families moving into the district for these offerings—while circle reviews seldom list comparable organized program depth or institutional parent booster support.
candidate_defs.square entries record clearer facility,: Square reviews provide specific facility/health evidence (collapsed ceilings, mold, cockroaches, sewage leaks), overcrowding/short passing times, dated textbooks and budget cuts, and explicit allocation tradeoffs (new football field/gym vs. no books), whereas circle reviews rarely raise this level of physical‑plant or budget‑allocation detail.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete, in: Square reviews repeatedly give named, specific accounts of counselor errors, IEP/504 noncompliance, administrative favoritism or bullying, grading opacity and promotion practices, and also identifiable staff responsiveness in some cases (e.g., transcripts mishandled, 'IEPs not followed', 'teachers offer extra hours', 'principal turnaround'), whereas circle reviews typically lack this same level of operational detail about governance, counseling, special‑education, and grading practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: This bucket captures descriptions of frequent fights, lockdowns, arrests, weapons/drugs on campus, and claims that bullying and violence are chronic or dismissed (e.g. “lock-down almost every day,” “many arrests,” “Thugs run the community,” “you will get bullied every single day”) — plus reviewer evidence that anti‑bullying efforts are performative or administrators fail to enforce consequences; circle entries repeatedly lack or directly contradict these safety claims (e.g. “almost bully free,” “very little bullying”).
candidate_defs.square entries document wider extremes i: This groups concrete claims about AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/CTE/vocational certifications and notable college placements alongside reports of remediation needs, grade‑inflation/credit‑recovery misuse, and weak state/AP results — e.g. “IB, AP, Dual Enrollment, CTE certifications,” “Has produced National Merit semifinalists,” and opposing complaints like “Credit Recovery is a disgrace,” “students pass classes then fail state tests.” Circle entries rarely cite this same breadth of named advanced programs or the same mix of extreme outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more overt admin: This bucket covers reviewer claims about leaders and governance (nepotism, overpaid or absent principals, grade‑tampering allegations, transcript/fee coercion, arbitrary punishments, and board/district failures) with examples like “administrators are intensely overpaid,” “principal nowhere to be found,” “they will hold your transcripts,” and “no sense of quality control.” Circle entries do not emphasize this pattern of systemic leadership misconduct or the same scale of governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, more visi: This groups concrete program and facility evidence — both positive and disruptive — such as award‑winning bands/theaters and state sports championships, modernized gyms/theaters and CTE shops, plus overcrowding and renovation disruptions (e.g. “best performing arts center,” “Blackfoot Broncos took state,” and “overcrowded—desperately needs expansion,” “stalled school renovations obstructing traffic”). Circle entries typically do not list the same range of named programs, facilities, or large renovation/capacity effects.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frontline stu: This bucket collects reports of absent/ineffective counselors, denied medical or 504 accommodations, poor special‑education services, mental‑health harms tied to school climate, and unreturned parent emails or teacher nonresponse (e.g. “my freshman met her guidance counselor only once,” “refused to acknowledge my anxiety disorder,” “The special education program is terrible,” and “Most of the teachers do not respond to e-mails in a timely matter”), whereas circle entries more often describe accessible, individual staff support or do not report these systemic support failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews report concrete curricular assets—AP/IB offerings, dual‑credit and associate-degree pathways, career academies (health/CTE/STEM/Governor’s School), and elite college placements—far more often than circle (examples: “12 AP classes… admitted to MIT,” “AP/IB/dual credit… graduate with Associates,” “health academy,” “#1 robotics program”). Falling here means reviewers emphasize structured, measurable advanced-course access and postsecondary outcomes rather than the limited/basic academics described in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews recount concrete safety failures—guns/drug incidents, weekly fights, gang activity, arson, pervasive bullying, racial harassment and students leaving for safety—with administrators often portrayed as ineffective or ignoring problems (examples: “a student came to school with a loaded handgun,” “so many fights…trash cans set on fire,” “racism is prevalent…administrators let it happen,” “students selling drugs behind school”). Membership means the school narrative centers on tangible threats to student safety and inadequate disciplinary response.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Reviewers list a wide, high‑visibility array of clubs/teams and documented successes—nationally ranked sports, state championships, world‑champion color guard, top‑rated band, travel clubs, extensive arts programs, ROTC, FBLA/debate, large stadiums and PACs—more often than circle (examples: “WGI world champs Colorguard,” “stadium of a staggering $60 million,” “travel club to China, Russia and Egypt,” “band ranked 3rd in US”). Falling in this bucket means the school is characterized by scale, awards, and diverse extracurricular pathways not seen in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: These reviews describe leadership problems, opaque or hostile governance, coercive monetization (pay-to-stop-extortion tactics, inflated fees), punitive policy enforcement (rigid dress/eligibility rules, exclusionary suspensions), misinformation or intimidation of parents, and contested budget/board decisions (examples: “they worry so much about dress code…not teaching,” “$2 bribe for yearbook,” “principal lied to save district money,” “parents reprimanded for Facebook complaints,” “school board poor quality”). Inclusion means the dominant evidence points to problematic decision‑making, policy abuse, or fiscal/governance conflict rather than the collaborative leadership narratives in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent,: These reviews document failures or wide variability in on‑site supports—IEP/504 noncompliance, poor or dismissive counselors, barriers to special‑education enrollment, inconsistent remediation/tutoring, long parent communication delays, or pressure to medicate—contrasting with circle’s accounts of accessible help (examples: “They do not comply with IEPs…get an attorney,” “counselor said he was just one of those kids,” “getting someone to answer a call has taken up to 3 days,” vs circle’s reports of counselors who help). Falling in this bucket means reviewer evidence centers on whether the school reliably provides legally required and practical academic/social supports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: These reviews describe concrete safety problems (frequent fights, riots, on-campus drug/alcohol use, vaping epidemics, sexual-assault allegations, pervasive bullying, gang activity, theft) and explicitly say administration fails to stop or properly investigate them ("bullying is swept under the rug," "nothing is done," "administration oblivious"). Examples: "violent fights, drug use in the bathrooms," "school has a r*pist . do not recommend," and "Bullying problem is for real ridiculous," which appear across many square entries but are absent or minimized in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger advance: Many square reviews enumerate concrete academic offerings and outcomes—extensive AP/Honors, IB or magnet programs, dual-credit, 5.0 GPA options, high AP exam success and detailed college acceptances—often with quantified metrics ("over 90% of graduates going to college," "students accepted to Harvard/MIT"). Representative evidence: "wide range of AP courses… students accepted into top US universities," and "full IB program… prepared for college," whereas circle entries lack this level of program detail and measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, better-do: Square reviews list many named clubs, arts and music programs, robust athletics, CTE/vocational shops, internships and industry/community partnerships (e.g., aviation hanger, JPL speakers, strong band, robotics, theatre, state playoff teams), and describe visible admin support for these activities; circle entries mention far fewer specific extracurriculars. Examples: "wonderful music department," "aviation… full hanger built on campus," and "guest speaker series… speakers from JPL," contrasted with circle's sparse activity listings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly contain concrete reports about leadership and policy: nepotism and favoritism (especially toward athletes), punitive/exclusionary discipline and pushout practices, fees or policies blocking graduation, administrators who hide incidents or ignore parents, plus detailed accounts of counseling/IEP/504 follow‑through (both positive and negative). Illustrative items: "Western is all about what your last name is…", "fees over $300… without paying him would not be able to graduate," "Counselors don't care…" and also specific IEP communication claims like "school communicates well, establishes a solid IEP game plan," showing square entries provide specific governance and individualized‑support evidence that circle entries rarely do.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviews contain specific, actionable facility and operations details—overcrowding, trailers, closed restrooms, mold/rodent/sanitation problems, elevator accessibility, recent remodeling, Smartboards/iPad rollouts (both positive and poorly integrated), scheduling/attendance policies, fragmented online platforms, and registration/transfer disorganization—while circle entries rarely provide this level of operational specificity. Examples include "building is ninety years old… smell mold or seeing a roach," "classes ended up in the trailers," "Each classroom has a Smartboard," and "transitioned to Plato… students failing despite completing work."
candidate_defs.square entries report more serious stude: This bucket groups reviews describing chronic or severe safety/discipline problems and ineffective enforcement—physical fights and assaults, drug/gang activity, pervasive bullying, vaping, locked/filthy bathrooms, and cases where administration/staff ignored or mishandled threats (examples: 'bully, beat up defenseless students', 'Many drugs,fighting ,drinking and few gangs', 'There are fights literally every single day', 'they did nothing' after threats). It merges incidents and the school's failure to protect students (including calls for metal detectors, police involvement, or suspension mismanagement) into one safety/climate theme.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and high: This bucket captures concrete programmatic strength and intensity: many square reviews list AP/IB offerings, dual-enrollment/college-credit, advanced STEM and CTE options, measurable college outcomes and extreme homework/rigor (examples: 'all AP classes eliminated in favor of IB' in policy change discussions, 'excellent dual enrollment...saved us thousands', 'enormous volume of homework; 4-6 hours per night', 'HYPS/MIT/Caltech admits'). It covers both availability of advanced tracks and the associated high‑intensity academic expectations and outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit admi: This bucket groups reports of systemic inequity and questionable management practices—claims of bias toward wealthy/athlete/white students, nepotism, ideological/exclusionary donor decisions, withheld incident documentation, and prioritized funding for athletics over academics (examples: 'If you come from money, you're good', 'nepotism... but with a recent change', 'they will NOT provide [incident] documentation', 'They value sports more than they value how their kids are taught'). It focuses on fairness, equity, and administrative decision‑making rather than isolated staff rudeness.
candidate_defs.square entries report more active, concr: This bucket groups evidence of teacher/counselor engagement and structured academic support—frequent examples of proactive teacher emails/responses, one‑on‑one attention in small classes, weekend tutoring, responsive guidance counseling, and successful special‑education accommodations (examples: 'teachers emailed at 2 am... surprisingly they responded', 'They also offer tutoring... as well as Saturday's', 'The counselors do a wonderful job...keeping up with the individual kids', 'son with Asperger's now in regular classes and honor roll'). It captures tangible in‑school support systems and their impact on individual students.
candidate_defs.square entries contain far more concrete: This bucket groups practical, operational issues and changes: building condition (old vs new), trailers and cafeteria closures, locked bathrooms, overcrowded classes, transportation problems and paid bus fares, block/4x4 schedule controversies and mid‑year transfer/credit problems, tuition/extra fees and IB/AP charges, and enrollment/waitlist/permit policies (examples: 'rented trailer classrooms', 'GO BACK TO 7 CLASSES A DAY', 'LCHS only accepts La Canada residents first and waitlisting', '$200/class IB fee billed in October', 'The buses are late or delayed a lot'). It captures logistical constraints and facility/capacity effects on daily schooling.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger advanced: These reviews describe square schools as offering system-level advanced pathways (IB, many AP/honors options, magnets like Science & Technology, UC/dual‑enrollment centers and concurrent‑enrollment credit) and concrete elite matriculation outcomes (students going to Ivy/Pac‑12/major conservatories, full‑ride scholarships), whereas circle reviews lack sustained evidence of comparable advanced-program breadth or elite college outcomes (examples: 'Wall to Wall IB program', 'UC Center...take SSU courses', 'students sent to the Ivy's' vs. circle's absence of IB/AP program detail).
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pr: Square reviews repeatedly name abundant clubs, award‑winning arts programs, state‑level competitive teams, and large sports facilities/complexes (marching band at Kennedy Center/Mayor's office, Mock Trial #1 in State, 'sports complex is top notch'), while circle reviews generally mention only a few programs and no comparable high‑profile extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more school safe: Square texts contain frequent, concrete reports of student misconduct and safety incidents (drugs, fights, weapons, sexual harassment, Nazi graffiti), repeated police/shelter‑in‑place events, and claims that discipline is uneven or ignored—often tied to athletic favoritism—whereas circle reviews offer little or no evidence of pervasive safety crises (examples: 'drugs...happen in the hallways', 'shelter in place every 2 weeks', 'armed guards on campus', contrasted with circle's 'very little teasing or bullying at all').
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: Many square reviews allege unresponsive/hostile guidance offices, failure to implement IEPs/504s, bureaucratic red‑tape, budget misprioritization, favoritism toward athletes/band, and high leadership turnover—concrete operational harms to students—whereas circle reviews more often describe helpful, communicative administration and effective counseling (examples: 'no IEP coordinator...denying special help', 'counselors hide in meetings', 'they only care if you’re the football team' vs. circle's 'the new principal is phenomenal', 'Counseling staff truly cares').
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize practical vocat: Circle reviews disproportionately highlight career/vocational pathways, in‑school college courses/dual‑enrollment alternatives and measurable school improvement (ROP/SkillsUSA/Construction programs, 'College in the High School', Running Start alternatives, 'award for most improved HSPE scores'), and portray concrete administrative fixes (new principal, improved supervision), while square reviews focus more on advanced‑academic and extracurricular prestige rather than this distinct, career‑oriented, improvement‑focused portfolio.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more con: These reviews name AP/Pre‑AP, IB/Cambridge, dual‑enrollment, engineering/STEM academies, documented alumni admissions (Ivy/MIT/Stanford), high AP participation and school rankings — e.g., “Both my children went to University of Pennsylvania…”, “Many AP and Honors classes…”, “adding an IB program” — whereas circle reviews rarely list concrete advanced programs or comparable college matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Multiple square reviews describe frequent fights, bullying, physical assaults, drug/alcohol problems, vaping, K‑9 locker searches and even near‑lockdowns or a protest after a student suicide, often coupled with administrative failure to protect victims (e.g., “teacher now beaten by the students,” “DRUGS.ARE.EVERYWHERE.HERE,” “bullying goes unchecked”), claims not made in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document more systemic op: Square reviewers repeatedly cite concrete failures — missing grade portals, ignored emails, chaotic registration, counselor inaccessibility, nepotism, budget cuts and questionable spending, teacher hiring/retention problems, and altered/transferred records — e.g., “teachers are not required to update web‑pages,” “district tried to throw him under the bus,” and “not enough textbooks,” while circle reviews rarely report these detailed governance/operational failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more physical‑plan: Evidence includes overcrowded classrooms and 40+ portables, poor maintenance or pest/mold complaints, parking and heavy bussing/early start complaints, and construction or facility disruptions (e.g., “classes are packed with 27 students,” “40+ portables… kids get soaked when it rains,” “pick up/drop off needs improvement”), whereas circle entries emphasize modest/small size and do not report these pervasive facility/capacity strains.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a more consisten: Circle reviews more often portray a close, well‑organized environment — small classes, teachers who mentor/are approachable, orderly discipline and family‑like treatment (e.g., “wonderful atmosphere,” “the staff knows your teen… close family environment,” “they are always fair, show concern”), a pattern that contrasts with the fragmented, safety/leadership problems frequently reported in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger formal a: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete, institution-level academic strength in square schools (AP/IB/dual-credit access, magnet/STEM/arts/CTE pathways, higher test scores and documented college matriculation) versus circle reviews that describe limited advanced offerings or poor college readiness; examples include square claims of ‘‘IB/AP/dual-credit giving 18+ college credits,’’ ‘top state rankings,’ and named magnet programs, while circle reviews report ‘no AP,’ ‘poor college readiness,’ or counselors blocking advanced enrollment.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures descriptions of frequent physical fights, bullying, racial/sexual harassment, vandalism, vaping/drug incidents, bomb threats and repeated reports that staff/administration fail to stop or adequately discipline perpetrators in square schools; contrasting circle reviews often describe a safer, respectful or well‑managed student climate. Examples: square mentions ‘weekly fights,’ ‘daily racial slurs,’ ‘bomb threats,’ and ‘staff complacent about bullying,’ while circle states ‘students seem to respect each other’ and ‘they are safe.’
candidate_defs.square entries portray larger, program‑r: This bucket groups reviews emphasizing scale and physical/program assets in square schools — large enrollment, many clubs/arts/athletics, performance centers or new campuses — sometimes alongside overcrowding or space strain; circle entries instead emphasize small, close-knit settings and lack of comparable program breadth. Examples: square lists ‘dozens of clubs, state‑level marching band, PAC and new campus’ and also ‘trailers/too crowded,’ whereas circle highlights ‘about 400 students,’ ‘small town community,’ and fewer advanced extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket includes concrete operational and governance problems reported more often in square reviews: counselors who botch schedules or risk graduation, teachers tutoring students for pay, opaque/biased grading, rehired superintendents or rapid principal turnover, and claims of favoritism (especially toward athletes) and cover‑ups; circle reviews seldom make these same governance/misconduct allegations and more often praise responsive staff. Examples: square cites ‘counselor scheduling errors that nearly cost graduation,’ ‘teachers refer students to paid tutoring approved by principal,’ ‘awards based on popularity,’ and ‘revolving door of principals.’
candidate_defs.circle entries describe smaller, close‑k: This bucket covers circle reviews that emphasize individualized attention, stable/good teachers, long-term parental satisfaction and an inclusive peer climate (AVID/college trips, active parent communities), in contrast to many square reviews that stress impersonal scale, variability of teacher quality, or community stratification. Examples: circle reviewers say ‘small school…parents truly care,’ ‘good teachers…my daughter thrives,’ and ‘students are accepting,’ while square reviews more often describe large, impersonal classes, cliques, or inconsistent teacher performance.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger advanced: These reviews describe square schools with extensive AP/IB/honors/dual‑credit catalogs, named specialized academies, and concrete college metrics (e.g., multiple AP credits, dual‑enrollment participation, '98% go to college', students accepted to top colleges), whereas circle entries lack comparable advanced‑course inventories or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries show broader, higher‑qual: Square reviews repeatedly list large club rosters, award‑winning band/arts, NJROTC/Jazz/BPA national teams, many athletic teams and booster support (marching band at Greek Theater, state‑ranked teams), while circle reviews rarely name such breadth or external honors and often report limited activities.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater facility d: Square content documents mold, sewer/odor issues, cracked ceilings, trailers, overcrowded classes/buses, locked or trashed bathrooms and repeated lockdowns—concrete infrastructure and space constraints not reported in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviewers describe gangs, drugs, frequent fights, vandalism, serious assaults/suicides, unlocked entrances and policy shifts after violent incidents (e.g., banning off‑campus lunch), and often frame safety as a dominant, unresolved issue—claims largely absent or far less severe in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviews name overloaded or hostile guidance offices, college‑counseling sabotage, unresolved harassment, principal turnover or auditing scandals, arbitrary/favoritism discipline and biased treatment of POC/low‑income students, poor parent communication, and contested budget priorities—patterns of operational and governance breakdowns that circle entries do not report at the same scale.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reviews that describe recurring fights, gang targeting, physical assaults, suicidality linked to bullying, pervasive drug/alcohol use or pot smell on campus, lockdowns and police involvement (e.g., “there is a fight daily,” “the whole school smells like pot,” “at least two suicides due to bullying,” “gangs targeting white kids”), all of which appear far more often in square than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Includes complaints about ignored parent calls/emails, principals who won’t respond, administrators protecting bad teachers or privileged students, reassigning low‑performing staff instead of accountability, hostile front‑office conduct, and punitive responses to complainants (e.g., “never pick up the phone,” “the school office protects the bad teacher,” “when parents file a complaint they waste no time making claims against you”), patterns emphasized in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, named a: Captures explicit program breadth and demonstrable outcomes present in many square reviews — AP/IB/magnet/CTE tracks, dual‑enrollment and college‑credit programs, STEM/biomed pathways, award‑winning debate/band/robotics, scholarship totals and selective college acceptances (examples: ‘IB and AP offerings,’ ‘SLU 1818 program,’ ‘over $26 MILLION in scholarships,’ ‘state and national championships’), features far more frequently documented in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: Groups critiques of classroom practice and supports — widespread ‘horrible’ or underqualified teachers, frequent teacher no‑shows, lax classroom management, high turnover, ‘sink or swim’ culture, refusal/denial of IEP accommodations and parents hiring advocates (e.g., ‘math teachers will not help,’ ‘teachers aren’t even certified,’ ‘IEP rights denied—had to hire an attorney’), patterns that square reviewers raise far more than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight more extreme fa: This bucket captures reviews that report either notable new construction/high‑end athletics/performing‑arts facilities or, conversely, severe deferred maintenance, pest infestations, closed bathrooms, overcrowded halls, and explicit budget tradeoffs (e.g., ‘new $1M football field while arts are cut,’ ‘rat fell from ceiling,’ ‘one bathroom for 500 students,’ ‘major remodel coming’), a pattern of acute facility/resource extremes emphasized in square more often than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: These reviews repeatedly name concrete college‑prep offerings and in‑school academic supports (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment/CCP/Running Start, credit recovery, math labs, summer bridge, college reps) and claim measurable outcomes (high SAT averages, Ivy placements) that circle reviews do not. Examples: “AP and Early College programs are fantastic,” “first high school in Indiana to offer the International Baccalaureate,” and “Credit Recovery” and math labs supporting student success.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a broader, bette: Square reviews enumerate many named clubs, arts/performing‑arts achievements, CTE/vocational tracks, JROTC/leadership programs and high extracurricular participation, whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth. Illustrative evidence: “hundreds of clubs… choir, band, theater… culinary academy, medical program, robotics, ROTC,” and competitive arts/athletic placements cited by reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Many square reviews describe violent incidents, pervasive substance use, gang activity, repeated fights, weapon discoveries, sexual harassment, and reports that schools failed to remediate or escalate these problems; circle reviews contain far fewer or none of these claims. Examples include: “kids have been stabbed… shootings… bomb threats,” “drug dealers in every grade,” and “They do nothing about bullying… unless the child has been hit.”
candidate_defs.square entries document more politicized: Square reviews repeatedly allege favoritism toward athletes and wealthy families, unpredictable or punitive discipline, board secrecy and politicized personnel decisions, and hostile or unstable principals—patterns largely absent in circle. Representative lines: “dean allows his wrestling team members to get away with murder,” “board of directors keep unworthy teachers…,” “principal is heavy handed,” and reports of opaque grading/discipline policies and parental exclusion.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: Square reviewers frequently cite overcrowded classes/buildings, deteriorating or inconsistently maintained facilities, severe connectivity or banned‑app technology problems, cafeteria/food complaints, bus and records/registration errors, and disruptive construction—issues circle reviews rarely raise. Examples: “classrooms had an average of 35–40 students,” “THE WIFI IS TERRIBLE… banned everything,” “lost paperwork…put my kids in classes they had already completed,” and “dirty…tons of broken equipment.”
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student: This bucket groups reviews that describe frequent fights, weapons, open drug/vaping use, pervasive bullying (including racial/identity‑based harassment), sexual assaults, gang activity and threats, plus staff/administration that fail to intervene (e.g., 'fights 1–2 a week', 'drugs openly displayed', 'bullying is a major issue and the school does nothing', 'Vice Principal threatened my son they'll call police' and 'metal detectors/police are on site but enforcement is inconsistent'). It captures both the incidents themselves and reviewers’ claims that consequences and follow‑up are absent or inconsistent, distinguishing these safety/crisis realities from other operational or programmatic issues described in other buckets.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, formal: This bucket covers reviews that list concrete academic programs and outcomes—IB/IB participation, many AP/honors classes, Early College/dual‑enrollment, CTE credentials, National Merit/college acceptances and alumni trajectories (e.g., 'IB programme; over 63% take an IB class', 'students placed into top tier colleges', 'graduated with CNA license', 'concurrent enrollment so students may graduate with an Associate degree'). It captures explicit program inventories, participation rates, and postsecondary evidence that reviewers attribute to the school’s academic strength.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broad extracurr: This bucket groups reviews highlighting abundant or highly visible extracurriculars (competitive band, choir, theatre, robotics, vocational partnerships, travel trips) alongside a dominant sports culture, athletic facilities and community turnout, plus complaints that resources and leniency are skewed to athletes (examples: 'football stadium at the front', 'band traveled to China', 'pay‑to‑play fees', 'they literally invented the grade D‑ so that more people can play sports', 'funds go to football not academics'). It captures both positive program breadth and the recurrent criticism that athletics/stars receive preferential funding, discipline, and grading.
candidate_defs.square entries report administrative and: This bucket collects reviews alleging poor leadership, secretive/ politicized board behavior, fiscal mismanagement/nepotism, abusive or biased staff behavior, high‑level personnel investigations, and unresponsive or punitive administrative practices (e.g., 'school board meets secretly', 'administration is way too rigid and only cares about sports', 'ex‑principal resigned pending police investigation', 'teachers/staff show favoritism to parents with money'). It focuses on governance, hiring/discipline decisions, and leadership conduct separate from day‑to‑day discipline or facility shortcomings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: This bucket includes overcrowding and scheduling breakdowns, transportation unreliability, emergency‑drill and safety‑procedural failures, infrastructure/health hazards or recent modernizations, unequal material resources (underfunded art supplies vs. 1:1 devices), and operational errors (attendance/records mistakes)—for example 'classes with 40 students', 'buses never on time', 'asbestos found', 'every student has an iPad', 'drills are not practiced', and 'ceiling panels missing after Hurricane Sandy'. It groups physical, logistical, and capacity realities that shape student experience distinct from program quality, extracurriculars, discipline, or governance.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially br: These reviews emphasize that square schools offer many named AP/IB/CTE/STEM/dual‑enrollment pathways and external partnerships (examples: IB/AP/ACP/AVID, Project Lead The Way, cosmetology/mechanics, Early College/AA pathways, 3D printers/laser cutter/CNC, Running Start, dual enrollment with local colleges) and cite measurable postsecondary success (scholarships, multiple students attending selective universities), while circle reviews lack comparable, sustained program breadth or outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews repeatedly document fights, daily drug exposure and overdoses, hate symbols and racial slurs, suicidality tied to bullying, and claims that administration tolerates or mishandles these incidents (examples: 20–25 fights early in the year, confederate flags/swastikas, daily drug exposure, suicides, students punched a cop), whereas circle reviews do not report the same scale or severity of systemic safety/harassment problems.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pervasive a: Square reviewers report nonresponsive or punitive leadership, selective enforcement, cronyism in hiring/athletics, mishandled hearings/alternative‑school placements, scheduling and credit‑transfer errors, food service/meal‑shaming incidents, and facility/crowding mismanagement (examples: $500 wrongful fines, alternative‑school overuse, administrators protecting wealthy students, fire/emergency protocol failures, overcrowded trailers), while circle reviews lack these recurrent governance and operational failure patterns.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater internal var: Many square reviews contain sharp contradictions—strong STEM/math departments, award‑winning programs, or caring teachers alongside widespread reports of grade inflation, teachers not teaching (movies/games), post‑test instructional gaps, and alleged teacher cheating to inflate scores—producing high variance in classroom quality and student outcomes that circle reviews do not display at the same scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent: Circle reviews more often emphasize a small, safe atmosphere, accessible/caring teachers and counselors, proactive parent communication and community events, and leadership turnarounds that improved discipline (examples: 'small school,' 'teachers engage with students,' 'new principal brought back integrity,' free community concerts), features that are comparatively less prominent or far more conflicted in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket captures concrete reports about physical safety and the built environment (e.g., 'the school smells like pot all the time,' 'there's fights everyday,' 'bomb threats, gun threats, Fights,' 'walking through the hallways, all you can smell is mold,' 'Terrible insect problems,' overcrowding and chaotic hallways). It groups items describing on-campus violence, drug/vaping/gang activity, health hazards (mold, pests, food hygiene), theft, and overcrowding/campus supervision problems that square reviewers describe but circle reviewers generally do not.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially gr: This bucket groups concrete program- and outcome-level claims about non-academic opportunities and recognition (e.g., 'many clubs and activities,' 'state championships,' 'music/theater department is absolutely outstanding,' 'hands on career and technology classes,' 'dual enrollment pathways, Wildcat University, workforce certifications'). It covers the presence, variety, competitive success, and community/alumni ties for athletics, music/theater, CTE/vo-tech offerings and boosters that square reviews enumerate but circle reviews typically omit.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced ac: This bucket captures statements about course availability, rigor, and instructional substance: polarized coursework where 'AP/IB/honors teachers are very hard working' but 'regular/on‑level teachers give up,' complaints of missing AP/science courses and curricular misalignment ('curriculum is horrible', 'textbooks are outdated', 'labs underfunded'), and contested claims about rising versus falling test scores and college readiness. It groups evidence about academic offerings, rigor, materials, and college-prep/dual-credit structure—distinct from extracurricular breadth or administrative behavior.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups descriptions of how leadership and policy shape fairness and operations (e.g., 'prevalent sexism and racism amongst the staff,' 'kids in sports are overlooked,' 'preference is given to children of those families,' 'spend budget on landscaping instead of books,' 'they refuse to answer emails,' calls to replace principals). It covers unequal enforcement, selective discipline, nepotism/protected athletes, budget priorities, leadership instability or targeted criticism, and systemic poor responsiveness that square reviewers often attribute to administrators.
candidate_defs.square entries document more special-edu: This bucket includes reports about IEPs, special‑education practice, counseling/scheduling errors, and targeted interventions (examples: 'If you have special needs children do NOT come here,' 'they gave my child an IEP... all this did was enable my child to slack off,' 'councillor forgot to mention course was not UC approved,' and also 'teachers worked tirelessly for my child with learning disabilities'). It groups evidence about the availability, effectiveness, contestation, and concrete consequences of special-needs accommodations and counseling/advising services described in square reviews but absent or less-detailed in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more frequent: This bucket covers concrete safety and climate failures described in reviews: recurring physical fights, bomb/gun threats, daily violent incidents, drug use, sexualized coercion, suicides/attempts, pervasive bullying and body‑shaming, and the resulting unsafe after‑school dynamics (e.g., ‘fights are an everyday routine,’ ‘had very many bomb and gun threats,’ ‘drug use galore’). It also includes reviewers who say the school failed to protect students or address mental‑health crises; these are operationalized as real safety incidents and unmitigated peer harm rather than tone or sentiment.
candidate_defs.square entries document substantially ri: This bucket groups explicit programmatic and outcome evidence: named SAS/AP/IB programs, dual‑enrollment and college‑credit totals, National Merit / scholarship counts, concrete test‑prep gains and acceptance to elite colleges (examples: ‘two students granted early admittance to Columbia and Stanford,’ ‘graduating with 12 hrs of college credit,’ ‘over 20 APs offered’). It captures program breadth, credentialing, and measurable student‑achievement claims that circle reviews largely lack.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more organized,: This bucket captures programmatic extracurricular evidence and funding choices: strong marching bands, international music travel, state championships, booster fundraising for turf/stadiums, and explicit statements that athletics or band receive prioritized resources (e.g., ‘raised a million for turf,’ ‘one of the best marching bands in the state,’ ‘band kids get favored’). It also covers critiques that boosters or capital spending favor athletics/arts over academics when reviewers note contested allocation decisions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more tangible oper: This bucket groups physical‑space and logistics problems that affect instruction: overcrowded classes and lunchrooms, short class periods and lost instructional time, mold/asbestos/rodent/HVAC failures, bus and scheduling breakdowns, administrative paperwork errors that blocked graduation, and chaotic orientation/ID lines (examples: ‘way overpopulated,’ ‘mold and asbestos,’ ‘two hour and a half in a line to get the ID,’ ‘bussing system dangerous and unreliable’). These are concrete infrastructure and operational failures rather than staff attitude or curricular content.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger and more: This bucket covers variability and extremes in personnel and governance: named teachers/counselors praised for individualized support and outreach, alongside repeated reports of unprofessional administrators, favoritism (athlete/band nepotism), racial bias, ADA/special‑education noncompliance, poor parent communication, and record‑keeping errors that harmed students (examples: ‘guidance counselors are extremely helpful’ vs ‘they don't comply with ADA rights,’ ‘advancement based on last name,’ ‘file destroyed’). It focuses on concrete staff/board/policy behaviors and compliance that shape student access and equity.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and higher: This bucket captures reviews that list program breadth and prestige (IB/AP/honors, dual‑enrollment/transcripted college courses, strong marching band, CTE/auto/arts academies) and concrete outcomes (high GPAs, scholarship totals, Ivy/UC/college matriculation). Example evidence: Square mentions IB/AP, partnerships with Miami or RIT, students graduating summa cum laude and receiving large scholarship totals, and nationally ranked speech/debate or band—features Circle reviews do not enumerate.
candidate_defs.square entries report more bullying, rac: This bucket groups accounts of pervasive misconduct (bullying, racial slurs, homophobic harassment, fights, vaping/drugs, bomb threats) together with claims that staff/police/administration ignore or ineffectively respond. Example evidence: Square reviews describe racial slurs left in bleachers, weekly fights and daily smell of marijuana, students forced to leave or be homeschooled, and administrators who 'brush off' bullying—contrasting with Circle’s reviews that emphasize respectful students or active anti‑bullying priority.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: This bucket covers communication breakdowns, chaotic or politicized administration, hiring/retention problems, tenure‑complacency or favoritism, and abrupt policy changes that disrupt students (e.g., IB eligibility reversals). Example evidence: Square reviewers cite counselors/principals who don't return calls, 'bureaucracy is a nightmare,' many principals/teachers quitting, and accusations that admins favor athletes or affluent students—issues Circle rarely raises.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical cap: This bucket groups concrete infrastructure and scheduling problems that affect daily experience: extreme enrollment, 25–50+ students per room, disgusting/locked bathrooms, mold infestations, vermin, heavy drop‑off traffic and poor lunch/schedule logistics. Example evidence: Square mentions >2,500–3,000 enrollments, bathrooms 'disgusting,' mold forcing faculty loss, and single‑road drop‑off causing heavy traffic—complaints not present in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete, i: This bucket captures reviews that report explicit supportive services for struggling learners and special‑needs inclusion—detailed IEP/504 assistance, dedicated special‑ed staff, social workers, and in‑school interventions—even where other operational problems exist. Example evidence: Square reviewers note strong special‑needs inclusion and helpful IEP directors, social workers and interventions that helped students graduate, whereas Circle reviews generally omit such individualized support descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, broade: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete programmatic breadth and demonstrable college success (AP/IB/Dual-Credit, named magnet tracks, CTE/university partnerships, AVID/PACE/Running Start) and cite admissions/scholarships or national awards (e.g., AP/IB participation, UT-Austin/USC admits, Washington State Achievement Awards). Items here focus on the availability and success of formal advanced‑course pathways and programmatic college-prep supports that Circle reviews do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports of bullying, gang violence, pervasive drug dealing/use, assaults, frequent fights/lockdowns and school searches—often coupled with reviewer claims that administrators ignore, mishandle, or enact punitive/arbitrary discipline (e.g., ignored racist incidents, drug problems 'refused to deal with', ISS/harassment for minor dress-code issues, calling police on students). Circle reviews lack these sustained accounts of safety crises and official nonresponse.
candidate_defs.square entries describe worse and more v: This bucket groups complaints and examples about staffing and leadership: quantified high turnover and out‑of‑state recruiting, large gaps between excellent and ineffective teachers, protected low‑performing staff, low morale/absenteeism (including Covid-era complaints), poor or hostile guidance offices, and contested or chaotic principals/superintendents—features Circle reviews do not reliably show.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic favo: This bucket covers allegations that access and opportunity are unequally distributed—examples include nepotism and 'who you know' favoritism, preferential treatment for athletes/wealthy families, explicit racial bias or anti‑LGBTQ hostility from staff or peers, exclusion of students with disabilities, and fee structures that disadvantage low‑income families—patterns absent or contradicted in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater facility-,: This bucket contains concrete infrastructure and operational problems: mold/asbestos/poor HVAC, overflowing/crowded halls and modular classrooms, slow wifi/broken tech, complaints about misallocated discretionary spending (TVs/iPads vs. textbooks), pay‑to‑play fees, cafeteria/transport hazards, locked restrooms and rigid visitor/security practices—practical resource and campus logistics issues not described in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report a far worse studen: This bucket captures pervasive accounts of bullying, frequent physical fights, rampant substance use, self‑harm, gendered safety risks, and weak or inconsistent discipline—evidence includes claims like 'Bullying is not dealt with,' 'Drug use and drinking are rampant,' 'There were plenty of fights...', 'Girls cutting wrists,' and reports that victims are punished while bullies go unpunished; Circle reviews lack these sustained safety/crisis descriptions and instead report fewer or isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, stronge: This groups reports of extensive AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/CTE offerings, concrete college‑credit outcomes and elite matriculations, and vocational pathways—examples: 'full IB diploma,' 'lots of AP classes... my AP scores allowed me to start college as a sophomore,' 'graduate with an Associate Degree in cyber technology,' and 'placements were Harvard, MIT, Stanford'; Circle reviews tend to describe limited advanced/AP offerings and weaker college‑prep evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer extracurric: Included evidence documents award‑winning band/choir, many sports and clubs, strong traditions, large parental donations, and programs like Project Rise—e.g., 'state award winning choir, band & orchestra,' 'The Pride of Branson Bands,' 'many of the features of a private school due to... parent donations,' and 'free after school program called Project Rise'; Circle reviews emphasize fewer social/athletic opportunities and less school spirit.
candidate_defs.square entries report more physical infr: This bucket covers facility condition, capacity and logistics complaints such as overcrowded halls and classes, run‑down or unsanitary buildings, cafeteria/meal service failures, bus/schedule errors, and mixed construction/maintenance issues—examples include 'It is very overcrowded... hallways are always packed,' 'building is falling apart... no AC... lead pipes,' and 'third lunch students never have time to make it through the line'; Circle contains far fewer of these facility/capacity failures and often notes newer/cleaner buildings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This groups allegations about inequitable discipline tied to influential families or athletes, coach/staff favoritism, unresponsive or punitive administrators, hiring/turnover and recruitment problems, and even fiscal or personnel scandals—examples: 'kids with prominent families run rampant... give these kids a "pass",' 'I had to contact the superintendent,' 'administration are incompetent... drive away dedicated staff,' and 'business manager resigned and has been indicted'; Circle reviews rarely allege this scope of governance/favoritism or district‑level misconduct.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups raw terms where square reviews report explicit AP/IB/honors/dual‑enrollment offerings, specialty academies or CTE tracks, tutoring/retest policies, and named college matriculations or scholarship outcomes (e.g., “IB program… AP/Dual Enrollment… national merit finalists… full scholarship to Georgetown,” “engineering program with certifications,” “many students leave with college credits”), while circle reviews lack comparable concrete advanced‑program breadth or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This cluster captures accounts of gangs, regular fights/assaults, sexual‑assault allegations, routine drug/alcohol use, metal detectors, stabbings, bomb threats, EMS calls, and claims that staff/police provide inadequate protection (e.g., “overwhelmed by overcrowding, gangs, drugs… my child has been attacked,” “students arrested/EMS dispatched,” “metal detectors, thuggy kids”), contrasted with circle reviews that do not document this level of physical‑safety crisis.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater administ: This bucket gathers evidence of registrar/enrollment/scheduling failures, counselor overload, central‑office mismanagement, district financial scandals or leadership turnover, opaque policies, nepotism, and slow/absent responses to parent complaints (e.g., “money went missing… retire‑rehire scandals,” “process to enroll has been trying… Mrs. Lawson the registrar,” “principals won’t call you back,” “state supervised intervention needed”), whereas circle reviews typically lack these district‑level governance or chronic operational scandal claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more direct teache: This bucket groups teacher‑centered evidence—yelling, public beratement, unlawful phone searches, teacher bullying or snide parent communication, tenure‑protected poor teachers, inconsistent strictness, and also many accounts of highly committed individual mentors (e.g., “Algebra teacher yelled ‘shut up’… vice principal did nothing,” “teachers went above and beyond… Mr. McAdams”), capturing a pattern of polarized, teacher‑driven classroom experiences that circle reviews do not describe as extensively.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced so: This bucket contains raw terms alleging that money, athlete status, race or being a nonlocal drive who gets opportunities and who is punished (e.g., “if you don’t have money… be prepared to be left out,” “staff favor wealthy/white students,” “students rude to outsiders… don’t come here unless born here,” “racial profiling… pride flag torn down”), while circle reviews either describe more inclusive countywide/community orientation or frame exclusion as limited favoritism without the same breadth of systemic socioeconomic/racial exclusion claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures descriptions of on-campus safety problems and their direct impacts—fights almost weekly, vaping/drug use, guns and lockdowns, locker thefts, gang activity, police presence, and students visibly anxious or arming themselves—often paired with accounts that staff sometimes fail to control these behaviors (e.g., “I have smelled pot in the halls,” “been on lockdown twice…kid brought guns,” “a student wore a kevlar suit because they were so anxious”). These items are about the raw incidence and severity of student misconduct and its effect on campus climate, not about administrative policy or facilities alone.
candidate_defs.square entries describe worse staff and: This bucket groups concrete operational and governance problems: unresponsive or disorganized front offices/registrars, lost records, mis‑distributed devices, punitive attendance/tardy rules and arbitrary suspensions, inconsistent enforcement, secrecy/nepotism, and budgetary choices that harm programs (e.g., “No one calls back… schedules arrive wrong… ISS for being late five times,” “district is managed poorly…spent on the wrong priorities”). These items focus on how the school/district is run, including communication, logistics, discipline policy design/enforcement, and fiscal governance.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: This bucket covers concrete academic-program strength and outcomes: availability and success of IB/AP/STEM academies, internship pipelines, dual enrollment, high ACT scores, National Merit and scholarship counts, and named college matriculations (examples: “International Cambridge/IB program,” “STEM Academy…top scores,” “30 on ACT…full scholarships”), reflecting substantive curriculum offerings and tracked postsecondary results rather than subjective praise.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and high: This bucket captures program breadth and quality in non‑academic domains—robust marching band, choir, drama, numerous clubs, vocational teams, award-winning arts, and also patterns of athletic privilege/grade-inflation or recruitment (e.g., “THE best music program…band instructors are top notch,” “If you aren’t rich or good at sports you’re in trouble,” “recruit girls from 8th grade”), emphasizing what activities exist, their quality, and how they shape student experience.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic ineq: This bucket groups descriptions of unequal or harmful policies/practices: forced or manipulative special-ed placements, IEP/Title IX failures requiring outside advocates, racially segregating tracking, lack of accommodations for learning disabilities, and socioeconomic elitism or exclusion (examples: “Average students forced into special ed to keep scores down,” “didn’t follow our daughter’s IEP…had to get an advocate,” “segregated classes…Jim Crow like system,” “low income family very little assistance”). These items concern equitable access, legal/educational supports, and discriminatory or excluding institutional practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe recurrent physical safety problems and student misconduct (fights, visible blood, sexualized behavior on campus, bomb threats, frequent vaping/smoking, gang/drug activity) and school inaction on those incidents; examples include “Alot Of Fights,” “students have sex on school campus,” “bomb threats every other week,” and “You can’t go to the restroom with out seeing 3 kids smoking.” Circle entries rarely describe such pervasive safety failures and typically report much milder or isolated behavioral concerns.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This bucket covers leadership and staff practices (rude or absent administrators, poor communication, cover‑ups, refusal to act, union‑protected unaccountability), misaligned priorities (funding athletics over academics), and harsh/policy‑driven discipline (overuse of suspensions, rigid tardy/attendance penalties); supporting evidence includes “The administration listens but does not act,” “covered up the misconduct,” “football players get special privileges,” and “sent to ISS and miss the entire class period.” Circle reviews lack systemic claims of such entrenched administrative failure and punitive governance.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and strong: This bucket groups reviews that cite concrete program breadth and outcomes (many AP/IB offerings, AICE, dual enrollment, robotics, strong performing arts, Career Technical Center programs, dozens of clubs, high scholarship/graduation/college admission claims); examples include “numerous (about 100) different student clubs,” “IB/AP scores exceed international average,” “Career Technical Center offers culinary arts, welding…,” and “gives out millions of dollars of scholarships each year.” These items reflect programmatic strength and measurable post‑secondary results distinct from staff behavior or facilities comments.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extreme facil: This bucket captures physical‑plant and capacity evidence—overcrowded hallways and classes, heat/AC failures, filthy bathrooms/food hygiene violations, construction impacts, or large bond‑funded renovations/new state‑of‑the‑art buildings and technology for learning; examples include “The school is overcrowded,” “Made students go to school when it was 112 degrees,” “huge roaches…51 health violations,” and conversely “the new high school…top notch athletic fields.” Circle reviews generally do not document these pronounced facility/capacity extremes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic ineq: This bucket covers allegations that specific student groups are marginalized—racial slurs and exclusion, homophobia, minority students getting less attention, newcomer/employee‑family exclusion, religious proselytizing, and legal failures on IEP/504 accommodations; illustrative claims include “Minority students are not given the same attention,” “racial comments are rampant in the hallways,” “teachers refuse to follow my IEP,” and “they don't welcome the employee's families and children.” These equity and inclusion failures are conceptually distinct from general administrative dysfunction or safety incidents described above.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of fights, drug use, vaping, sexual activity, hospitalizations, suicides, teen‑pregnancy, rampant bullying and students assaulting peers — plus claims that the school ignores or fails to investigate these incidents (e.g., “fights on a daily basis…drugs openly being sold,” “multiple kids were beaten up…hospitalized,” “2 suicides in past couple of years,” and parents/teachers saying leadership ‘ignored’ or ‘did nothing’). Items belong here when reviews describe concrete safety/health incidents and either ineffective or only reactive responses to them.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe broader and more: This bucket groups reports of concrete advanced offerings and outcomes (many AP/IB/dual‑enrollment classes, AP scores, SAT/ACT metrics, Ivy/college placements, college credits) together with reviewer evidence that instruction and college‑readiness are inconsistent across tracks (e.g., “they teach over 30 AP classes,” “earned a 4/5 on the AP exam,” but also “I got A’s without learning how to study…was unprepared in university” and “honors classes were 2 years behind”). Use this bucket when reviews document formal advanced programs, quantifiable outcomes, or explicit mismatches between program rigor and whole‑school academic preparation.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more administrat: This bucket covers complaints about leadership unresponsiveness or authoritarianism, nepotism/favoritism, rude front‑office staff, broken recordkeeping/transcript access, and managerial instability (examples: “principal wouldn’t respond…took four months for a reply,” “nepotism reigns supreme,” “staff refused transcripts,” and “administration failed to take responsibility”). Include reviews that focus on whether school leaders/office staff reliably communicate, enforce rules fairly, keep accurate records, or demonstrate transparent accountability.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pronounced co: This bucket groups evidence of facility extremes: new auditoriums/biotech labs/renovations and air conditioning on one hand, and mold, roaches, overflowing sewers, filthy bathrooms, missing desks, and severe overcrowding on the other (e.g., “new auditorium…state‑of‑the‑art lab” vs. “roaches everywhere…bathrooms unsanitary…overcrowding is horrible”). Use it when reviews describe building condition, health hazards, space constraints, or recent capital projects (including tensions between renovation and ongoing maintenance deficits).
candidate_defs.Square entries showcase wider and higher: This bucket captures extensive lists of clubs, career academies, championship athletics, elite music/performing‑arts facilities, robotics and journalism accolades, plus pay‑to‑participate costs and complaints that athletes are favored (examples: “won state championships…world champion qualifier robotics…performing arts center like Juilliard,” and “paid $300 for activities…athletes get preferential treatment”). Assign reviews here when they emphasize breadth/depth of co‑curricular programs, competitive success, fees, or claims that extracurriculars drive priorities or favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse student safe: This bucket captures reports of a hostile or unsafe student climate in square reviews—frequent bullying, fights, drug/alcohol availability, sexualized behavior and even allegations of mishandled sexual assaults—plus claims that staff/security do not supervise or respond (e.g., “They do nothing about the bullying…4 year old…black eye,” “Drugs are a HUGE problem,” “watched kids pass small bottles…dean drove right past,” and “S/A cases? Yeah they don’t do ANYTHING about that”). These items contrast with Circle reviews, which generally lack persistent safety crises and instead describe more orderly or supported student environments.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive A: This bucket groups concrete statements about advanced/rigorous academic offerings and measurable outcomes that appear more often in square entries—AP/IB breadth, dual‑enrollment and alumni college placement (e.g., “huge list of AP classes,” “one of the only schools in WA to offer the Cambridge International program,” “19/29…have gone on to college,” and alumni at MIT/Stanford). Circle reviews rarely list this programmatic breadth or specific outcome data and instead emphasize general college‑prep or counseling.
candidate_defs.square entries report more uneven and po: This bucket covers classroom‑level instructional failures that square reviewers describe more often: inconsistent/poor teacher competence, favoritism, unfair grading and assessment, excessive homework, reliance on substitutes/self‑teaching, and overcrowded classes limiting individual attention (examples: “many of the teachers fall short…do the minimum,” “quizzing us over things we hadn't gone over,” “teachers expect kids to teach themselves,” and “teachers have a lot of kids…can't pay attention to all of them”). Circle reviews rarely contain these same concrete classroom‑practice complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups organizational and adult‑system problems reported more in square: inconsistent or biased discipline, transcript/scheduling mistakes, long term substitute/coverage issues, poor guidance/IEP management or special‑education failures, frequent administrative turnover and even corruption claims (e.g., “constantly messing up students transcripts,” “guidance counselors have no idea what they are doing,” “IEP is a joke,” “3rd principal in 7 years,” and “forced into retirement by bribery”). Circle reviews contain far fewer such operational or governance complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, named: This bucket includes concrete, named co‑curricular strengths and community engagement that square reviewers more often enumerate—award‑winning band/choir, orchestras, NJROTC, many sports and clubs, parent PTAs and fundraising (e.g., “full orchestra, outstanding Arts Department,” “BEST BAND I’VE EVER HEARD,” “Parents volunteer through PTSA, Magnet Foundation”), as well as statements that athletics are prioritized or require payment (e.g., pay‑to‑play or funding skewed to football). Circle reviews rarely list many named programs or the same level of parental/volunteer infrastructure.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more n: This bucket captures program-level academic strength: square reviews repeatedly name IB/AP/magnet/AVID/CTE tracks, dual‑enrollment and explicit college matriculation (e.g., ‘‘IB Diploma Programme,’’ ‘‘take many APs,’’ ‘‘one son is now a chemical engineer,’’ multiple Ivy/MIT/Johns Hopkins admits), while circle reviews lack comparable advanced‑program lists or concrete post‑secondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews contain frequent, concrete safety incidents and failed responses (fights every day, drug availability, knife/assault episodes, bomb threat/lockdown, resource officers not following up), plus accounts of ignored bullying and victim‑blaming; circle entries do not present this level or frequency of safety incidents or the same mishandled follow‑up.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: Square reviewers repeatedly cite leadership instability, bureaucratic miscoordination, lost records, punitive or inconsistent discipline, monetization/fee barriers, wealthy‑parent influence and use of police in parent disputes (e.g., ‘‘7 principals over 4 years,’’ ‘‘parents run the school,’’ ‘‘they lost her transcripts’’), whereas circle reviews rarely describe this breadth of governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer, broader, a: Square reviews enumerate extensive co‑curricular programs and accomplishments (JNROTC, exceptional band/marching history, state/national championships in sports/one‑acts, thriving theater/robotics programs, many clubs and strong school spirit), while circle reviews generally do not list comparable extracurricular breadth or documented competitive achievements.

candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures critiques of school/district leadership in square reviews—accusations of nepotism/athlete favoritism, cover‑ups or failure to notify parents, refusal to return calls, militarized security/search practices, and demands for principal removal (e.g., 'principal needs to be removed', 'superintendents refuse to return voice messages', 'added steel gates and K9 searches'), whereas circle reviews rarely describe such institutional corruption or authoritarian tactics and more often describe accountable, communicative leaders.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict more consistent, c: This bucket contains reviews where circle schools are characterized by dependable staff and constructive adult support—approachable teachers, stable committed administration, strong counselor/teacher responsiveness, and sustained alum/parent pride (e.g., 'teachers have been above awesome', 'commitment of the administration is phenomenal', 'I completely miss it'), while square reviews more often document uneven teacher quality, burnout, or erratic leadership.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, san: This bucket groups concrete physical/operational complaints concentrated in square reviews—unsanitary conditions and pests, leaking or aging buildings, overcrowded halls and large class sizes, short lunch times, parking and schedule/block issues, and contested maintenance priorities (e.g., 'roaches', 'leaks everywhere', '20 minutes for lunch', 'overpopulated/too many students'), while circle reviews generally do not report the same level of facility neglect or system‑wide logistical strain.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more routine s: This bucket groups reports of fights, drug use, lockdowns, hate‑speech/Title IX incidents, and claims that school security/staff failed to protect victims (examples: “fights every day,” “almost everyone does drugs,” monthly K‑9 searches, “school goes on lockdown very frequently,” and parents hiring attorneys after unresolved sexual-harassment complaints). It captures both the prevalence of unsafe incidents and repeated reviewer claims that administration/security responses were inadequate or punitive, a pattern repeatedly present in square but absent or minimal in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger advance: This bucket groups concrete descriptions of AP/IB/dual-enrollment programs, high district/state scores and college-credit claims (examples: AP/Dual Enrollment partnerships, “highest scores in the city,” engineering/IB academies), together with square reviewers’ concurrent reports of tracking, honors vs. standard-class disparity, online credit recovery use, and grade‑inflation (“A+ online courses,” “standard classes nearly impossible to fail,” pronounced honors/AP vs. weak regular classes). It captures that square reviews describe both stronger formal academic offerings and program-integrity/ equity problems in the same schools — a distinction not present in circle.
