candidate_defs.square entries report more problems with: This bucket covers unprofessional staff behavior, failure to discipline or hold teachers accountable, administrative favoritism or bias (including toward athletes/wealthy families), confidentiality breaches, punitive micromanagement, and special‑education/IEP neglect (examples: “Teachers will cover for each other,” “principal is extremely biased,” “do not hire minorities,” “refused to provide IEP services,” and threats of punitive consequences like juvenile‑hall warnings). It isolates interpersonal, ethical, and governance failures distinct from safety incidents or program offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This bucket groups overcrowding, poor building maintenance/cleanliness, broken bathrooms/AC, parking and transit burdens, outdated or missing classroom technology, and concrete operational failures (examples: “very overcrowded…almost to the point of danger,” “bathrooms are horrible,” “no computers,” “parking—insanely hard,” and lost paperwork/registration errors). These are physical- and operations-level deficits that reviewers link to safety and instructional strain, and which appear far more often in square than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: This bucket groups robust, named extracurricular successes, Fine Arts and music praise, booster/parent engagement, visible school pride, and district/community partnerships (examples: championship marching band, outstanding choir/choir directors, strong booster support, “lots of clubs,” and community college dual‑enrollment links). It captures both positive program breadth/achievement and the visible community backing that square reviewers frequently cite — a contrast to circle’s lack of comparable extracurricular/community program evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student-: This bucket groups items where square reviews describe frequent physical fights, bullying, gangs/drugs, sexual misconduct, suicides, police/SRO involvement, weapons/drug sweeps, and allegations of administrative cover‑ups or non‑reporting (e.g., “fights almost every day,” “students bringing guns… hush hush,” “highest suicide rate… assemblies held,” “bomb squad search twice”), while circle reviews lack comparable reports and often emphasize relative safety and care. Membership means the review documents concrete student-safety incidents, substance or violence problems, repeated formal security responses, or systemic failure to remediate them—features far more prevalent in square than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe richer and more: This bucket captures square reviews that enumerate AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, vocational certifications, specialized magnet/magnet-vs-resident tracks, award‑winning extracurriculars (band, NJROTC, robotics, engineering academies), and elite college placements (e.g., ‘AP/IB programs… one graduated from Harvard… PTECH, CNA/EMT, college credit’), whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth or measurable elite matriculation. To belong here, a review must provide concrete program names, pathways, or outcome metrics (AP/IB/college credits, certifications, National Merit, scholarship/college placements) indicating substantive curricular or extracurricular opportunity differences.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups evidence of administrative problems in square reviews—unresponsiveness, lost transcripts, refusing records, nepotism, concealment, arbitrary/punitive discipline, policy prioritizing appearance over safety, and top‑down unilateral decisions (e.g., “I had sent Johansen multiple letters… he doesn’t reply,” “refused to release nurse records,” “principal…throw the children out,” “nepotism in distribution of student opportunities”)—claims that circle reviews do not make or make far less often. Membership means the reviewer points to organizational failures, deliberate opacity, biased or punitive leadership actions, or systemic coordination breakdowns at the school/district level.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete, de: This bucket holds square reviews that discuss physical plant and operations in detail—renovations, poor sanitation, overcrowding/capacity metrics, lunch schedules and menu logistics, parking, swimming‑pool absence, bus/transportation gaps, security hardware or hotlines, and capital spending (e.g., “new renovations… no swimming pool,” “overcrowded cafeteria hundreds over legal limit,” “computers/laptop program is a major plus,” “$12million toward athletic facility”). Circle reviews rarely discuss facilities or operational logistics at this level of specificity. A member review thus cites tangible infrastructure, capacity, scheduling/food service, transportation, or security resources/problems.
candidate_defs.square entries contain far more teacher‑: This bucket groups square reviews that give concrete classroom and support‑staff evidence—teacher availability after school, named influential teachers, AIS/remediation classes, detailed special‑education/504/IEP battles or successes, counselor accessibility or ineffectiveness, and high variability or turnover in teacher quality (e.g., “they will stay after with you,” “AIS classes…,” “I fought with the district on getting him his 504 plan,” “half the teachers act like they’re teaching college and the other half… day care”). Circle reviews seldom provide this level of teacher/practice‑level detail and instead give more general statements; membership requires explicit claims about teacher behaviors, counseling/sped supports, remediation programs, or variability/turnover in instructional staff.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, formal: These reviews describe concrete program infrastructure (IB/AICE/AP, multiple academies, dual-enrollment, career centers, PLTW/biomed tracks) and quantifiable outcomes (scholarship totals, Ivy/elite admits, AA degrees) that square reviewers repeatedly cite — e.g., “25 AP/Dual Credit Classes offered,” “the only school in Polk county with 5 academies,” and “This year’s senior class has already received over $1.7 million in scholarships!” — while circle reviews lack comparable concrete pathway, dual-credit, or consistent college-outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: Square reviewers repeatedly allege pervasive conduct and safety breakdowns plus weak enforcement — e.g., “Bullying is a huge problem… faculty and staff fail to address it,” “drugs are everywhere… teachers either have blinders on,” and “fights every day between classes” — whereas circle reviews emphasize student kindness, cohesion, or only isolated minor cattiness and disciplinary fixes.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Many square reviews describe leadership turnover, nepotism, cover-ups, inconsistent policies, and poor incident response — e.g., “administration is so cluttered…most incompetent staff,” “nepotism is now the new norm,” and “Admin here hides all problems and refuses to take action” — while circle reviews more often describe caring, responsive staff and constructive administrative direction.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced ph: Square reviewers provide concrete facility/operational complaints (mold, leaking ceilings, no soap/toilet paper, broken escalators), capacity and scheduling problems (“way over crowded…3000 students,” conflicting AP schedules), unsafe bus stops and unreliable wifi, and shortages of core instructional materials, whereas circle reviews rarely cite such chronic physical or district-logistics failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: Circle reviewers frequently highlight small-school/community warmth, caring teachers and staff responsiveness, individualized counseling and supports, and consistent college-prep help — e.g., “Very student focused…Great relationship between school and community,” “Very good support for ADHD, very inclusive,” and “teachers gave me the tools...to complete twelve AP classes” — a pattern of cohesive, supportive school-community practice less emphasized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report administrative unr: This bucket captures schools where reviewers allege leadership fails to respond or be held accountable, prompting organized parent complaints and calls for leadership change (e.g., 'ADMINISTRATION is horrible. Big pay and no action' and parents 'in an up`roar' who 'Sent an email to the superintendent...He never returned my email or call'). It groups evidence about leadership inaction together with the resulting public/parent mobilization aimed at administration.
candidate_defs.square entries describe inconsistent dis: This bucket groups reviews that document uneven application of rules and punishments across students and staff (e.g., 'Inconsistent with which rules and guidelines are followed depending on the student and staff member' and examples of coaches/teachers favoring some students). It specifically covers variability and unpredictability in discipline and rule enforcement inside the school.
candidate_defs.square entries report staff favoritism a: This bucket covers allegations that staff show favoritism that affects student safety and case outcomes, including claims that staff 'let people assault children and suspend the victim' or 'plays favorites' that influence who is protected or punished. It focuses on favoritism that directly undermines student safety or leads to mishandling of incidents rather than general procedural inconsistency.
candidate_defs.square entries report classroom overcrow: This bucket groups concrete facility/staffing issues where reviewers cite packed classrooms and strained staffing (e.g., '1 teacher to 30 students... at some schools it is 1 teacher to 20 students... these over populated schools'). It is about tangible capacity problems—class size and staffing levels—affecting instruction and supervision.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe organized events: This bucket captures reviews that emphasize constructive programming and staff support—organized events, active clubs, and positive endorsements from families and students—rather than the administrative complaints found in square entries (circle reviews note supportive staff and organized events with no evidence of administrative inaction). It groups positive, programmatic, and community-support evidence distinguishing circle schools.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially st: This bucket captures reviews that report concrete curricular depth and credentialed pathways at square schools — e.g., IB programs, large AP/IB offerings, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit partnerships, specialized academies (business, engineering, medical), career/CTE certifications, and documented college acceptances/AP score gains — claims that are absent or far less detailed in circle reviews (examples: 'has excelled to become an IB school', 'early college program…associates degree WHILE IN HIGH SCHOOL', 'partnership with Miami University', 'lots of AP and Honors courses', '46 college credit hours').
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize athletics, spor: This bucket groups items where square reviews describe a school identity and spending skewed to athletics — upgraded bleachers/football stadiums, top‑notch sports complexes, coach praise coupled with accusations that funds were diverted from academics/health (examples: 'spent millions to build a football stadium…instead of getting air conditioning', 'the emphasis here seems to revolve around football and cheerleading', 'our Football team is great and they just upgraded our Bleachers'), a pattern much more prominent than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers reports of concrete safety harms and weak enforcement at square schools: recurring fights and assaults, gang issues, drug incidents and random testing, bullying (including racialized harassment) with inadequate administrative follow‑up, and extreme warnings about suicidal risk (examples: 'tried to stab staff with a pencil', 'Gummy Bears with a substance that sent a few kids to the hospital', 'lots of racial discord…staff does nothing', 'We get threats every single week'), claims that are far less frequent or severe in the circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document more systemic st: This bucket groups human‑resource and governance failures described in square reviews: teachers 'lazy' or 'underqualified', substitutes reporting rude front‑office staff, principals criticized or praised for turnover effects, union strikes, guidance counselor instability, and chronic unresponsiveness/communication breakdowns (examples: 'teachers with 190 students', 'nepotism galore', 'guidance counselor has been ignoring us for months', 'The principals and administration all continue to receive raises…'), a cluster distinct from student safety incidents and from programmatic strengths.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe smaller, more pe: This bucket captures the opposite direction: circle reviews repeatedly emphasize small‑school scale, close teacher mentorship, individualized attention, safe/accepting environments, and steady instructional support (examples: 'Because of the small school population, there is opportunity for one‑on‑one attention', 'teachers for the most part were approachable and seemed to care', 'Surrounded by nature…quiet Manoa Valley', 'has always felt safe and accepted'), features that contrast with many of the scale, safety, and staffing problems described in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive a: These reviews repeatedly cite concrete, formal programs in square schools (AP/IB/honors expansion, dual‑enrollment, award‑winning music/band/arts, language offerings, vocational shops, academies like CCT or Media & Entertainment) and measurable outcomes (college acceptances, scholarships, alumni success), whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth or college-prep pathways. Examples: square mentions IB, growing AP/Honors tracks, 1:1 tech initiative, award‑winning band and dual‑enrollment; circle offers few or no equivalent program details.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many square reviews document recurring violent incidents, drug and gang presence, weapons or searches, frequent fights, teen‑pregnancy/drug issues and describe staff/administration as slow, punitive, or dismissive in addressing them; circle reviews contain far fewer or only isolated safety incidents. Illustrative evidence: square cites weekly fights, K9 searches, students hospitalized after attacks, frequent vape/drug searches, and statements that bullying/violence is swept under the rug.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater inconsiste: Square reviewers repeatedly document unstable staffing, high teacher turnover or many weak teachers, scheduling/transcript/counseling errors, overloaded counselors, and both failures and occasional strong special‑education cases—while circle reviews more often describe steady, responsive teachers. Representative examples: square notes teacher shortages and substitutes, counselors 'never in school' or misadvising (outdated UC approval), mis‑coded transcripts, and special‑education services that are either awful or strictly teacher‑dependent.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize tangible facili: Square reviews frequently describe physical campus features and budgeting choices—new/upgraded schools, large athletic complexes and fundraising for sports, 1:1 tech programs—while also calling out overcrowding, poor sanitation, food safety, library closures, and pay‑to‑play or privatized lesson barriers; circle reviews rarely combine this level of facility detail with the same resource‑allocation critique. Examples include new athletic fields built while books are unfunded, multiple cafeterias and large campuses, but also hair/spoiled food complaints, closed libraries for testing, and charges for music/sports participation.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more pol: Square reviewers describe vivid peer hierarchies, wealth- and program-based exclusion (IB or athletes being favored), cliques, racial microaggressions or religious practice conflicts, and small‑town political ties that shape inclusion; circle reviews emphasize community warmth or isolated interpersonal problems rather than this concentrated, structural social stratification. Examples: square cites ‘stick to AP classes to avoid troublemakers,’ coaches’ children getting special treatment, prayer/policy disputes before games, and wealthy/student‑elite exclusionary practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more severe st: This bucket captures reviews that describe pervasive bullying, frequent fights, vandalism, on-campus drug use/overdoses, sexual harassment, theft, intruders, and other violent or chaotic student behavior (e.g., “bullying is completely out of control,” multiple freshman overdoses, weekly fights, sexual acts reported), problems that Circle reviews do not or only rarely raise.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger/more nume: This groups notes that Square reviews repeatedly list AP/IB/magnet/STEM/dual‑enrollment programs, National Merit and internship outcomes and scholarships (e.g., IB/AP, Science & Technology magnet, dual enrollment, National Merit counts), while simultaneously describing big disparities in teaching quality, missing AP offerings, course-gaps, and honors-vs-general track inequality that make access and preparation uneven — a combined program‑strength + instructional‑variability pattern not present in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This covers complaints about leadership churn, administrator unresponsiveness, lost transcripts/record errors, secretive school-board behavior, nepotism/corruption allegations, chaotic registration, strict/opaque residency enforcement and poor crisis response (examples: transcripts lost, principals who 'never respond,' ‘school board meets secretly’ and parents advised to transfer), themes far more common in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader extracu: This groups reviews that cite very large clubs/arts/music/theater offerings, unique programs (Cirque, aviation, state arts centers), strong booster/levy fundraising and families moving for the school, while also reporting athletics-dominant budgets, coach favoritism, and athletes getting preferential treatment (e.g., extensive music scholarships and top bands vs. claims that 'all they care about is athletics'), a pattern that contrasts with Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report weaker targeted su: This captures reports of denied 504/special‑education accommodations, mishandled mental‑health or medical needs, counseling failures or late reactive help, push‑out practices for pregnant/struggling students, and failures to transfer or review prior records (e.g., refusal to acknowledge anxiety disorder, 504 meeting neglect, being told to 'look somewhere else'), problems that appear more often in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, organi: These reviews report explicit, school-run academic pathways (IB/Full-IB, robust AP and dual-enrollment/CCP offerings, STEM/academy tracks, honors sequences) and tied outcomes (high AP/ACT/SAT performance, students entering college with credits, scholarship winners). Examples include named IB/UC/dual-credit programs, claims of large IB participation and students going to top colleges, whereas Circle reviews lack such concrete program lists, metrics, or college-credit evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe and fr: These entries document concrete safety problems inside buildings and on campus—fights, gangs, regular drug/alcohol use (bathroom smoking, very high prevalence estimates), weapon incidents, sexual harassment/Title IX allegations, teen suicides and vandalism—often accompanied by parents transferring children out; Circle entries do not describe this cluster of high-severity safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries detail more concrete faci: Reviews enumerate overcrowding and space failures (overcapacity halls, shared classrooms, students without lockers), aging/unclean or partially renovated facilities, inconsistent A/C, budget shortfalls that force parent fundraising, and inequitable resource choices (e.g., athletics prioritized over other programs); Circle reviews generally do not report these capacity/maintenance/resource-allocation failures or parental fundraising burdens.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater systemic s: These reviews describe missed scholarship/counseling deadlines, ignored large petitions, rude front-office staff, nepotism/overpaid administration, demotions and rapid teacher attrition, inconsistent discipline enforcement, and unresponsive communication from counselors/principals; Circle reviews by contrast contain few or no examples of this level of systemic leadership failure or chronic staff instability.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight stronger, bette: Many square reviews list nationally/state-recognized arts and band programs, specialized magnets (theatre, performing-arts centers), wide extracurricular breadth, active PTAs/nonprofits funding trips, and visible alumni/community pride—while Circle reviews lack comparable named, high-level extracurricular accomplishments or organized community fundraising support.
candidate_defs.Square entries document stronger, broade: This bucket captures reviews that name many AP/IB/dual‑credit/STEM offerings, early‑college or AA pathways, high SAT/AP metrics, and alumni college success (e.g., students earning 60 college credits, Ivy/Top‑tier admits, US News rankings, 'students started College at FSU with 20+ credits'), contrasts that with circle entries which lack comparable course catalogs or measurable college outcomes; it groups any evidence of extensive advanced coursework and concrete college-readiness results.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more robust, visib: This bucket groups reviews that highlight large, sustained extracurricular life—named marching band/orchestra/show choir, state/national competition wins, enduring leadership positions (cheer captains), major fundraising ($300k), and well‑supported theater/arts facilities—while circle entries typically do not list comparable program breadth or high‑profile achievements.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe worse student sa: This bucket covers reports of frequent fights, daily police presence, thefts, OD/ drug incidents, pervasive bullying and racism, sexual misconduct, lockdowns, and administrators who ignore or mishandle complaints (e.g., 'students jumped... admin said ignore it', 'police walk students out daily'), contrasted with circle entries that rarely report such sustained safety crises.
candidate_defs.Square entries emphasize pronounced faci: This groups reviews that simultaneously praise new construction, smartboards and renovated gyms/theaters and also report overcrowded new schools, leaking buildings, roaches, broken locks, long lunch lines, and spending tradeoffs (big football/field investments vs classroom needs), whereas circle reviews rarely combine these concrete facility/space complaints or renovation claims.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger evidence: This bucket captures accounts of systemic barriers and uneven implementation—restricted AP enrollment and 'sorting hat' tracking, athletic/legacy favoritism, inconsistent dress‑code/device enforcement, counselors pushing easy options or failing students, biased rehiring/blacklisting and alumni‑dominated hiring—that describe how programs and discipline are applied unequally, a pattern less present or described differently in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more extensive ad: These reviews describe concrete program inventories and college-prep results (AP/IB/dual-enrollment/STEM/medical academies, fab labs, distance-learning, internships, seven+ AP classes, students admitted to MIT/Harvard/Princeton, millions in scholarships) that are repeatedly present in square but absent or only vaguely referenced in circle (circle gives general 'rigorous' claims without program detail). Examples: square cites IB/STEM academies, dual‑enrollment credit, sustained National Merit and scholarship totals and named elite college placements; circle lacks comparable program-level evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews frequently document on-campus incidents and peer misconduct—regular bullying, vaping and drug use, gang problems, fights, sexualized harassment, arson and vehicle crashes—that reviewers say degrade learning and safety; circle reviews either omit these events or portray a safer, more regulated environment. Examples: square lists 'vaping IN the school,' 'students bullied day after day,' 'lots of drug activity' and repeated fight/arson reports; circle emphasizes 'safe environment' and anti‑bullying efforts.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Square reviewers report operational and governance problems—unresponsive or rude administrators, abrupt/unauthorized records transfers, favoritism toward athletes or staff relatives, grade manipulation, misuse of funds, scheduling failures, and opaque communication—whereas circle reviews rarely allege this level of district/administrative misconduct. Examples: square cites 'principal favors Math/Sci/show choir,' 'invented the grade D-,' 'records transferred without consent,' and 'district tried to throw him under the bus'; circle does not make comparable claims.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater extremes and: Square reviews contain both detailed praise for new/upgraded specialized facilities and technology (new buildings, fab labs, remodeled theater, modern tools) and contrasting reports of severe upkeep/resource failures (rodent/roach infestations, leaky ceilings, worn classrooms, lack of textbooks, overcrowded 36–40+ classes, parking/transportation chaos), while circle’s facility/resource comments are milder and more uniform. Examples: square mentions 'the new facility is excellent' and elsewhere 'a rat fell out of a ceiling tile' and 'classes of 36 or more'; circle only notes general cleanliness or lacks such extremes.
candidate_defs.square entries present larger within‑sch: Many square reviews describe intensely heterogeneous student experiences—pockets of elite AP/IB instruction and high achiever outcomes alongside illiterate graduates, inconsistent teacher competence, variable counseling (life‑saving support vs. dismissive counselors), and tracked class-placement bias—whereas circle reviews are more uniformly characterized and do not display the same internal extremes. Examples: square juxtaposes 'students admitted to MIT' with 'one in five graduates illiterate,' notes 'AP teachers outstanding; half of teachers don’t know what they’re teaching,' and documents both strong guidance help and overloaded/uncaring counselors.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program pathways (AP/IB/AICE/Cambridge, dual‑enrollment, magnet/CTE tracks), award‑winning arts and competitive teams, internships, and explicit college admissions results (Yale, Ivy acceptances, AP pass rates), whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable programs or measurable post‑secondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Many square reviews document daily fights, open drug use, racial harassment, suicides or severe assaults and describe administration/staff enabling or ignoring incidents (failed investigations, ignored reports), while circle reviews contain few or no comparable accounts of pervasive violence, substance visibility, or systematic nonresponse.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more systemic ad: Square reviewers repeatedly allege mismanagement at school/district levels (cheating to inflate scores, hiring for image, siphoning funds to football, aggressive fundraising), widespread favoritism/clique politics, punitive one‑size discipline or inconsistent enforcement, and high teacher turnover — issues circle reviews do not consistently report.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete fac: Square reviews give many specific operational examples — long lunch lines, broken air conditioning, nonfunctional fire alarms, locked bathrooms, renovation disruptions, bond/levy debates and overcrowded classrooms — whereas circle reviews rarely provide this level of facility/operations detail.
candidate_defs.square entries include far more detailed: Square reviewers both praise and fault concrete special‑education and counseling practice (e.g., 'first school I didn't have to fight to get IEP followed', and conversely 'IEP was not worth the paper', plus reports of helpful guidance counselors and also ignored suicidal crises), while circle reviews largely omit detailed descriptions of these support services.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse school s: These reviews describe frequent and severe safety incidents (daily fights, bomb/shooting threats, on‑campus drug sales, vaping fires), widespread peer bullying and racial/identity harassment, and often ineffective or tolerated staff responses — e.g., “There are fights literally every single day,” multiple bomb/shooting threats, students openly selling drugs, and complaints that “they do nothing about bullying unless the child has been hit.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more c: Square reviews enumerate AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment partnerships, National Merit and Ivy matriculations, scholarship totals and specific college credit outcomes (e.g., “AP and IB started college at sophomore level,” “Harvard, MIT, Stanford placements,” “12 National Merit Semifinalists”), while circle contains only vague or limited college‑prep claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more serious facil: These accounts document overcrowding, large campus logistics, broken/unsanitary facilities, maintenance failures, long lunch lines, unreliable busing, mandated technology/fee burdens, and contested spending priorities (e.g., leaking roofs, roaches, ‘HUGE school’ crowds, required laptop fees, and criticism that money is spent on athletics/technology over core courses), reflecting both physical capacity and resource‑allocation issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Reviewers cite nepotism, biased discipline, punitive or retaliatory administrator behavior, mismanaged transcripts/grades, residency/expulsion threats, leadership instability, and poor accountability (e.g., “nepotism... pay raises to their friends,” principal refusing to return calls, transcript errors that ‘ruin the GPA,’ and parents threatened with lawsuits), indicating governance and procedural breakdowns beyond routine communication problems.
candidate_defs.square entries depict stronger and more: These reviews emphasize affluent/choice‑based enrollment, socio‑economic snobbery, exclusionary clique cultures, racial tensions and mixed claims about LGBTQ or special‑needs inclusivity (e.g., parents ‘renting a place over there to get your children enrolled,’ ‘the richer you are... the more friends you will have,’ alongside reports of both a huge rainbow flag and trans students being disrespected), showing pronounced social stratification and contested inclusion in the school community.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger, more co: This bucket captures reviews that list IB/AP/STEM/honors tracks, dual‑enrollment or PTECH offerings, frequent AP participation and high AP/test scores, and named college placements or scholarships (e.g., “IB, Advanced Placement…graduates go to Princeton/Duke/Emory”, “6 AP courses…passed AP exams”, “concurrent college courses”), distinguishing schools described as having explicit college‑prep pathways from Circle reviews that lack such programmatic detail or outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Includes accounts of regular fights, gang/drug activity, sexual harassment/assault allegations, lockdowns, weapons threats, pervasive bullying, and administrators or SROs failing to stop or consistently discipline these behaviors (e.g., “fights broke out everyday,” “many arrests…gang violence and drug issues,” “there is a serious bullying problem that the administration insists does not exist”).
candidate_defs.square entries mention physical faciliti: Covers concrete discussion of buildings, renovation/technology investments, overcrowding and space constraints, cafeteria/food quality and sanitation, bathroom access, and device programs — both positive (major remodels, new science wings, one‑to‑one iPads, good stadiums) and negative (severe overcrowding, mold/unsanitary kitchens, closed bathrooms, long cafeteria lines) — e.g. “new state of the art science wing…3000 students, way over crowded,” “mold in the food,” “one-to-one iPad program.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater administ: This groups reports of opaque or tone‑deaf leadership, frequent principal/AD turnover, district mismanagement, favoritism/nepotistic hiring, bungled scheduling and counseling/IEP failures, and punitive or inconsistent office practices (e.g., “administration is not always consistent…change graduation requirements every other day,” “high turnover…no leadership,” “IEP/504 not implemented; parents must fight”), distinguishing systemic governance/operations failures from Circle’s comparatively fewer or different leadership complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries portray a broader, named: Groups mentions of robust, award‑winning programs (band, theater, robotics, FFA, vocational classes, competitive academic teams) together with reports that access or selection is uneven (hand‑picked teams, family/alumni favoritism, coaching mismanagement or nepotism) — e.g. “band and color guard are the best…marching band Tennessee State Champions” alongside “principal and AD handpicked teams…only people with family members get placed in the front.”
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and broad: This bucket captures reviews where square schools list concrete curricular breadth and outcomes (many AP/IB/honors/dual‑credit courses, vocational pathways, academies, AP funding, and named college‑admissions/scholarship results) that circle reviews do not (e.g., 'JF offers the most AP classes… VASS grant pays for AP tests', 'home of the International Baccalaureate program', '1.2 million dollars in scholarships'). It groups items about program variety, specialized tracks (STEM, CNA/EMT, business academies), and documented college readiness/placement evidence distinct from routine classroom supports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers reviews describing recurring fights, filmed attacks, pervasive bullying/cliques/racism, drug problems, teen pregnancies, and mental‑health consequences (therapy, attorneys, suicides) at square schools, frequently paired with staff inaction (e.g., 'fight happening every day', 'kids filmed a brutal attack', 'had to withdraw… obtained an attorney', 'bullying runs rampant… administration does nothing'), whereas circle reviews rarely report this scale or severity of safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete st: This bucket groups reviews in which square schools provide specific, operational evidence about supports across levels — both positive and negative examples — such as named counselors/IEP processes, academic centers, paid AP test support, in‑school tutoring, and after‑school study programs (e.g., 'ESS kids thrive', 'her IEP was ignored by nearly all her teachers', 'AP test paid for by grant', '20 minute activity period allows extra help'), while circle reviews largely lack this programmatic detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers reports of poor/admin communication and follow‑through, favoritism (athletes/connected families), punitive responses to complaints, grade‑manipulation or collusion, board/district corruption or political interference, and staffing instability (e.g., 'unreturned parent calls', 'teachers play favorites', 'district had a policy... round grades up', 'principal is inaccessible', 'replace the whole management'), which are described far more often for square schools than for circle schools.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete evi: This bucket groups reviews that report tangible infrastructure and resourcing details at square schools — both positive (new buildings, science centers, pools) and negative (overcrowded classes, canceled tutoring, outdated textbooks, blocked web tools, athletics getting priority funding) — examples include 'new Math and Science Center', 'massive budget cut… cancellation of afterschool tutoring', 'File manager is blocked', and 'classes are too big', topics largely absent or far less detailed in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute student: This bucket groups raw terms describing repeated on-campus fights, bathroom drug/vape use and overdoses, hate symbols and racialized harassment, daily bullying and threats, fire-alarm evacuations due to vaping, and accounts that staff/security do not or cannot stop it (e.g., “boys fight in the bathrooms every single day,” “Heavy drug use by students,” “trashed bathrooms… graffiti…swastikas,” and reports that administrators/security ‘do nothing’ or normalize fights). These are concrete incident-level safety/discipline failures that appear much more often in square reviews than in circle ones.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: This bucket groups raw terms listing IB and magnet programs, large AP/Honors catalogs, dual-enrollment and community-college partnerships, robust CTE and vocational certification pathways, and concrete college-success claims (e.g., “IB program… many IB students accepted to top universities,” “dual enrollment with Bunker Hill Community College,” “graduate with about 25 AP credits,” and alumni at top colleges). These programmatic depth and outcome signals distinguish square reviews from circle’s lack of comparable, concrete college-prep evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete, in: This bucket groups terms about IEP/504 denials or noncompliance, overloaded or unhelpful counselors, explicit Life Skills and speech-therapy praise, and documented casework (e.g., “IEP supports removed,” “administration unwilling to work with 504,” and “Life Skills classes… very attentive” and “guidance office overloaded”). Square reviews more often provide specific examples of special-education/counseling practice and failures (or exemplary programs), whereas circle reviews largely omit or lack such concrete SPED/counseling incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket covers complaints about leadership turnover, unresponsive or secretive administration, inconsistent policy enforcement, records and scheduling errors, program cuts, and favoritism (e.g., “administration is horrible…resistant to criticism,” “rules are inconsistently enforced,” “athletes/JROTC get favoritism,” “IEP files lost,” and “they refuse to fire a problematic teacher”). These governance and process failures are reported far more in square reviews than in circle ones and are distinct from student-safety incidents or program descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries report wider and more pol: This bucket groups descriptions of very broad extracurricular and arts offerings, championship athletics, music/choir national recognition, CTE and trade labs, and explicit facility investments (new gyms, tracks, technology rollouts) alongside repeated critiques of overcrowded classes, trashed bathrooms, mold/ceiling problems, construction disruption, or mismanaged device programs (e.g., “many clubs…award-winning music program,” “new gym and track,” and simultaneously “overcrowded hallways,” “trashed bathrooms… graffiti,” and “construction has made it hard to walk around”). Square reviews report both the breadth of extracurricular/facility strengths and acute capacity/maintenance problems much more often than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, named: These reviews emphasize formal offerings and outcomes (IB, AP, dual‑enrollment, honors, National Merit, concrete college‑attendance rates like “98% go to college,” and national/state rankings) that circle reviews do not. Examples: repeated praise for IB/dual‑credit/AP pathways, AP credit filling a year of college, and US News/college‑readiness metrics are frequent in square but absent from circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews document bullying, repeated physical fights, gangs, on‑campus drug/smoking use, sexual incidents, and claims that staff/administration ignore or mishandle these problems; circle reviews lack comparable safety incident reports. Illustrative evidence: “bullying mercilessly… administration turns a blind eye,” “serious gang issue,” student drug sales in hallways, and security/response failures described in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more explicit admi: Square reviewers repeatedly name cover‑ups, retaliation, nepotism, prioritizing awards/appearance or graduation rates over student learning, and heavy‑handed or absent principals—claims that circle reviews do not make. Representative items: “the school does everything it can to keep things quiet,” “nepotism reigns supreme,” “principal is heavy handed/bully,” and complaints about administration protecting certain students or suppressing programs.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader and bet: Square frequently documents strong fine‑arts, championship athletics, many clubs/boosters, and booster/parent support (and sometimes pay‑to‑play controversies or athletics‑first budgeting), whereas circle rarely lists comparable extracurricular breadth or high‑level athletic achievement. Examples: state titles and national athletic reputation, “fine arts program is exceptional,” active PTSO/boosters, and named successful programs in square versus little or declining extracurricular detail in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete da: Square reviews contain many specific operational details—overcrowded classes and trailers, outdated tech and textbooks, substitute‑reliance, scheduling/credit transfer problems, counselor caseload shortages, uneven IEP/504 follow‑through, and both strong examples of teacher tutoring/parent contact and counterexamples of minimal instruction—whereas circle provides far fewer of these concrete operational reports. Sample evidence: “class sizes over 30,” “subs are in classes more than actual teachers,” “no IEP set in place,” “teachers exchange cell numbers for daily contact,” and pervasive tech/facility complaints in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety, bully: This bucket collects reports of on‑campus threats and misconduct (drugs, guns, frequent fights, vaping, theft, cybercrimes) plus repeated reviewer claims that staff/administration ignore or mishandle reports (sheriff calls, arrests, students passing alcohol on campus, bullying ignored, staff driving past incidents). Examples: “notorious for drug availability,” “we are sick to learn yet another student had a gun on campus today,” and “countless reports of students bullying kids and the principal pushes it to the side,” contrasted with Circle’s lack of comparable safety/crime claims.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger advance: This bucket groups claims about breadth/depth of rigorous coursework (many APs, IB, STEM/business/CTE academies, magnet programs), concrete college‑prep infrastructure (Naviance, College & Career Centers) and explicit placement/test outcomes (high SAT averages, Ivy/major university admits). Examples: “22 AP and 8 dual‑credit classes,” “IB…24 college credits,” “helped me a lot with my SATs…and get into the college of my choosing,” which are details Circle reviews do not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader extracur: This bucket covers both the extensive extracurricular and arts/CTE offerings (marching band, choir, theater, hundreds of clubs, CTE pathways, internships) and reviewer complaints that resources/favors are unevenly distributed (coach‑dominated admin, pay‑to‑play, arts deprioritized, favoritism in cast/slots). Examples: “THE BAND IS ALL THAT MATTERS!!!!,” “hundreds of clubs and activities,” alongside “sports has always been #1” and “music dept is not dedicated to teaching all kids,” contrasts with Circle’s lack of comparable program breadth or such favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.square entries expose more administrativ: This bucket captures critiques of leadership and governance: school‑ or board‑level politics, curriculum policy changes tied to falling scores, inconsistent discipline/enforcement, censorship/book bans, nepotism/corruption, and mismanaged initiatives or facilities spending. Examples: “The School board is uneducated and very politically motivated,” “curriculum choices resulted in lower scores… petition ignored,” “suspended seven books,” and “most of the staff only really cares about athletics (where all the budget goes),” issues not attributed to Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal greater variabilit: This bucket groups evidence about highly mixed teacher practice (from ‘go above and beyond’ to verbal abuse or apathy), high substitute/turnover problems, tenure‑protected poor staff, and inconsistent counseling/special‑ed supports (some strong paraeducator/IEP praise vs. reports of ignored 504s and ineffective guidance). Examples: “many teachers don’t teach well… I honestly feel scared,” “an astounding number of classes are STILL being covered by subs,” and “huge student services department… Dover is a model,” showing variability that Circle’s reviews do not display.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures repeated accounts of day‑to‑day danger and peer harm plus institutional failure to protect victims — e.g., “fights every single day,” bomb threats, “This school is full of drugs,” racial harassment at sporting events, systematic bullying and retaliation for reporters — contrasted with Circle reviews that emphasize safety or report only isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: Includes concrete program and outcome evidence that Square reviewers name but Circle largely does not — e.g., full IB/AICE offerings, extensive AP and dual‑credit classes, Project Lead The Way, parent‑run College & Career Center, internship pipelines, multiple orchestras/bands, and measurable college/scholarship outcomes (Ivy admits, full scholarships).
candidate_defs.square entries report more uneven, polar: Groups reviews documenting variable teacher performance and professional failures — destroyed education files, counselor errors that blocked graduation, inconsistent discipline/favoritism, IEP non‑enforcement, district lawsuits and opaque leadership — producing polarized praise and criticism within the same school; Circle reviews do not show this depth of administrative/process breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Covers physical‑plant and resource themes: chronic overcrowding and split campuses, flooding/structural complaints, requests for cosmetic/major renovation, contradictory notes of recent capital improvements, traffic/parking congestion, and complaints funds favor athletics over labs or arts — issues Circle reviewers generally do not raise.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more complex com: Captures school‑community patterns that affect student composition and outcomes: prevalence of private supplemental tutoring and affluent parents, Choice or open‑enrollment growth and transfers out to private schools, multigenerational family attendance, boarding programs, and reports of racial/class exclusion or segregation — contrasted with Circle’s simpler, stable enrollment narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete academic-program breadth and rigor (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment, STEM certifications, college-credit pathways) and measurable outcomes (graduation rates, AP/IB participation, admissions to selective colleges) being present at the school; examples include 'AP program is amazing', 'IB program...prepared for college', 46% AP exam participation and 94% graduation, and alumni to MIT/UCLA/Harvard — claims Circle reviewers do not substantively make.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive,: This bucket captures documentation of broad extracurricular offerings, high-level competitive recognition, and an outsized sport/music culture — e.g. band playing at the Greek Theatre and Normandy, state‑ranked sports teams, 'top of the line athletics, JROTC, music program', plus repeated claims sports are prioritized over academics — features Circle reviews usually omit or report far less of.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers accounts of sustained peer violence, daily bullying, pervasive drug/vape exposure, classroom violence and even sexual assaults, together with failures or inconsistency in school response (police/home armed responses, admins ‘do nothing’, students returned to class after violent incidents) — e.g. 'HUGE bullying problem', 'weekly fights, drug use', 'rapists attend/attended bhhs and administrators did absolutely nothing' — contrasted with Circle reviews that generally lack these severe safety claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviewer claims about unfair personnel practices and governance failures — nepotism and advancement tied to last names, administrators publicly humiliating or harassing students, allegations of 'a lot of pedo teachers', union protection of ineffective staff, and school‑board/district unresponsiveness or community escalation — e.g. 'advancements...based on what your last name is', 'Mr. Lawless...said she looked "whorish"', and appeals to state education officials — issues Circle rarely reports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket collects tangible operational and infrastructural evidence — overcrowded classrooms and huge enrollments, mold/unsanitary conditions, scheduling and lunch logistics, pay‑to‑participate fees, textbook shortages vs. tech purchases (iMacs/SmartBoards/vape detectors), and both major renovations and maintenance shortfalls — e.g. '3500+ students', 'overrun with mold', 'they make us pay $60', 'textbooks over 10 years old while new iMacs purchased' — items Circle reviews mostly limit to cosmetic facility notes or do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures reviews that cite concrete advanced‑curriculum offerings and outcomes (e.g., “30+ hours of credit from AP courses,” “IB magnet program,” “dual‑enrollment/associate degree pathways,” high AP/SAT pass rates, Ivy/ selective‑college matriculations). Falling here means the review provides program names, counts, partnerships, or quantified outcomes that show a robust college‑prep pipeline — evidence repeatedly present in square but absent or weaker in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This groups descriptions of leadership or teacher failures: ignored parent emails/phones, administrators ‘overwhelmed’ or protecting staff, favoritism by coaches/teachers, failure to investigate bullying/sexual harassment, and repeated discipline/crime incidents (drugs, weapons, lockdowns). Reviews in this bucket document operational breakdowns and specific mishandled incidents that undermine safety and accountability — a pattern much more common in square than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries discuss facility conditio: Includes concrete physical‑plant evidence: reports of brand‑new campuses, new stadiums/pools and modern tech, alongside many entries about crumbling buildings, roaches, mold, broken A/C, overcrowded halls, and active bond/capital campaigns. Membership means the review focuses on tangible infrastructure or space problems or recent facility investments — topics emphasized in square reviews far more than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, better‑re: Covers detailed extracurricular and career/technical program evidence: award‑winning bands, state‑champion sports teams, robotics/aviation/CTE pathways, international music trips, and many clubs; sometimes also funding/priority complaints tied to these programs. A review falls here if it names specific extracurricular programs, achievements, or CTE credentialing that materially extend student opportunities — a distinguishing feature of many square entries versus circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures or i: This bucket groups accounts of inadequate special‑education services, legal noncompliance, pressure to medicate, shipping low‑performing students to alternative schools, economic/racial exclusion, and elite‑program favoritism (IB/HPT separation). Reviews here describe how vulnerable students are marginailzed or denied proper supports or accommodations — detailed equity and access failures that appear much more often in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: These reviews emphasize concrete curricular breadth and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, academies, dual‑enrollment, college credit and elite admits) in square schools compared with circle; examples include mentions of concurrent enrollment, SAS/IB/Engineering Academies, students leaving with Associates credits, and claims of higher test scores or selective college placement, indicating square schools report clearer formal advanced-program infrastructure and measurable postsecondary success.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑ac: Square reviews repeatedly list extensive competitive extracurriculars — marching band, theater, speech/drama, award‑winning sports, robotics and dozens of clubs — and also note athletic prestige and favoritism toward athletes; circle reviews rarely enumerate comparable arts/athletics depth and instead omit or highlight narrower program sets.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square content contains repeated concrete accounts of fights, assaults, gang presence, drug/alcohol problems, racial harassment and bullying and alleges weak, inconsistent or punitive administrative responses (ignored reports, enabled bullying, invasive searches), whereas circle entries lack or downplay these ongoing safety failures.
candidate_defs.square entries document more operational: These reviews give detailed personnel and support-system evidence: teachers absent daily or unqualified, substitute-teacher cooperation problems, high turnover, contradictory praise for dedicated staff alongside accusations of special‑education neglect and IEP noncompliance, and inconsistent guidance counselor responsiveness; circle reviews do not show this same breadth of operational HR and student‑support detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviews document overcrowding and portables, unsanitary restrooms, aging/poorly maintained buildings, outdated or malfunctioning technology, scheduling and lunch-line failures, pay‑to‑play fees and district funding complaints — sometimes alongside notes of recent bond-funded improvements — while circle entries generally lack these specific facility/capacity or district‑finance reports.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews report concrete, expanded academic offerings (AP/IB/dual‑credit, new AP classes, named career academies, STEM/medical pathways), structured remediation/tutoring, and alumni/college‑placement evidence (scholarships, graduates at top universities), whereas circle reviews lack comparable program breadth or measurable college‑prep outcomes; examples include “Each year, a quarter of the students are enrolled in dual credit courses,” “The number of AP classes has doubled,” and multiple alumni claiming strong college preparedness.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize abundant, high‑: These reviews detail wide extracurricular breadth, competitive/award‑winning arts and standout athletics (marching band, theater, state playoff teams), often noting institutional prioritization or favoritism toward athletes and sports budgets, while circle reviews name few or narrower activities; examples: “award‑winning Drama Magnet…invited to the SE Theatre Conference,” “football team has been to the state play‑offs,” and complaints that “the budget for some classes is very low because it is being used on sports.”
candidate_defs.square entries report worse facility con: These reviews provide many concrete infrastructure and operational problems — overcrowded classrooms and hallways, pest and health‑violation reports, leaking ceilings/power outages, dangerous bus stops, registration delays and event‑communication failures — none of which circle reviews document to the same degree; examples include “the campus is pretty dirty and is infested with bugs and rats,” “There were fights at least once a week. The halls were so crowded,” and “a 5‑week delay due to them on the start of the semester.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews recount repeated physical fights, drug use, gang‑targeting, rampant bullying, even multiple suicides, and explicitly describe staff or administrators who ignore, minimize, or participate in the mistreatment, whereas circle reviews rarely report comparable safety crises; examples: “There are multiple fights each day,” “Bullying is rampant…faculty rarely deals with bullying,” and “teachers do nothing to stop the bullying and even go as far as picking on her themselves.”
candidate_defs.square entries document more systemic ad: These reviews allege district‑ or school‑level misconduct and mismanagement (nepotistic hiring, favoritism to wealthy/athlete students, alleged grade bumps tied to evaluations), misallocated budgets, and persistent unresponsiveness or miscoordination from counselors and offices, while circle reviews do not present comparable evidence of systemic governance failure; examples include “The entire system…is corrupt,” “grades had been drastically bumped up in order for the teachers to look better,” and “Parents concerns are not well received and often dismissed.”
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more num: This bucket captures claims that Square schools offer more AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, vocational certifications, structured pathways (e.g., internships, Career/College academies), and documented alumni/award outcomes (National Merit, college credits) — e.g., reviewers noting 'AP classes, college credit, SU/RI cooperating programs,' 'students graduate with transcripted college work,' and 'National Merit Scholars,' while Circle reviews lack comparable program breadth or measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, better‑re: This groups descriptions of abundant clubs, award‑winning band/theatre, many competitive sports, high participation and school spirit, and claims that athletics/music receive visible institutional support — e.g., 'so many clubs,' 'one of the best music programs,' 'state champion teams,' and 'extreme focus on athletics' — whereas Circle reviews typically note few on‑site sports, limited after‑school options, or lack comparable extracurricular infrastructure.
candidate_defs.square entries document worse physical i: This bucket covers concrete facility and capacity problems reported more for Square: aging or falling‑apart buildings, mold/lead/health hazards, closed/insufficient bathrooms, overcrowded classes, and missing instructional materials or outdated technology — e.g., 'no AC, you can't drink the water (lead pipes),' 'only one girls bathroom open for 500 students,' 'we have no math or Spanish books,' while Circle reviews generally omit such severe facility/resource failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups accounts of pervasive peer violence, targeted racial/sexual orientation harassment, an entrenched drug culture, suicides/self‑harm clusters, and either inconsistent enforcement or harsh punitive responses (suspensions, invasive searches) — e.g., 'drug issue is a cultural norm,' 'white supremacist symbols... family forced to move,' 'suicide rate seems very high,' and examples of extreme suspensions — whereas Circle reviews do not report this scale or severity of safety/crime incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced ad: This bucket captures governance and operational dysfunction described more for Square: unstable or unqualified leadership, old‑boys networks, staff gossip/abuse, uneven discipline tied to influence, mishandled transcripts/fees, poor scheduling/grade‑posting, and parent‑school communication breakdowns — e.g., 'admin turned a blind eye,' 'they will hold your transcripts if you don't pay,' 'many teachers are quitting,' and 'PowerSchool/portal not updated weekly' — while Circle reviews rarely allege systemic cronyism, records mismanagement, or this level of administrative dysfunction.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger, broader: This bucket captures descriptions where square schools list concrete advanced offerings (IB, many AP/honors, Dual‑Enrollment, academies/medical/engineering pathways), dedicated college counselors, AP/Running Start placements, and claimed higher test/college matriculation metrics (e.g., IB diplomas, 20+ college credits, 'top 20' admissions), while circle reviews lack or downplay such structured college-prep detail.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This groups accounts of pervasive safety problems at square schools — repeated fights, drug odor/use, gang activity, sexual harassment, student assaults and chronic bullying — plus claims that administration often fails to intervene (cover-ups, victim‑blaming, minimal consequences); circle entries either do not report these issues or describe far milder/discrete behavior problems.
candidate_defs.Square entries report larger enrollment,: This bucket covers complaints of severe overcrowding and big-campus logistics (3,000+ students, packed hallways, insufficient bathrooms/lockers), concurrent renovations or trailers, facility maintenance and sanitation failures (leaks, pests, no AC, yellow water), and resource shortages (no paper, broken tech), while circle entries typically describe smaller scale or no such capacity/facility crises.
candidate_defs.Square entries document greater staff va: This groups reports that square schools have highly inconsistent teacher quality (some excellent but many incompetent), named incidents of teacher misconduct or bullying, administrative favoritism toward athletes/connected families, politicized governance/protectionism, paid‑tutoring conflicts, and repeated failures on Special Education/IEP supports — whereas circle reviews generally report more consistent, caring staff and fewer governance/favoritism allegations.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe stronger, more n: This bucket captures square schools' accounts of abundant clubs and award‑winning programs (marching band, debate, robotics), sustained athletic dominance and scouting visibility, visible booster/PTA fundraising and turnout at events, multi‑generational alumni pride, and community rituals/traditions — features that circle entries rarely document or that circle reports describe as diminished or absent.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups reviews that report concrete curricular depth and measurable academic pathways in square schools — e.g., abundant AP/Pre‑AP and IB courses, magnet programs, dual‑enrollment/5.0 GPA options, career/CTE tracks (cosmetology, automotive, nursing), and documented college-placement claims — while circle reviews lack or downplay these offerings. Examples: 'three magnets… highest AP pass rates,' 'Dual Credit… Associates Degree in cyber technology,' versus Circle’s comments that advanced offerings are minimal or absent.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: This bucket captures reviews describing concrete safety incidents and hostile peer climates in square schools (fights, stabbings, frequent bullying, drugs/alcohol on campus, racial/sexual harassment, even alleged concealment of incidents) and often an ineffective or dismissive response by staff. Examples: 'My friend has been bullied for 3 years… nothing has been done,' 'there was once a stabbing on school grounds,' and 'kids bringing guns… they go to great lengths to cover up,' whereas circle reviews rarely report such violence or systemic safety failures.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups operational and governance complaints in square reviews — lost paperwork/registrar enrollment errors, monetization/fee practices, arbitrary/inconsistent discipline or dress‑code enforcement, transfer denials for funding, and visible misallocation toward athletics — contrasted with circle reviews that do not raise these procedural/systemic failures. Examples: 'lost the school they were transferring in from paperwork,' 'They only want your money… pay $80 to take tennis,' 'administration favors athletes… give them leeway,' versus Circle’s lack of such operational allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries list broader, higher‑perf: This bucket covers concrete evidence of extracurricular breadth and achievement in square schools — strong band/choir/theatre, national/state championship teams, speech & debate excellence, robust club lists, active booster/alumni support, and community fundraising — whereas circle reviews typically omit or report few such sustained programs. Examples: 'marching band 1st in state 5 of last 6 years,' 'DECA, Robotics, FBLA, FFA, award‑winning ROTC,' and 'huge network of famous alumni,' contrasted with Circle’s minimal extracurricular description.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket groups reviews that recount failures or strain in student supports at square schools — IEP/504 noncompliance, families hiring advocates/attorneys, massive counselor caseloads, weak college advising, and lack of teacher tutoring — while circle reviews do not document these systematic support breakdowns. Examples: 'teachers refuse to follow the 504 plan,' 'probably 500 students per counselor,' 'lacking in college guidance,' and 'no tutoring support at all (by teachers).'
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger, more nu: These reviews name concrete curricular offerings and results (AP/IB courses, academies (STEM/arts/culinary), dual‑enrollment/college‑credit partnerships, large AP counts and state rankings) and cite college matriculation and scholarship evidence — e.g., “30+ AP classes,” “IB program,” “GearUP/College & Career Center,” and alumni admitted to elite colleges — while circle reviews largely lack named advanced tracks or measurable college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑qu: Square reviews repeatedly list a wide menu of clubs, championship teams, standout band/choir/drama programs, booster‑backed athletics, and facility investments (e.g., top band program, over 100 student clubs, new construction/overrides), whereas circle reviews generally do not document that scale or named flagship extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain repeated concrete safety claims — daily bullying, constant fights, drug use, gang presence, bomb threats, sexual‑misconduct rumors, arrests/lockdowns and added security guards/cameras — whereas circle entries rarely describe comparable violent or pervasive safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries display a more polarized: Many square reviews describe teachers who provide one‑on‑one help, extensive tutoring, counselors and AVID/one‑on‑one interventions AND, in the same school, report grade inflation for minimal effort, regular classroom disruption, inconsistent grading, or poor support for middle‑of‑the‑road learners and special‑education gaps (e.g., strong AP/IB instruction vs. ‘regular’ classes that are unchallenging or poorly differentiated); circle reviews lack this pronounced polarization.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly document concrete governance issues — unresponsive office staff, unanswered parent calls, punitive discipline/fee policies, favoritism in extracurriculars, misuse of funds, leadership turnover or harmful policy changes — describing systemic administrative dysfunction and arbitrary enforcement more often than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, more ad: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and rigor — numerous AP/IB offerings, CTE/dual‑credit tracks, niche electives (medical apprentice, electronic music), nationally competitive band/arts and championship sports, and repeated Ivy/UC placements — claims that Circle reviews do not (e.g., many Square notes of ‘IB program,’ ‘nearly 30 AP classes,’ ‘Early College/Dual Credit,’ band trips to Carnegie Hall, and top‑university matriculation). Falling here means the school is portrayed as offering many structured, high‑level pathways and measurable postsecondary results absent from Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These comments recount concrete safety and climate problems — drug use and overdoses, fights, sexual‑assault allegations, vaping, bomb threats, racial slurs, homophobia, and pervasive bullying — often paired with claims that staff/admin failed to stop or adequately respond (e.g., 'drugs in every school', 'I was bullied constantly. No one even tried to stop the bullying', 'I've never heard more racial slurs'). Membership here means reviews document frequent serious student‑behavior or discrimination incidents and ineffective or inconsistent discipline/anti‑bullying enforcement.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: These reviews point to leadership and office‑level failures — lost student records, unresponsive counselors, discouraging guidance advice, multiple principal/superintendent turnovers, punitive attendance/fee policies, and calls for systemic leadership replacement — plus chronic poor parent communication (e.g., 'they couldnt find his info', 'Guidance told him there was no hope', 'the administration does not return phone calls'). Falling in this bucket means the school is characterized by weak office systems, erratic leadership, and ineffective college/guidance services.
candidate_defs.square entries show larger internal vari: Reviews describe a wide spread of teacher quality — some teachers lauded as lifelong role models or unusually available, and others described as disengaged, incompetent, complacent with tenure, favoritism toward athletes/high achievers, or unable to control classrooms (examples include 'great teachers... and everything in between', 'teachers are either hit or miss', 'they highly favor students that participate in athletics', 'teachers are very easy to fool'). Inclusion here denotes explicit, co‑occurring accounts of highly effective teachers alongside systemic teacher‑quality problems.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This cluster covers physical and resourcing issues: overcrowded cafeterias and classrooms, severe maintenance and sanitation problems (roaches, broken desks), insufficient security/SRO coverage, problematic tech rollouts (iPads unused), punitive billing/asset mishandling, and contested capital spending choices (e.g., performing arts center despite poor program outcomes). Reviews placed here describe tangible space, maintenance, staffing, or resource allocation problems (or visible misprioritization) that impede day‑to‑day operations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety incidents and student misconduct plus staff/supervision failures (e.g., “I have smelled pot in the halls,” “a fight every other day,” “lots of drugs and sex in the bathrooms,” “stabbing, fire,” and gang presence) whereas circle reviews contain no comparable catalogue of violent/drug-related incidents or pervasive bullying. Content in this bucket signals a school whose primary distinguishing problem is uncontrolled student behavior and inadequate on-campus supervision or enforcement.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more e: Square reviews repeatedly name IB/AP/STEM breadth and alumni/test outcomes (e.g., “wall-to-wall IB,” “30+ AP courses,” “national merit finalists,” high SAT scores, students skipping college semesters) whereas circle reviews emphasize lack of AP/rigor and remediation (e.g., summer school because a teacher didn’t do her job, students unprepared for college). This bucket captures programmatic depth and documented postsecondary outcomes versus reviews that report instructional failure and remedial recovery.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize heavy athletic/: Square reviewers often praise strong sports, band and arts and facility assets (state‑of‑the‑art pool, stadium, thriving band, CIF appearances) and simultaneously complain classrooms lack textbooks or supplies (“spend most of the money on uniforms and sports rather than textbooks”), whereas circle reviews rarely highlight such robust extracurricular/facility prominence. This bucket groups claims about resource allocation priorities and the presence/quality of extracurricular programs and campus infrastructure.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent ad: Square reviews contain direct allegations about administrators and staff—cover‑ups, bias toward athletes/wealthy parents, shutting off a valedictorian’s mic, calling parents into the superintendent’s office for criticizing the district, and claims of no background checks—while circle reviews include far fewer or no parallel accusations of institutional intimidation or malpractice. This bucket captures governance/ethics problems, uneven enforcement, and adult-led favoritism or suppression in the school community.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: Many square reviews describe concrete student supports (autism programs and paraprofessionals, vocational certificates, dual‑credit, active boosters, virtual options) alongside systematic failures (IEP denial, counselors overloaded, reliance on online credit recovery like E‑2020, or legal‑level special‑ed breakdowns), whereas circle reviews seldom mention special education or these mixed support-system extremes. This bucket groups review evidence about how the school identifies, funds, and operationalizes services for diverse learners and the inconsistency of those supports.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: These reviews report concrete offerings and results — AP/IB/AVID, honors/dual‑enrollment, rigorous Pre‑AP curricula, high AP pass rates, National Merit and elite college matriculations — whereas circle reviews rarely list specific advanced programs or documented college placements (examples: multiple square notes of IB/AVID, AP/Calc/Calc‑3 success, many students accepted to Harvard/MIT/Caltech/MIT/USC; circle contains only generic claims about being 'prepared').
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Square reviews contain repeated allegations of drug use in bathrooms, ongoing fights, racial and anti‑Muslim incidents, sexual harassment, and statements that 'administration does nothing' or that legal action may be required; circle reviews mention bullying or discipline more mildly and do not report the same scale/severity or administrative toleration of safety breaches (examples: 'Drugs run wild,' 'Thugs run the community,' bomb‑threat searches and mishandled evacuations in square vs. circle's absence of comparable safety crises).
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more documented a: These reviews name front‑office rudeness, unanswered calls/emails, budget misallocation (funds to athletics/tech gadgets over textbooks), selective enforcement favoring athletes/wealthier families, deleted reviews, and reported staff misconduct (swearing, harassment, physical aggression), while circle reviews rarely combine so many concrete governance or staff‑misconduct allegations (examples: 'they keep deleting my review,' 'principal spends money on football not books,' teacher grabbed student's head).
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete, op: Square reviewers frequently describe building condition and scale — severe overcrowding, new/modern facilities alongside roaches/asbestos/mold, one‑to‑one laptops, block scheduling, Arena scheduling failures, bus/zone/parking complaints, and failed emergency drills — whereas circle reviews rarely give this level of facility/operational detail (examples: 'very overcrowded 2300+ kids,' 'no elevator for disabled students,' 'laptops for all students,' 'fire/tornado drill mismanagement').
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete, pro: Square reviews commonly describe named supports and programs — proactive counselors calling parents, PBIS, daily tutoring, math skills classes, functioning IEP teams, alternative high school/freshman academy, vocational/CTE pathways and internships — while circle reviews seldom list this level of specific support infrastructure (examples: 'They use PBIS and offer tutoring any day,' 'helpful special education/dyslexia program,' 'Information Technology Systems CTE program praised').
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, broader: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete higher‑level academic offerings (AP/IB, dual‑enrollment, Running Start, Calc III, honors/Freshman Academies), measurable outcomes (graduation rates, ACT/AP performance, alumni college matriculation) and explicit college‑prep supports; e.g., many square entries list IB/AP/dual credit, unique courses and alumni college success whereas circle reviews lack named program evidence or measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pe: This captures evidence of extensive non‑academic programming and high achievement—marching bands, state championship sports, theater awards, robotics, CTE academies and numerous clubs—where square reviews name multiple ensembles, national/state honors, and vocational academies while circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth or accomplishments.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seri: Includes raw items documenting fights, gang/drug presence, bomb/gun threats, sexual misconduct allegations, life‑threatening bullying episodes and repeated parental claims that administration failed to protect students; circle entries, by contrast, rarely document this level or frequency of violent/abusive incidents or systemic non‑response.
