candidate_defs.square entries describe more detailed op: Groups reviews that give concrete facility and logistics evidence—cafeteria shortages, locked bathrooms, overcrowding, renovation status, parking, lost busing, 1:1 tech programs, contested spending (marquees vs. textbooks), and calls for a second high school—where square entries provide specific operational accounts and funding complaints that circle entries do not.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater internal: This bucket covers reviews reporting wide variance within the same school—some award‑winning, highly supportive teachers and principals versus many inexperienced/abusive teachers, favoritism/nepotism, high turnover, inconsistent discipline and mixed special‑education compliance—so square entries present sharply polarized coexisting realities, whereas circle entries tend to show more uniform (though often negative) characterizations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more advanced acad: This bucket groups items where reviewers describe concrete, school-level academic strength and college-prep infrastructure—wide AP/IB/honors catalogs, dual‑enrollment/PSEO/Early‑College programs, remediation/homework centers, and named alumni college successes (e.g., graduates at Penn/Carnegie Mellon, high scholarship totals). Examples: many square reviews list extensive AP/honors/IB/dual-credit offerings and concrete postsecondary outcomes, whereas circle reviews lack comparable evidence of sustained college-preparatory depth.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader e: This bucket captures descriptions of abundant clubs, award‑winning band/robotics/JROTC/STEM academies, CTE certification pathways, no‑cut sports, and athletics-centered funding/identity: reviewers praise state championships, marching band excellence, STEM/aviation academies and many on‑campus arts/CTE options; circle entries rarely catalog comparable program breadth or high‑level extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket groups accounts of pervasive student misconduct and attendant safety crises—recurrent fights, drug/alcohol use, bomb/gun threats, repeated shelter‑in‑place/lockdowns, racial targeting and homophobic harassment—and reviewers’ claims that victims are insufficiently protected; circle reviews more often describe low bullying, fewer fights, or a safer social climate.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers reviewer claims about leadership and office practices (unresponsive or rude administrators, arbitrary enforcement, frequent unnecessary police involvement, camera/searching/phone‑searching, lost records, 504/IEP noncompliance, and counseling breakdowns) that undermine student support and due process—patterns repeatedly attributed to square schools and not to circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: This bucket groups concrete, physical and logistical shortcomings: overcrowded classes and course access limits, dilapidated or pest‑infested facilities, bathroom/cleaning problems, late buses and parking permit issues, budget shortfalls and material shortages—conditions repeatedly cited in square reviews but infrequently mentioned in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more pervasive: This bucket covers concrete accounts of fights, gang activity, frequent lockdowns, drug use, sexualized shaming and physical assaults plus staff inaction or punishing of victims (e.g., “There are fights everyday,” “Bullying is RAMPANT… The staff do NOTHING,” “weekly fights,” and “Shooting incident”), contrasted with Circle’s lack of comparable safety/crime reporting or its praise of handled incidents. It groups reports of both the behaviors themselves and failures of staff/administration to prevent or remediate them (e.g., victims told to have ‘thicker skin’ or administrators minimizing incidents).
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more systemic adm: This bucket captures reviews describing record‑keeping and enrollment breakdowns, ignored parent emails, fiscal scandals, leadership turnover, protected staff, and public misconduct trials (e.g., ‘superintendent indicted for stealing 400k,’ ‘we never received his report cards… he dropped out,’ ‘grade‑changing trial,’ and ‘you can never get in contact with the administration’). It groups operational failures (late counseling appointments, lost paperwork, intrusive/punitive policies) together with governance problems (nepotism, favoritism, board dysfunction, and calls for state takeover) that distinguish Square schools from Circle ones.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially st: This bucket includes explicit program inventories and outcomes found in Square reviews—IB/AP/Honors, dual enrollment, AVID, tech/robotics, pre‑med partnerships, award‑winning arts, and documented scholarships or Ivy/Stanford placements (e.g., ‘full IB program,’ ‘95% of college credits transferred,’ ‘AP/IB students sent to top conservatories’). It groups program breadth (electives, career/CTE tracks, dual credit) and concrete college/career results that Circle reviews generally do not document.
candidate_defs.square entries mention special‑education: This bucket collects both positive and problematic special‑education evidence in Square reviews—from praise for a well‑run special‑ed program to concrete accommodation failures and IEP noncompliance (e.g., ‘Special ed program is extremely well done,’ ‘special needs kids fall through the cracks,’ ‘IEP not followed,’ ‘restricted parent observation policy’ and reports of exploitative tasks assigned to special‑ed students). It groups any detailed operational or policy-level claims specific to special‑education supports and disputes that are largely absent in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more sal: This bucket captures social‑climate and community patterns described in Square reviews—popularity/snobbery and tight cliques, favoritism for well‑connected students or athletes, strong booster/parent involvement, alumni pride, or community relocation choices (e.g., ‘students focused on popularity,’ ‘outsiders have a tough time,’ ‘show choir fees $1,200,’ ‘tight knit, supportive community’ and families moving into the district for safety). It groups peer hierarchies, social exclusion, demographic/status narratives and organized family/community engagement as distinct from administrative or instructional issues.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize tangible program breadth and measurable academic strength at square schools (more AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, magnets and career academies, vocational certs, robotics/STEM labs, higher testing/graduation/college‑placement claims) while circle reviews repeatedly note limited AP/elective options and weak college prep (examples: ‘‘IB program,’’ ‘‘many AP classes,’’ ‘‘higher testing scores/IVY placements’’ vs. ‘‘no advanced placement classes offered,’’ ‘‘almost no choices in elective classes’’).
candidate_defs.square entries report worse student safe: Square reviews contain frequent concrete safety incidents and system failures—weapons/lockdowns, daily fights, pervasive bullying, vaping/drug epidemics, metal detectors and security breaches—and describe ineffective or inconsistent enforcement of discipline (examples: ‘‘multiple lockdowns…kid brought a gun,’’ ‘‘bullying happens at least four times a day…administration does absolutely nothing,’’ ‘‘drugs run rampant’’), whereas circle accounts rarely describe comparable severe safety or daily‑violence patterns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent fail: Many square reviews call out concrete compliance and support breakdowns (504/IEP plans ignored, case‑manager nonresponse, refusal of teacher accommodations), plus insufficient counseling/mental‑health supports and stress from academic pressure (examples: ‘‘504 plan has NOT been followed,’’ ‘‘serious deficiencies with special education and students with IEPs,’’ ‘‘many kids suffer from mental health problems because of the amount of stress’’), while circle reviews largely omit or do not document the same pattern of special‑education or mental‑health failures.
candidate_defs.square entries document more facility, c: Square reviews repeatedly cite physical and operational breakdowns that affect daily schooling—extreme overcrowding and trailers, broken HVAC/intercom/plumbing, scheduling/locker chaos, cafeteria/food and bus shortages, and shifting fees passed to families (examples: ‘‘class sizes huge…no seat some days,’’ ‘‘some rooms 115°F,’’ ‘‘scheduling at start was awful,’’ ‘‘$30 per 9‑weeks parking pass,’’ ‘‘student portal system is horrible’’)—whereas circle reviews rarely describe this combined set of capacity/infrastructure/logistics failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more mixed or prob: Square reviews more often describe uneven teacher quality and instructional passivity, administrative rudeness or incompetence, poor parent communication, perceived favoritism or inequitable access, and disruptive staff turnover (examples: ‘‘administration is extremely incompetent,’’ ‘‘very few teachers show any competence,’’ ‘‘wealthy and popular take all opportunities,’’ ‘‘many teachers broke contract and left’’), while circle entries tend to report more consistently helpful or stable staff and clearer communication.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially br: These reviews repeatedly list named AP/IB/dual‑enrollment programs, magnet/ROTC/CTE tracks, competitive music/theatre/art teams, varsity athletics, and explicit college‑credit outcomes (e.g., “AP and concurrent enrollment,” “PLTW engineering,” “dual magnet/ROTC,” “enough AP and dual credits to enter Purdue as a sophomore,” “top marching band, drumline, Colorguard”), whereas circle reviews largely omit program names and advanced pathways and give no comparable evidence of broad, organized college/career offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews document concrete safety crises and poor enforcement—fights and videos of students being choked in class, drugs used in classrooms, overdose and suicide deaths, sexual‑assault allegations, police handcuffing students, and covert online monitoring—paired with claims that administration fails to stop or covers up incidents; circle reviews either do not mention such incidents or explicitly describe a safer, kinder, low‑fight environment.
candidate_defs.square entries evidence greater administ: Square reviewers repeatedly cite authoritarian or abusive leadership, nepotism/favoritism (especially toward athletes), secretive cover‑ups, refusal or delays in sending transcripts, strict/punitive discipline practices, budget mismanagement, unpaid mandated trainings, and active gatekeeping of parents—claims that contrast with circle reviews, which focus on more limited leadership complaints and do not document the same pattern of alleged secrecy, recordkeeping failures, or politically driven favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: Square reviews contain many specific facility and operational complaints—extreme overcrowding (e.g., thousands of students, chaotic lunches), rented trailer classrooms, flooded fields, collapsing ceilings, mold/rodents, broken A/C or heat, unreliable buses and weather‑access problems—while also sometimes noting renovations or new pools/tracks; circle reviews rarely describe this combination of chronic space, health, and transportation failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater instruct: Square reviews frequently report a two‑tier academic experience—very strong instruction and accountability in honors/AP/IB tracks but weak, under‑resourced regular classes (teachers lacking subject certification, mood‑driven teaching, students forced to self‑teach), inconsistent guidance/special‑education services, and wide teacher variability—whereas circle reviews present more uniform (if sometimes underperforming) classroom experiences and do not show the same degree of internal stratification or certification/placement failures.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger advanced: These reviews describe square schools as offering many AP/IB/honors classes, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit courses, rigorous pathway sequences and documented elite college placements or high standardized‑score results (examples: “wide range of honors and AP courses,” “IB diploma with DE Calculus 2/3,” “usually one of the top National Merit schools,” and students admitted to Ivy/Princeton), whereas circle reviews rarely list AP/IB/dual‑enrollment options or documented high college‑placement outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more numerous, hig: Square reviews repeatedly name extensive extracurricular breadth and prestige—state‑competitive band/choir, UIL/theatre, championship sports, robotics/debate, robust booster/PTA and alumni support (examples: “State competitive band,” “softball team won 5A State Championships,” “Parent-Teacher Association has spearheaded greater outreach”), while circle entries contain little comparable program detail or list far fewer high‑level extracurricular successes.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse campus safet: Many square reviews document frequent fights, assaults, bullying, drug/alcohol problems, bomb scares and staff/office failures to enforce consequences (examples: “fights every other day,” “bullying is common,” “students bring large amounts of drugs,” and alleged officer misconduct), contrasted with circle reviews which either omit such severe safety incidents or describe administrative interventions (restorative justice) rather than chronic violence or neglect.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviews show repeated leadership turnover, lost records, poor parent communication, punitive responses to advocacy, selective discipline, and explicit funding or resource misallocation claims (examples: “Katella averages a new principal every two years,” “8 MONTHS to notify us,” “preferential treatment for athletes,” and “high funding for buildings, low funding for textbooks”), whereas circle reviews contain fewer or less severe accounts of such systemic administrative mismanagement.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal greater inequities: Reviews of square schools frequently allege athlete‑first cultures and grade/favoritism advantages, alongside neglect or exclusion of economically disadvantaged, special‑education, newcomer or non‑local students (examples: “If you don't play sports you don't really matter,” “Special Ed students have to clean up trash,” “students who commute from Juarez are harassed,” and warnings that disadvantaged students feel uncomfortable), while circle reviews do not present this pattern of systemic exclusion or targeted inequitable treatment.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket captures reviews that list named AP/IB/Honors/STEM/dual‑enrollment/academy programs and cite measurable outcomes (AP pass rates, ACT/ACT scores, scholarship offers, Ivy/elite acceptances, transferable college credits); examples include long AP lists, PACE/CIC/AVID/CTE pathways, 'multiple scholarship offers,' and detailed dual‑enrollment credit counts—features that circle reviews generally lack or describe only vaguely.
candidate_defs.square entries report a worse student sa: This bucket groups accounts of frequent or severe safety incidents (weekly fights, armed student threats, gang mentality, pervasive drug/vaping use, self‑harm) and reviewers' claims that bullying and harassment go unpunished or are selectively enforced—e.g., 'bullying problem is for real,' 'drugs are everywhere,' and 'bullying rules only apply when they want'—where Circle reviews tend not to report comparable violence or failed responses.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Reviews in this bucket allege ineffective or punitive administration, protected/underperforming teachers, front‑office rudeness, district‑level turnover or corruption, and the need to contact superintendents/state panels to resolve issues—examples include 'administration acted ineffectively and, at times, cruelly,' 'caught them red‑handed and was let go,' and 'you have to call over & over or contact the superintendent.'
candidate_defs.square entries report broader curricular: This bucket covers reviews that enumerate many clubs, award‑winning performing arts, vocational/trade programs, career pathways and structured small‑school academies—e.g., 'a million groups/clubs,' 'North Valley Arts,' 'vocational programs are first rate,' and strong show‑choir/choir trophies—while circle reviews typically list few or no comparable extracurricular or pathway offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: This bucket groups evidence of physical‑plant and operational strain—overcrowded classrooms and buses, decaying buildings and pest infestations, unsanitary conditions, budget‑driven program cuts, hazardous busing and logistics, and mismanaged events—examples include 'portables caved in from cockroaches,' '30 per teacher,' 'major underfunding,' and 'dangerous buses.'
candidate_defs.Square entries document stronger advance: These reviews describe concrete curriculum depth and outcomes at square schools—many named AP/IB offerings, college‑credit pathways, high AP counts, IB candidacy, AP/IB exam and SAT success, scholarship totals, and alumni matriculation to selective colleges—while circle reviews rarely list comparable AP/IB breadth or specific postsecondary metrics (examples: “over 25 AP courses,” full IB programme, students earning a year of college credit, $4M in scholarships vs. circle’s generic ‘advanced courses’).
candidate_defs.Square entries report worse safety, bull: Square reviews repeatedly document violent fights, bomb/gun threats, drugs, sexual assault mishandling, hate graffiti, pervasive bullying, teacher/coach favoritism, and claims that administration fails to protect victims or even punishes them, whereas circle reviews largely lack these specific safety crises and often emphasize low bullying or caring staff (examples: “beaten by students,” “lots of drugs,” “Nazi graffiti,” and “they don’t do ANYTHING about S/A cases” vs. circle’s ‘very little teasing or bullying’).
candidate_defs.Square entries show more frequent admini: These items report concrete operational dysfunction at square schools—unreturned parent e‑mails, scheduling/assignment errors that jeopardize graduation, counselor overload or incompetence, poor course catalog/registration processes, high teacher turnover, and district hiring/retention problems—while circle reviews rarely describe chronic admin/process failure and often note stable or responsive staff (examples: “they can’t even answer their e‑mail,” “13 teachers in one year,” counselors causing missed graduation credits).
candidate_defs.Square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square reviews frequently enumerate large, diverse extracurricular portfolios (bands, theater, JROTC, vocational courses, many sports) and visible capital spending or booster funding for facilities (new turf, stadiums), often coupled with complaints that athletics/facility projects are prioritized over instructional materials or equitable access; circle reviews emphasize limited sports or volunteer-run music and do not report similar booster investments (examples: ‘80% student participation, nationally‑recognized band, $400k turf’ vs. circle’s ‘no music programs established’).
candidate_defs.Square entries report more severe overcr: Many square reviews cite concrete physical and capacity problems—extreme enrollment, modular classrooms, lack of desks, narrow halls, filthy restrooms, vermin/asbestos/odors, and COVID‑space concerns—while circle reviews rarely raise these facility or health‑hazard issues and sometimes describe well‑maintained buildings (examples: “2700+ students, 8 modular buildings,” “mice and cockroaches,” “asbestos in the building,” “bathrooms closed after vandalism”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe far more concret: These reviews name specific rigorous pathways and student-support programs (AP/IB/Honors, dual‑credit, Early College, GT tracks), formal college-guidance counseling, and documented IEP/504 implementation (both good and problematic examples), whereas circle reviews rarely list program inventories or structured college/special-ed supports; e.g., square cites wide AP lists, dual-credit/college-credit participation, a dedicated freshman counselor mapping four‑year plans, and explicit IEP/Gifted‑Track reports that Circle does not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews repeatedly document fights, weapon/drug activity, police calls, physical assaults, sexual/teacher misconduct, student-on-student and staff-on-student bullying, and claims that complaints are ignored—i.e., a pervasive safety/climate problem and ineffective protection; Circle reviews do not present this scale of violent/drug/bullying incidents (they focus on social drama or isolated discipline issues instead).
candidate_defs.square entries document a broader, bette: Square reviewers enumerate many clubs, competitive teams, award‑winning music/theater programs, strong athletics, and major community capital projects (PACs, new buildings, multimillion-dollar renovations, large fundraisers), signaling richer extracurricular breadth and visible investment; Circle reviews seldom list comparable program variety, awards, or large community-funded facility projects.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more detailed all: Square reviews commonly call out concrete governance issues—administrative favoritism (athlete/donor/staff-family advantages), micromanagement, opaque or unethical decisions, accreditation threats, legal threats, and explicit policy choices (strict/no‑tolerance codes tied to suspensions)—whereas Circle reviews rarely provide this level of operational/governance detail and instead offer general complaints about leadership or morale.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviews give specific operational evidence—high/uneven class sizes, crowded hallways, portables, dusty/decaying rooms, food‑safety incidents, buggy computers or Smartboard/WiFi rollouts, faulty lunch/pay systems, tardy/attendance policy impacts and device distribution problems—while Circle reviews do not present this rich set of daily logistical details.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports that the school experiences pervasive unsafe student behavior (e.g., drug sales, gang activity, daily fights/riots, vaping epidemic, sexual harassment/coercion, theft, overdoses) and consequences to student mental health; many square reviews also describe victims’ harm. Examples: “constantly dealing with drug sales, fights… averaging 2 to 3 or arrest a day,” “sexually harass you,” “vaping epidemic,” and reports of anxiety, self‑harm ideation after bullying—none of which circle reviews document.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, formal: This bucket groups claims of extensive curricular and co‑curricular offerings and measurable outcomes—AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, career certifications, internships, dozens of clubs, travel and award-winning arts/teams, and scholarship/college‑credit evidence. Illustrative square evidence: “almost 30 different programs… direct route to employment,” “IB program… proven track record,” “over 40 clubs,” and graduates with college credits/scholarships—whereas circle rarely lists this programmatic breadth or concrete college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report a sports‑/athletic: This bucket covers square reviews that say athletics are culturally central and materially prioritized—big stadium/field investments, coach‑centric staff, athlete favoritism, and arts cuts in favor of sports. Example claims: “This school worships their football players,” “new football field (over $1M),” “arts programs cut bit by bit each year while the sports budget rises,” and high community turnout at Friday night games, contrasts absent from circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report systemic administr: This bucket captures structural leadership and personnel problems that reviewers tie to poor student outcomes and family distrust—overloaded/unhelpful counselors, wrong advice that endangers graduation, scheduling chaos, alleged cover‑ups of teacher misconduct, nepotistic hiring, and punitive or inconsistent discipline policies. Examples: “guidance counselors… not helpful… wrong information 3 times,” “lost assignments and principal covered up misconduct,” “170 teachers leaving,” and “administration is as unprofessional as they come.”
candidate_defs.square entries report worse facilities,: This bucket contains concrete physical‑plant and operational complaints: aging or outdated buildings, mold and health complaints, fire‑code‑level lunch overcrowding, mass bussing/overcrowding, dangerous pick‑up/drop‑off traffic, and renovation disruptions. Representative square items: “walking through the hallways, all you can smell is mold,” “many cases of severe over crowding during lunch,” “4,200 students… overcrowded,” and “pick up drop off needs improvement,” which circle reviews do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more severe an: This bucket captures concrete safety and behavior problems (fights, bullying, gangs, in-school drug dealing, weapons/lockdowns, sexual assaults, suicides, repeated thefts) that reviewers attribute to lax enforcement or ineffective supervision — e.g., ‘guns on campus… nearly all day lockdowns,’ ‘drug dealers in every grade,’ ‘2 suicides in past couple of years,’ and ‘bullying allowed with no help from administration.’ Circle entries largely lack these kinds of repeated, severe safety incidents and instead describe inclusion or isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: This groups items naming IB/AP/dual‑enrollment, magnet and career-technical programs, robust arts/band/theatre, measurable college outcomes and scholarships, together with reviewer claims about whether teachers prepare students for those programs (positive or negative). Example evidence: ‘IB, AP, dual-enrollment, full tuition scholarships,’ ‘1:1 Apple laptop program,’ and the counterpoint ‘AP teachers didn’t prepare us for the tests’ — while Circle reviews rarely list such named advanced programs, college‑credit pathways, or concrete scholarship/matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report substantially more: This captures the cluster of parental reports about delayed diagnoses, having to fight for 504s/IEPs, IEP noncompliance or changed notes, segregation of special‑needs students, shaming by staff, as well as separate accounts of excellent IEP support and successful inclusion — e.g., ‘it took 6 years to realize he had a learning disability,’ ‘they do not enforce the IEP,’ and contrastingly ‘inclusion worked; honor roll now.’ Circle entries rarely discuss formal special‑education processes at all.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more systemic admi: This bucket groups governance and personnel practices: grade‑tampering, nepotism/favoritism (athletes or staff relatives), rehiring of accused staff, failure to return calls, public cover‑ups, punitive or abusive deans, forced retirements/layoffs, and district‑level politicization or fiscal mismanagement — examples include ‘VP changing grades,’ ‘welcomed back without warning [a teacher who touched my daughter],’ ‘they do not return phone calls,’ and ‘forced a number of good teachers into early retirement.’ Circle reviews may note administrative problems but do not allege this breadth or severity of systemic misconduct.
candidate_defs.square entries report wider and more ext: This captures concrete building/operations evidence (deferred maintenance, filthy/ freezing bathrooms/classrooms, HVAC failures, renovations, overcrowding, parking/evacuation chokepoints, scheduling/calendar disruptions, supply shortages) plus contested funding choices (spending on athletics vs textbooks, renovations vs basics) and visible tech/CTE investments — e.g., ‘bathrooms super dirty,’ ‘pool in desperate need of refurbishing,’ ‘over 2000 students / short class time,’ ‘reconstructing the gym,’ and ‘money spent on football not textbooks.’ Circle entries rarely report this same mix of chronic maintenance/logistics problems or contested resource allocation.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more severe stud: This bucket captures reports of active safety/behavior problems and ineffective protective responses in square reviews — e.g., repeated fights, stabbings, sexual assault, gang presence, pervasive drug/alcohol use, suicidality, and allegations that administrators failed to investigate or discipline ("a student was stabbed in the hallway", "sexual assault…admins did not respond", "drugs are an enormous issue"). Circle entries either omit these severe incidents or describe milder, isolated peer cruelty and organized safety training instead.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher-: This groups items where square reviews list concrete, high‑level offerings and competitive outcomes (IB, many APs, dual‑enrollment, magnet tracks, strong STEM/CTE, award‑winning band/Academic Decathlon, state championships, many clubs and travel teams — e.g. "IB and Dual‑Enrollment," "11 state championships," "many AP classes and awards"), while circle reviews generally lack comparable evidence of sustained advanced programs or competitive success.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects critiques of selective treatment and gatekeeping in square reviews — e.g., favoritism tied to donations or connections, athletes or wealthy students getting grade/discipline leniency or lead roles, coaches blocking opportunities, and unfair program/admissions placement ("It's all about who you know," "Athletes get their grades inflated," "lead roles reserved for children of the elite"). Circle reviews do not make the same, repeated claims of systemic elitism or access manipulation.

This covers operational leadership failures and communication breakdowns described in square reviews — examples include ignored parent emails, unresponsive counselors and front office staff, failure to follow IEPs or provide promised evaluations, board/leadership dysfunction, and parents kept uninformed about major incidents ("emailed teacher with no response... counselors were extremely unhelpful", "had to get an advocate…we filed a Title IX"). Circle reviews generally contain fewer or no such governance/communication failure narratives and often note responsive teachers/staff instead.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extreme facil: This bucket captures concrete facility and resource claims in square reviews, from positive capital investments and 1:1 tech rollouts to stark deficits — renovated/new buildings and athletic facilities or district laptop programs alongside overcrowded classrooms, broken HVAC/bathrooms, pest infestations, bus problems, limited special‑ed slots, and scheduling/grade‑posting issues ("new school and facilities are top notch", "cockroaches in the cafeteria", "buses are always late and/or double loaded", "they run out of slots for those students"). candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: This bucket captures concrete program breadth and measurable outcomes—AP/IB participation, PLTW/engineering pathways, dual‑enrollment/CTE certificates, high AP test and college‑placement claims, and explicit alumni success—reported in square entries but absent or weaker in circle.
