candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups structural governance problems and biased leadership behaviors: frequent principal turnover, selective discipline and athletic favoritism, administrative lying or deceptive responses, lost records and enrollment/credit mishandling, and defensive or uncooperative communications. Examples: '7 principals over 4 years,' 'athletes get grades inflated,' 'the principal lied to save district money,' and 'lost transfer paperwork / threatened to take her credits,' contrasted with Circle's fewer such governance accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: This bucket covers physical‑plant and operational evidence—overcrowding and hallway/cafeteria strain, health/pest hazards (mold, rats, asbestos), cafeteria food complaints, late buses/traffic, plus named modernizations (new wings, smartboards, Wi‑Fi) and contentious tech rollouts. Examples: 'building ninety years old... smelled mold/roaches,' '3000 students; overcrowded halls,' 'Smartboards in every classroom and whole campus has WiFi' versus Circle's lack of comparable facility/resourcing detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit stud: This bucket groups mentions of counseling, SEL programs, tutoring and academic supports, special‑education accommodations, and also reported mental‑health outcomes and guidance failures—i.e., square reviews more often name programs (after‑school tutoring, Safe Schools Healthy Students mental‑health therapists, AVID/Puente, college/career centers) and specific counseling successes or breakdowns (outstanding counselors vs. ineffective guidance and suicide response problems). Examples: 'free after school tutoring... mental health is valued,' alongside 'guidance counselors are ineffective... administration minimized response after a student suicide,' which Circle rarely documents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket groups reviews that detail concrete program breadth (AP/IB/TAG, large AP catalogs, IBCapstone, STEM pathways, concurrent/dual enrollment, career/tech credentials) and quantified postsecondary results (ACT/SAT scores, scholarship totals, college acceptances, students graduating with associate credits)—features repeatedly cited for square but absent or unquantified in circle (examples: AP/IB programs, ‘‘1 to 1’’ tech rollouts, concurrent enrollment leading to an associate degree, seven‑million dollar scholarship class vs. circle’s lack of outcome metrics and low AP pass rates).
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: This bucket captures classroom‑level evidence about teaching practice—square reviews simultaneously contain many accounts of teachers who ‘go above and beyond’ (late help, volunteer coaching, named effective instructors) and many accounts of inconsistent/poor delivery (outdated textbooks, missed lessons, substitutes, grading inconsistency, students forced to self‑teach), whereas circle reviews lack the same mix of concrete teacher support plus variable delivery. Examples include parents praising late-night homework help alongside complaints about 'no books' or teachers not covering material.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: This groups reports of extensive extracurricular breadth and recognized arts/athletic achievement—strong band/music cultures, marching‑band/state/national awards, plentiful clubs, vocational shop/auto programs, and high school spirit—attributes emphasized in square reviews but largely missing or described as small/weak in circle (examples: 'THE BAND IS ALL THAT MATTERS', state‑level music/performing arts center, many clubs and vocational pathways).
candidate_defs.square entries report worse student safe: This bucket covers recurring reports of safety and behavioral problems at the student‑level—frequent fights, lockdowns, weapons/drug incidents, severe bullying/harassment, sexualized misconduct, and either lax enforcement or overly punitive/arbitrary discipline (delayed punishments, excessive suspensions, unlawful phone searches)—whereas circle reviews tend to describe better‑managed or family‑like climates and lack these specific safety crises. Examples include lockdowns for a student with a gun, daily fights, and allegations of staff failing to stop bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries evidence more administrat: This bucket groups operational and governance failures described in square reviews—unreturned parent communications, withheld incident documentation, superintendent/district favoritism, residency surveillance, selective resource allocation to athletics/wealthy students, poor special‑education services and counsel/IEP mismanagement—contrasted with circle reviews that more often describe engaged, accessible leadership and clearer parent channels. Illustrative examples: repeated unanswered calls, withheld transcripts, staff favoring richer kids/athletes, and reviewers advising hiring a lawyer for special‑needs services.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures hard safety incidents and on‑site misbehavior that reviewers attribute to the school (e.g., “lots of fights,” gang presence, stabbings, students having sex on campus, vaping/drug use, multiple suicides) plus evidence that security or staff are slow to intervene or punish (e.g., random searches, slow breaking up of fights, bullied students suspended while aggressors are not). Circle reviews rarely describe these kinds of chronic, severe safety events.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe stronger and bro: This bucket groups concrete curricular strength and outcomes: many Square reviews name AP/IB/Honors, Cambridge/Early College magnets, dual‑credit, specialized research academies and cite college acceptances or large scholarship totals, whereas Circle reviews lack sustained AP/IB offerings and describe weaker long‑term academic preparation.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more numerous, hig: This covers program breadth and public successes — Square reviewers repeatedly praise championship athletics, top‑tier band and theater, strong CTE/technical offerings and community fundraising/parent boosters; Circle reviews generally omit or report weak extracurricular/arts achievement.
candidate_defs.Square entries discuss counseling, speci: This bucket captures concrete student‑support services and their outcomes: Square reviewers frequently reference on‑site counselors, IEP teams, life‑skills classrooms, newcomer counseling and either praise (responsive counselors, good IEP teams) or document failures (denied accommodations, inadequate life‑skills supports, mishandled special‑needs cases); Circle reviews contain little to no comparable detail about special‑education or counseling services.
candidate_defs.Square entries contain more evidence of: This bucket groups management and governance issues: Square reviews allege nepotism, principal bullying, inconsistent/punitive discipline (e.g., extreme tardy/truancy enforcement), frequent teacher turnover or long‑term subs, misuse/prioritization of funds (stadiums over classrooms), and opaque grading/transfer decisions; Circle reviews do not show the same pattern of institutional misgovernance.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student: This bucket covers reviews that describe pervasive student‑safety failures (bullying, fights, sexual assault, guns), substance and gang activity, and inadequate supervision or counselor response—e.g., reports of 'many fights,' 'a gun found...in a backpack,' 'drug issues,' severe bullying that caused trauma or withdrawal, and claims counselors/teachers 'did nothing.' Circle entries generally contain no comparable catalog of violent incidents or systemic supervision failures, so material about acute safety, weapon/drug/gang presence, and related trauma belongs here.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader and stro: This bucket groups reviews that list concrete advanced‑course and career pathways (IB, numerous AP courses, dual enrollment, PLTW/CTE tech wings) and named college outcomes—e.g., 'IB program,' '25 AP courses,' 'students got into Yale/HYPSM,' 'Project Lead the Way with college credit.' These are program‑level, curriculum and outcome claims (advanced courses, transcripted credit, college placement, vocational labs); circle entries generally lack similarly specific, high‑level academic program evidence and outcomes, so those comparative program strengths fall in this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more inconsistent: This bucket captures claims about highly variable or politicized adults in the building—examples include principal favoritism and nepotism ('rules do not apply to all'), accusations of bribery/overpaid executives, protected/underperforming teachers, punitive retaliation for complaints, and contradictory reports of both strong and 'incredibly punitive' leadership. These are governance/discipline/HR patterns distinct from student conduct or curriculum; circle entries typically show steadier, less politicized staff behavior and do not contain the same mix of corruption, favoritism, and turnover allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: This bucket groups substantive claims about extracurricular breadth, athletic prominence, booster/PTA activity, and visible facility/funding tradeoffs—e.g., 'sports complex is top notch,' 'many clubs,' marching band/theatre trophies, athletic scholarships, but also complaints that 'money goes to football while band instruments fall apart' or 'old buildings need renovation.' These are concrete programmatic and capital/resource patterns (what activities exist, facility quality, fundraising priorities) that circle reviews largely do not document at the same scale.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight greater inequal: This bucket contains reviews describing unequal access and contested equity—examples include explicit discrimination and exclusion of marginalized students, unmet or litigated IEP/IEP noncompliance, both praise and warnings about special‑needs supports, parents 'renting a place' or choice‑in enrollment, and claims that wealthy/connected families monopolize opportunities. These are systemic equity/access patterns (who can access programs, who is served or pushed out) distinct from staff incompetence or curricular richness, and they appear far more often in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger advanced: These schools describe concrete AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/STEM pathways, measurable college outcomes, and counselor/credit systems (e.g., 'many AP classes', 'IB program', 'dual credit', 'students regularly gain acceptances to top tier universities', 'I graduated with 18 college credits'), while circle entries lack comparable programmatic depth or explicit college‑matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews name frequent fights, on‑campus drug problems, bomb/weapon searches, victim‑blaming, and law‑enforcement style interventions (e.g., 'bomb squad search', 'loaded handgun', 'there are physical fights here daily', 'supports bullying, punishes victims', 'k‑9 teams search lockers'), whereas circle entries either omit such severe safety claims or describe bullying/fights as less frequent and better handled.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, award‑w: Square schools list dozens of clubs, championship athletics, nationally recognized band/theater/journalism and competitive STEM/arts teams (e.g., 'Mock Trial and Robotics have won state and national awards', 'band ranked third best in US', 'state championships', 'over 100 student clubs'), while circle entries rarely enumerate comparable competitive extracurricular breadth or awards.
candidate_defs.square entries show more administrative: These reviews point to leadership turnover, unresponsiveness, chronic phone/email failures, district budget cuts or athletic‑first spending, and examples of favoritism or scandals (e.g., 'Principle and dean support her and not the students', 'several consecutive rounds of cuts', 'money spent on football and baseball', 'preference given to children of town favorites', 'retire‑rehire scandals'), whereas circle entries generally lack sustained claims of such governance, financial scandal, or chronic communication breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit high within‑schoo: Square reviews repeatedly contrast pockets of rigorous, high‑achieving tracks with watered‑down or weak general tracks and variable teachers (e.g., 'a few students headed for Princeton and a few headed for prison', 'hard teachers and easy teachers for the same AP subject', 'IB/AP strong but much of the work is dumbed down'), producing starkly different student experiences that circle entries do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: This bucket captures claims that the school offers coherent, high‑end curricular tracks and measurable college outcomes — e.g., multiple AP/IB/Academy programs, Governor’s School or magnet tracks, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit courses, AVID, and concrete outcomes like high SAT averages, scholarship totals, or Ivy/elite placements (examples: “25 AP courses,” “IB program sets it apart,” “highest SAT average in Maine,” “$4.1 million in scholarships”). Content in this bucket emphasizes program breadth/depth and documented postsecondary preparation that circle entries do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that allege frequent fights, gang activity, drug and alcohol use, sexual harassment/assault, and chronic bullying — paired with claims that staff/administration fail to protect victims or enforce discipline (examples: “violent fights, drug use in the bathrooms,” “sexually harassed… wanted to commit suicide,” “reported it time and again but evidently there is no zero tolerance,” “lock‑down due to gunfire”). These items document school safety climate and adult nonresponse as central operational problems.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff and lea: This bucket captures allegations about adults’ behavior and governance: abusive/degrading teachers or deans, routine favoritism (athlete/legacy bias), punitive policies (forced transfers, online surveillance punishments), poor parent/teacher communication, opaque or corrupt administration, and high staff turnover (examples: “dean slapped… threatened expulsion,” “favoritism runs rampant,” “very poor communications with parents,” “teacher turnover rate over 30%”). These items focus on personnel conduct and leadership accountability distinct from curriculum or facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, concret: This bucket groups reviews that list specific, functioning out‑of‑class offerings and external ties — award‑winning band/arts programs, many clubs and sports, vocational shops and labs, formal college partnerships/articulation, active booster/PTA fundraising and alumni support (examples: “band program… 24 state championships,” “metalworking, electrical or woodworking… UCONN classes are offered,” “raised $129,217 for local families,” “parent Booster organization”). These items describe tangible extracurricular and community resources that circle entries rarely enumerate.
candidate_defs.square entries report more tangible oper: This bucket includes concrete physical and policy features: overcrowding and space constraints, block scheduling and transfer/credit loss, separate ninth‑grade campuses affecting ratings, metal detectors/security measures, cafeteria/sanitation complaints, and district policy changes (e.g., cancelling advanced classes or removing class‑rank/physics grad requirement) — examples: “extremely overcrowded,” “4x4 system…crammed into 18 weeks,” “Joshua Ninth Grade Campus should be included,” “metal detectors at HAHS,” “they stopped reporting class standings to colleges.” These are operational/structural realities distinct from staff behavior, safety incidents, curricular quality, or extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries document far broader, nam: This captures reviews that list concrete program breadth and accomplishments (AP/IB/AICE, dual‑enrollment/PSEO, STEM/CTE academies, award‑winning band/theatre, state championships, scholarships and elite college matriculations) — e.g., Square: “IB Program,” “8 National Merit Scholarship winners,” “students to MIT/UCLA/Harvard,” “Carnegie Hall”; Circle generally makes generic claims about rigor or lacks comparable named programs or quantified outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: This groups safety and conduct evidence: repeated fights, gang affiliation, pervasive drug use, weapons/armed‑student incidents, sexual harassment, police/armed‑guard involvement, and reviewer claims that staff often ignore or mishandle these problems — e.g., Square: “2–4 fights a week,” “AR‑15 brought to school,” “drug users in every bathroom”; Circle’s accounts focus on isolated bullying or social exclusion without the same scale/severity.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater administ: This covers governance and policy-level complaints (poorly run initiatives, principal/board criticism, favoritism toward athletes/alumni/coaches, nepotistic hiring, arbitrary or punitive discipline/attendance policies, and alleged budget misuse) — e.g., Square: “Small Schools initiative horribly mis‑managed,” “principal favorites teachers/athletes,” “waste of district money”; Circle rarely levels the same breadth of governance or fiscal critiques.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical pla: This groups concrete facility and capacity evidence: dirty/outdated buildings, broken HVAC, overcrowded classes and lunch transitions, parking/logistics issues and classroom acoustics — e.g., Square: “extremely dirty,” “classes are overcrowded,” “A/C constantly broken,” “insanely hard to get into parking lot”; Circle generally omits or reports fewer facility/capacity complaints (and sometimes reports different, smaller facility details).
candidate_defs.square entries provide more explicit, na: This covers concrete student‑support practices — credit recovery, retake/"learning to proficiency" policies, dual‑enrollment access, documented special‑education or IEP actions (including cuts or denials), remote‑learning provisions, counseling caseloads and college/career centers — e.g., Square: “Credit Recovery,” “retake policy,” “dual enrollment with Ohio Northern,” “very helpful for remote learning,” and also detailed counselor failures; Circle rarely names such concrete support programs or case‑level accommodations.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more frequent: This bucket captures reports of fights/assaults, stabbings, police on campus, widespread vaping and drug sales, chronic bullying, and claims that victims are punished or investigations fail (e.g., 'stabbing, a fire,' 'police in the halls,' 'Vape epidemic they can’t control,' 'If your child is attacked…both will be punished,' and 'my child was attacked…the principal failed to clearly view the video'). It groups raw terms about the prevalence, severity, and schoolwide disciplinary climate (including sensational misconduct and failures to protect students).
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: This bucket groups concrete programmatic and outcome evidence such as AP/IB/dual-credit/Calc III offerings, STEM and specialized academies, high SAT/ACT/AP results, Newsweek/award rankings, and alumni college placements (examples: '30+ AP courses', 'IB program…many accepted into top universities', 'AP and dual credit…shave a year off a college degree', 'Newsweek…one of the best high schools'). It captures claims about institutional rigor, advanced-course availability, and measurable postsecondary outcomes that are present in many square reviews but absent or weaker in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive (an: This bucket covers reviewers' concrete statements about physical resources, campus logistics, and extracurricular breadth—both positive (state-of-the-art gyms, multipurpose stadiums, marching band/state championships, robust JROTC/robotics programs, new construction) and negative (overcrowding, confusing layout, pest infestations, unsanitary bathrooms, traffic/entrance bottlenecks, poor food). Examples include 'multi-purpose stadium with lights,' '11 state championships,' 'cockroaches and mice,' '2,000 plus students…crammed school,' and 'building is state-of-the-art.' It groups operational/facility conditions together with the scale and competitiveness of after-school programs and facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete st: This bucket groups evidence about how staff and leaders communicate and support families/students—examples include proactive parent outreach and digital portals ('principal holds regular coffee meetings', 'Automated updates through email', 'log onto the system'), structured supports (PBIS, FLEX, AVID, dedicated college counselors, tutoring/after-school programs), but also administrative failures (missed scholarship/IEP deadlines, turnover, hiring/training complaints). It captures the many square reports that name specific supports or specific administrative dysfunction beyond generic praise/critique.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic favo: This bucket groups allegations of entrenched preferential treatment and discriminatory climates—athlete/elite favoritism, socioeconomic two‑class dynamics, racial slurs and microaggressions, religious/political hostility, and homophobia (examples: 'This school is about their sports…anyone else will be pushed through the cracks', 'every day i go to school and someone’s saying the n word', 'two class system', 'extreme amounts of religious and political bias'). It captures social stratification and equity complaints that are described as systemic in many square reviews but are absent or far weaker in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews repeatedly name IB/AVID/AP/magnet/dual‑enrollment/Early College pathways, high AP pass rates and concrete post‑secondary outcomes (e.g., “IB program…dual enrollment…can graduate your student as a sophomore in college,” “three magnets…highest AP pass rates,” “Early College…get two years of college”), while Circle reviews rarely list such sustained, school‑level academic pathways and measurable college‑prep evidence. This bucket groups program breadth (AP/IB/CTE/magnets), documented academic outcomes, and instructional rigor/weed‑out practices described as school policy or programmatic reality.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more safety incide: Many Square reviews describe fights, daily drug deals, bomb threats, police armed responses, systemic bullying (including race‑based harassment), wealth‑based cliques, and wide mental‑health concerns (e.g., “Drugs are a HUGE problem…multiple drug deals, fights…bullying, racism…police come in armed response”), whereas Circle reviews lack these recurring safety and toxic‑culture allegations. This bucket captures on‑campus safety events plus the peer‑culture problems and staff inaction that reviewers tie to student well‑being and school climate.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers repeatedly recount unresponsive or disorganized offices, failing recordkeeping/transcript problems, counselor nonresponsiveness or huge caseloads, special‑education legal noncompliance, and inconsistent or punitive policy enforcement (e.g., “they refused transcripts…took forever to speak to someone…guidance counselors were pathetic…School doesn't follow the law when it comes to special needs,” and rigid tardy/ISS rules), while Circle reviews contain far fewer such concrete procedural breakdowns. This bucket groups operational governance, complaint resolution, guidance/counseling support, and formal policy implementation issues.
candidate_defs.Square entries emphasize broader, longst: Square reviews enumerate many sustained extracurriculars (marching band, award‑winning music, AFJROTC, FFA, debate, extensive sports) and also document active parental fundraising and contested resource allocation (e.g., “a million for turf…curriculum suffers,” “one of the BEST in Wrestling, Lacrosse, Football”), including accusations of athletic favoritism and grade‑skewing for athletes; Circle reviews rarely show the same breadth or the same athletics‑centered funding/ favoritism dynamics. This bucket groups programmatic extracurricular scale, community fundraising/priority decisions, and sport‑centered favoritism or political dynamics.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more facility/ca: Square reviews frequently cite severe overcrowding, class sizes of 30+, trailers, long lunch lines, locker shortages, scheduling/block‑schedule problems, poorly designed new buildings or recent renovations that still cause space deficits, and tech/connectivity complaints (and occasionally 1:1 laptop programs) — e.g., “hallways are crowded…no lockers…lunchroom runs out of food…THE WIFI IS TERRIBLE…new building…too small, poorly designed” — while Circle reviews do not repeatedly report these operational capacity or daily logistics failures. This bucket covers physical capacity, food/service logistics, scheduling structures, campus design, and schoolwide tech/connectivity realities.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews report concrete, school‑level academic infrastructure and outcomes (AP/Pre‑AP/IB/Cambridge, dual‑enrollment, magnet/specialty centers, documented AP pass rates, high graduation/college‑placement percentages and named university acceptances) that circle reviews do not provide; examples include explicit IB/IB magnet praise, abundant AP/dual‑credit listings, claims of 97–98% graduation and Ivy/competitive college admits, and district AP funding supports absent from circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews recount fights, assaults, drug use, sexual harassment, gangs, vandalism and outsider security breaches plus either inadequate staff responses or highly punitive/performative enforcement (e.g., ignored assaults, police/security presence, excessive detentions, bag checks/’prison feel’), whereas circle reviews consistently describe a safer, better‑managed student climate.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pervasive s: Square reviewers cite problems across personnel and leadership—tenure‑protected poor teachers, favoritism toward select programs or athletes, rude/unresponsive front offices, repeated guidance/scheduling/records failures, IEP/special‑needs mishandling, leadership instability and mass teacher exoduses—while circle reviews report more consistent, accessible or committed staff.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and high: Square reviews enumerate many specific, recognized out‑of‑class programs (award‑winning band/theatre/forensics, national/international trips and performances, robotics/aviation/ROTC, numerous clubs, competitive sports championships and vocational/technical tracks) that circle reviews seldom specify, highlighting richer extracurricular breadth and prestige in square schools.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater facility,: Square reviewers repeatedly document physical and resource contrasts—severe overcrowding and portable classrooms, broken or unsanitary facilities and food violations, lack of AC, or conversely recent high‑cost renovations and new athletic facilities—and note uneven budgeting priorities (e.g., expensive athletic upgrades vs. outdated textbooks), conditions not reported in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and stro: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and academic pathways (IB/AP/GATE/academies, ~100+ clubs, award‑winning band/theatre, CCT magnet tracks, internships, college credit via CCP/CLEP) and specific outcomes (AP scores, named college acceptances, dual‑credit associates) that Circle reviews do not recount; examples include 'numerous (about 100) different student clubs,' 'outstanding IB, AP, and arts programs,' and an international trip to France organized by a foreign‑language teacher.
candidate_defs.square entries report more bullying, vio: Many Square reviews recount severe safety incidents and ongoing misconduct plus weak or inconsistent remedies (stabbings, guns, arson/trash‑can fire, in‑class dealers/high students, student sexual assault) and describe administration failing to protect victims or follow up; representative lines include 'trash can fire, fights, a stabbing, and a gun problem,' 'Now, drugs run rampant... my son sits next to kids who are high all day,' and 'Teachers do not care... Your child will be bullied.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers frequently describe governance problems—authoritarian or careerist principals, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy donors, blocked parent groups, outdated/absent communications, or repeated managerial reshuffling—evidenced by comments like 'The principal favors specific people, mainly star athletes,' 'the website is RARELY updated,' 'There is still no PTA available or allowed,' and 'she replaced people who disagreed with her notions on management.'
candidate_defs.square entries report worse and more var: Square reviews contain numerous concrete classroom‑level failures—unqualified or ineffective teachers, rote test‑focused instruction, arbitrary/punitive grading and makeup rules, delayed grade posting, and repeated special‑education/IEP breakdowns or poor counseling—for example, 'Most of the teachers can't teach... My job is to get you to pass the SOLs,' 'Teachers wait until the last day of the grading period,' 'If your child is learning disabled... don't even think about it,' and 'my daughter has Mr. Everson as a counselor. He is terrible!'.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extreme facil: Square reviews repeatedly document overcrowding/portables, hygiene and maintenance deficits, and contested budget choices (athletic stadiums vs. arts supplies), alongside occasional major capital projects—e.g., 'primarily portables (102 to be exact),' 'bathrooms... perpetually broken,' 'the arts programs are cut bit by bit... while the sports budget rises,' and also 'starting construction on a pool'—a pattern of pronounced facility/resource variability not described in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete ad: These reviews give specific program names, course lists, and documented postsecondary success (AP/IB, dual‑enrollment, AVID, SAS, G/T, scholarships, Ivy/Stanford/Columbia admits) and therefore signal an internally observable college‑prep infrastructure that Circle reviews lack (examples: “IB and AP courses,” “dual enrollment…Zell Miller scholarship,” “two students granted early admittance to Columbia and Stanford”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many Square reviews document concrete violent or safety incidents (gang fights, stabbings, repeated fire‑alarm evacuations from vaping, students injured), pervasive bullying and substance use, and claim inadequate staff discipline or anti‑bullying follow‑through, whereas Circle reviews lack these recurring high‑severity safety accounts (examples: “There are fights everyday,” “HUGE drug problem,” “plagued with the worst follow‑thru of an anti‑bullying campaign”).
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: Square reviewers repeatedly cite lost transcripts, enrollment/registrar nightmares, having to escalate to superintendents, counselors who miss opportunities or are unavailable, and IEP/504 noncompliance, indicating systemic process and support breakdowns not described in Circle (examples: “They lost my volunteering hours,” “had to contact the superintendent,” “we do NOT follow 504s or IEPs,” “counselors keep 0 track of anything”).
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize athletics/extra: Multiple Square reviews highlight sustained competitive teams, spirited game traditions, heavy financial/administrative support for sports, and explicit claims that athletics are prioritized over academics or other programs — distinct program‑level emphasis that Circle reviews do not report (examples: “sports teams are second to none,” “too much on football,” “much more financial and administrative support that goes towards sports,” large theater/music programs).
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced re: Square reviews frequently describe tangible resource shortages or overcrowding (no books, 35:1 ratios, broken tech), visible contrasts in teacher quality and turnover, and formal two‑tier program separation (IB/elite vs regular), signaling structural inequalities and uneven student experiences that Circle reviewers do not similarly document (examples: “NO BOOKS,” “35 students per 1 instructor,” “If you are in IB, you are basically not even a part of our school,” “most of the staff seems to dislike their jobs”).
candidate_defs.Square entries emphasize stronger advanc: These reviews name concrete program breadth and measurable outcomes—AP/IB availability, academies, dual‑enrollment, CTE/CTE centers, high college matriculation and scholarships—far more often than Circle (e.g., “IB program… meaningful teacher relationships,” “Dual College program with Bunker Hill,” “lots of AP and Honors… top public university”). This bucket captures claims of rigour, accelerated courses, pathway programs and alumni/scholarship evidence that Square reviewers repeatedly report and Circle largely omits.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more severe studen: Square reviews contain frequent allegations of fights, gang activity, drug/alcohol incidents and even sexual assault, threats or suicidality (e.g., “fights almost every week,” “smells like pot… bathrooms,” “I was sexually assaulted… administrators did nothing,” “bomb and gun threats”), whereas Circle reviews contain only much milder or infrequent behavior complaints. Use this bucket for concrete, repeated safety/climate failures and severe student harm described more often in Square than Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more administrat: These items describe governance and enforcement problems—administrators not returning calls, hiding incidents, protecting athletes/feeder‑school/PTO cliques, and uneven or punitive discipline (e.g., “administration is afraid to tighten the screws,” “they sweep things under the rug,” “football players get away with anything”), contrasts that Circle reviews rarely portray. This bucket groups complaints about leadership, communication breakdowns, political or socioeconomic favoritism, and inconsistent or secretive disciplinary practice.
candidate_defs.Square entries highlight broader, higher: Square reviewers frequently praise or document strong performing‑arts and athletic programs, upgraded facilities, external private investment and major co‑curricular opportunities (e.g., “band/top notch theatre… state awards,” “new gym, stadium, theater,” “private sector internships, major scholarships”), while Circle rarely describes such broad/high‑profile extracurricular infrastructure. Use this for tangible facility, arts/athletics program strength and community/district investment described in Square but missing in Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete oper: This covers hands‑on supports and operational policies: before/after‑school tutorials, SAT/Regents prep, work‑based learning, counseling and special‑education inclusion (and conversely, contested grade‑retake or grade‑inflation practices and accommodation enforcement failures) that Square reviews frequently enumerate (e.g., “tutorials… rewrite papers or retake tests,” “transition program for special ed,” versus allegations like “504 accommodations not enforced,” “multiple retakes given so students aren’t allowed to fail”). It groups concrete, programmatic student‑support and assessment/accommodation practices that Square details more than Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger, more ex: This bucket groups raw terms that describe concrete curriculum offerings and tracked outcomes—AP/IB/dual-enrollment/Running Start, STEM and CTE specialties, AP credit counts, honor rolls, university acceptances, and cited test/college statistics—claimed more often in square reviews (e.g., “Provides an incredible array of AP courses,” “IB program… accepted into every University,” “~50% pass rate… 28 AP credits”) while circle reviews rarely list such program breadth or measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pe: This bucket covers descriptions of wide extracurricular breadth, competitive success (state/national wins, scout visibility), strong music/theatre/band programs, active PTSA/booster involvement and alumni support that appear repeatedly in square reviews (e.g., “great marching band,” “sports teams always going to state,” “active PTSA… parents & volunteers”) and are mostly absent or described as diminished in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more frequent an: This groups raw items reporting concrete safety problems—gang members in halls, repeated fights/lockdowns, pervasive drug/alcohol use, documented violent assaults and hate-crime accounts, and reviewers’ claims that administration failed victims (e.g., “racially harassed… brutally assaulted… punished for reporting,” “so many fights, 3 gun lock downs,” “drugs are a HUGE problem”), which are reported far more often in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This bucket captures evidence of space- and logistics-driven dysfunction—overcrowded hallways and classes, high student:teacher ratios, auditorium SAT/ACT testing on lapboards, transit/busing mismanagement, construction disruptions and insufficient classrooms (e.g., “hallways too crowded… arrive late to classes,” “1 teacher to 30 students,” “Do not take SAT/ACT here; given in auditorium on lap boards”), reported repeatedly in square reviews but rarely in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pronounced: This bucket groups allegations about administration and staff practice—nepotism, wealthy‑parent or athlete favoritism, punitive/exclusionary discipline, unresponsiveness or unilateral decision‑making, plus inconsistent teacher quality and special‑education/guidance support (e.g., “nepotism reigns supreme,” “teachers burned out… do not enter grades,” “Guidance is SWAMPED,” “suspend students who can't afford dress code”), showing that square reviews report both strong engaged leaders and frequent opposite failures in administration and student support much more often than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: This bucket groups reports of on-campus violence, fights, gang presence, frequent lockdowns, widespread drug/alcohol/tobacco/vaping use, and claims that bullying and threats are ignored or poorly handled (e.g., “at least 3 bomb threats per year,” “students showing up drunk and high…,” “Horrible problems with bullying no one does anything,” and “lock-down almost every day”), all contrasted with circle reviews that contain no comparable accounts of repeated safety incidents or systemic failure to address them.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket captures concrete program and outcome evidence—extensive AP/IB/Honors offerings, dual-enrollment/college-credit partnerships, and alumni college placements or big scholarship totals (e.g., “huge list of AP classes,” “full IB program,” “graduated and got accepted to 2 Ivy League schools,” and specific AP/college-credit pathways)—whereas circle reviews largely lack such documented advanced-course breadth or measurable college-credit outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher-pr: This groups descriptions of thriving music/arts/band and many clubs alongside administration/team prioritization, athlete favoritism, and user-fees (e.g., “the band program is the best…invited to play in Normandy,” “too much on the football team,” “Sports and marching band are pay to play,” and “Teachers let football players have a pass”), contrasted with circle reviews that do not raise similarly prominent extracurricular strength or institutional favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report overcrowding, agin: This bucket covers physical-plant and logistics problems—severe overcrowding and split campuses, old/dark or infested buildings, mold or cleanliness and HVAC failures, unreliable transportation, cafeteria/fee complaints, and scheduling/substitute shortages (e.g., “very overcrowded…2300 kids,” “infested with bugs and rats,” “buses are never on time,” “no substitute teachers so students go unsupervised”), while circle reviews generally do not document these combined space/facility/logistics breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more leadership in: This bucket groups evidence of frequent principal/administrator turnover, perceived nepotism or mismanagement, overloaded counselors and understaffed special-education support, inconsistent policy follow-through, and district prioritization problems (e.g., “averages a new principal every two years,” “intense level of nepotism…overpaid administrators,” “Counselors…large caseloads,” and “All parents with special education children should avoid this school”), contrasted with circle reviews that do not present the same pattern of governance instability or systemic staffing/IEP failures.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger/more nume: This bucket captures concrete programmatic strength plus the intense, grade/ranking focus described in square reviews — e.g., multiple AP/IB offerings, dual‑enrollment and Early College/AA pathways, specialty magnet/STEM tracks, frequent alumni college placements, and also heavy nightly homework and test‑prep pressure (‘‘lots of AP classes,’’ ‘‘graduate with an AA,’’ ‘‘5+ hours of homework/night,’’ ‘‘teach to the test’’). It groups evidence about course availability, acceleration/credit options, measurable outcomes, and the culture of college‑centrism/test‑score emphasis that square reviewers repeatedly cite (and which circle reviewers largely do not).
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups concrete incidents and enforcement patterns: square reviews report drug problems, overdoses, weapons, suicides, frequent bullying, spectator vandalism, roving mobs and lockdowns, alongside administrators who fail to stop abuse or inconsistently discipline (e.g., athletes/wealthy students getting leniency), whereas circle reviews generally lack comparable safety crises. It covers both the types/severity of student safety harms and the school’s day‑to‑day failure or inconsistency in responding to them.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more visible, ha: This bucket bundles claims about adult leadership and responsiveness: many square reviews praise named principals, engaged superintendents, accessible counselors and teachers who go above‑and‑beyond, or district responsiveness to parents; by contrast circle reviews frequently note no full‑time principal, high turnover, unresponsive front offices, or administrators who 'won't answer the phone' (examples: ‘‘Dr. Richard inspired improvements,’’ versus ‘‘no full time principal…you cannot get her on the phone’’). It covers who runs the school, visibility/stability of leaders, and whether staff/counselors proactively communicate and support families.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader extracur: This bucket groups evidence about physical space, program scale, and how money is used: square reviewers list extensive clubs/sports/music/theater, large marching bands, exchange trips and strong vocational/trade programs, plus parent/teacher donations and affluent community supports, yet also report overcrowding (multiple lunch shifts, long lines), mixed facility maintenance (leaks, mold vs some renovations), and disputed spending priorities (big athletic or bandroom buys instead of textbooks or paving). Circle reviews rarely enumerate comparable program breadth or the same mix of crowding vs high‑end extracurricular investment.
candidate_defs.Square entries reveal stronger evidence: This bucket captures the complex equity picture that square reviewers describe: many square reviews note racial/socioeconomic diversity and opportunities for belonging, while also documenting discriminatory tracking, biased suspensions, nepotism/favoritism (staff/athlete kids favored), exclusion of newcomers, and failures to serve special‑needs learners (e.g., ‘tracking harms students,’ ‘suspended more severely because of the color of his skin,’ ‘staff kids on teams’). Circle reviews generally lack this constellation of both explicit demographic diversity and the policy/practice level inequities that accompany it in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger formal ad: These reviews describe concrete, school-run academic assets (full IB programs, AP offerings with college credit, high state/AP/test rankings, scholarship totals, and alumni college placements) that are repeatedly cited as evidence of college readiness (examples: “full IB program,” “US News ranked them…,” “students finish with several AP college credits,” “over $26 MILLION in scholarships,” and graduates to UNC/Ivies). Circle reviews rarely include equivalent program names, test-score evidence, or longitudinal college-outcome claims and instead offer only general statements about preparation.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and higher: Many square reviews list extensive on‑site CTE and career pathways (cosmetology, carpentry, allied health, CNA/EMT certification), rich arts and travel opportunities, robust band/choir/theatre, and competitive wins (Mock Trial #1, state champions, international travel clubs), plus strong athletics facilities and community sports culture; Circle reviews generally lack this breadth of named programs and high-profile extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews frequently recount fights, weapons/drug searches, sexual assault allegations, systemic bullying, racial harassment and LGBTQ/transphobic climates and describe administration failing to investigate or even blaming victims (examples: daily fights with police present, race wars, slurs left in bleachers, administration ‘did nothing’ or turned off a mic during a speech). Circle reviews, by contrast, more often describe a safer, inclusive environment and staff who intervene or support students.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: Square reviews contain concrete operational complaints—extreme enrollment/overcrowding figures, large class sizes, lost transcripts, asbestos/textbook shortages, inadequate testing computers, bad HVAC/food/parking, and budget-driven program cuts—whereas Circle reviews rarely detail this constellation of campus-level infrastructure and logistic failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, o: Circle reviews repeatedly praise accessible, organized staff (helpful counselors, teachers who ‘want to help you succeed,’ strong communication and parent outreach), and offer examples of staff stepping in for students (band/coach supports, named teachers who ‘stayed with me’), whereas square reviews are far more mixed about staff responsiveness and show many more accounts of unresponsive or inconsistent counseling and parent communication.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe ongoing, severe peer-safety problems—e.g., “Bullying is OBSCENE,” repeated fights, widespread drug/heroin concerns, high suicide/cutter reports—and document leaders denying or failing to address those threats ("Bullying is prevalent and no one does anything"; lockdown drills called a "farce"). Any school text that centers recurring violence, substance availability, or systemic nonresponse falls squarely into this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive f: Square reviewers repeatedly name concrete programs and outcomes—IB, AVID, Math/Science Academy, early‑college/dual‑enrollment, DECA/FBLA, strong AP/college‑credit results, and CTE/CTE job‑readiness—often with quantified successes (AP scores, college credits, prestigious college placements). Use this bucket for reviews that emphasize program breadth, specialized academies, vocational pathways, and measurable college‑prep success.
candidate_defs.square entries report more dysfunctional: These items document operational failures in counseling and school processes—"The majority of counsellors are not helpful," poor college application advising, schedule/registration errors that almost block graduation, transcript/grade mishandling, and device/distribution/attendance policy breakdowns—i.e., procedural issues that directly impede student advancement. Reviews describing counselor unresponsiveness, denied class changes or IEP procedural failures, scheduling mistakes, or broken administrative processes belong here.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater staff vari: This cluster covers personnel behaviors and equity problems: large swings in teacher quality, preferential treatment of athletes/wealthy families, nepotism in parent/PTA influence, explicit racial/ethnic profiling and biased language by staff, and allegations of staff bullying or theft. Use this bucket for evidence about unequal enforcement, staff‑driven exclusion, discrimination, or unethical conduct by teachers/security/administrators.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic resou: Reviews here point to material constraints and physical-site problems—crowded classes/portables, falling‑apart books, broken water/AC issues, filthy/closed bathrooms, lack of bus drivers, tight budgets limiting travel/equipment, and bond‑funding/renovation narratives—that reduce program delivery and daily comfort. Any report emphasizing facility decay, large class sizes tied to funding, or logistical shortages should be classified in this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and bro: This bucket groups raw terms that describe concrete course offerings and results—AP/IB, dual-enrollment (UCONN ECE, community-college credit), specific ACT/SAT prep programs, pathway/major systems, and named college acceptances or credits—e.g., mentions of IB, 20+ APs, SLU 1818, earning 25 college credits, and Ivy/UNC admissions that Circle reviews do not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket captures reports of pervasive bullying, racist/slur use, homophobia/transphobia, drug use, sexual-assault allegations, PTSD from victimization, and repeated failures to remediate—even after law-enforcement confirmation—such as recurring bullying ignored by staff, drug/alcohol on campus, and administrators dismissing felony-level incidents; Circle reviews lack comparable safety/violence claims and often describe a more protective climate.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater administ: This groups complaints about phone/e-mail nonresponse, grade/schedule posting failures, lost paperwork, secretive governance, cover-ups of incidents, retaliation against complainants, rude office staff, and documented leadership turnover or nepotism—examples include no returned calls, three-month refunds only after legal threats, administrators assuring action that never occurred, and reports of school leaders protecting reputation over students; Circle reviews do not contain this concentrated catalog of operational failure and concealment.
candidate_defs.square entries show larger variability i: This bucket covers inconsistent teacher performance (excellent to apathetic), chronic absenteeism/substitute reliance, passive/video-based instruction, lack of tutoring or 504/IEP follow-through, inconsistent grading/favoritism, and neglect of average/struggling students—evidenced by teachers 'teaching <5% of semester,' 'no tutoring,' ignored 504 plans, and clustered high-quality instruction only in AP classes—contrasting with Circle's reports of more uniformly supportive, engaged teachers.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize tangible facili: This bucket groups physical-plant and funding evidence: explicit dilapidation, mold outbreaks causing illness, cockroaches/rat problems, no A/C, consolidation/overcrowded cafeterias, strikes/program cuts, and spending choices favoring athletics over academics (e.g., turf vs. teacher hires); Circle reviews rarely mention such hardware, overcrowding, pest, or contested budget priorities.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger, more co: These reviews repeatedly list specific rigorous academic offerings and outcome metrics for square: AP/Pre‑AP, IB Diploma, dual‑credit, large AP catalogs, high AP/SAT/ACT performance, National Merit counts, and tangible college/counseling help (e.g., “took nine APs,” “90%+ college‑bound rate,” “BC Calculus 4.7 average,” “full‑ride scholarship”), whereas circle reviews typically lack comparable catalogs, metrics, or concrete college‑credit/placement evidence and instead report limited advanced options or weak college preparation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many square reviews describe bullying, daily fights, drugs/weapons, lockdowns, gang activity and administration failing to protect students or alternatively using punitive pushout tactics (e.g., “incessant bullying,” “fights almost every week,” “students bring knives,” “they encourage dropouts”), while circle reviews rarely report this level of physical safety incidents and instead emphasize a safer, more structured culture.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, better‑: Square reviewers name extensive non‑classroom offerings and capital/partner resources—strong band/theater/arts, championship athletics, NJROTC, career centers and CTE, unique electives (medical apprentice, electronic music), facility renovations and campus partnerships—(e.g., “brand new science building,” “Cuyahoga Valley Career Center,” “AP Academy, Center for Advanced Studies”), whereas circle reviews rarely list such breadth, facilities upgrades, or external partnerships.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more specific, co: Square reviews frequently provide granular staff- and service‑level evidence—timely IEP communication or special‑ed failures, counselor responsiveness or broken Naviance systems, teachers ‘available after school’ or named ineffective instructors, and explicit favoritism claims (e.g., “his support teacher has been over the top,” “guidance counselor ignoring us for months,” “favoritism toward popular kids”), while circle reviews rarely include this level of concrete staff/service detail.
candidate_defs.square entries give more explicit descri: Square reviews more often situate the school in its local ecology—multigenerational alumni ties, parent/PTSA involvement or absence, wealth/affluence or poverty context, overcrowding and lunch/transportation pain points (e.g., “3rd generation to attend,” “well funded by affluent area,” “overcrowded,” “Lilly Rd is a pain”), whereas circle reviews generally omit or give far less concrete community, demographic or operational detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket captures claims that a school provides AP/IB/Honors, broad CTE/dual‑enrollment pathways, abundant arts/sports programs, and visible outcomes (scholarships, college credit, state championships); examples include square mentions of 'full IB program', '18+ AP courses', 'dual enrollment/associate degree paths', many CTE tracks (welding, culinary, automotive), nationally‑recognized band, and 'more scholarships this year'—assets that circle reviews largely omit or say are lacking.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This groups reports of frequent fights, bullying, drug/vape epidemics, sexual harassment, bomb/gun threats and on‑campus fatalities, often paired with claims that staff or security are ineffective or overwhelmed (e.g., 'fights everyday', 'Vape epidemic', 'bomb threat and a soft lockdown', 'students do drugs in classrooms', 'sexual harassment unaddressed'), whereas circle entries rarely report this severity.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This covers complaints about unreturned emails/voice messages, lost paperwork and VOEs, chaotic scheduling/enrollment glitches, leadership churn, front‑office failures, and refusals to cooperate (e.g., 'superintendent never returned my email', 'grades not posted on time', '3 principals in 4 years', 'lost VOE documentation'), contrasted with circle reviews that describe more visible principal presence or steady communication.
candidate_defs.square entries report more instructional: This groups accounts of many teachers quitting or classes taught by subs, teachers who 'don’t teach' or assign only busywork, inconsistent course rigor, athletic favoritism/grade protection, and subject‑level failures (e.g., 'classes covered by subs a full semester', 'many teachers are quitting', 'administrators favor athletes'), whereas circle reviews emphasize more consistent teacher support and classroom instruction.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures or c: This bucket includes IEP/504 noncompliance, parents 'having to fight' for services, segregation of students with learning differences, explicit racial/socioeconomic exclusion and language‑access gaps (e.g., 'fight with the district to get his 504 plan', 'students with learning differences are separated', 'This district is racist', 'low income students left behind'), while circle reviews contain little or none of these specific accommodation/equity allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures recurring concrete accounts of daily fights, gang activity, drug use/overdoses, lockdowns, sexualized behavior, teen pregnancy, and pervasive homophobic/racial harassment in square reviews (e.g., “Fights broke out everyday,” “Extremely high gang activity,” “There are drugs in every school,” “can't go a single day without hearing a crack about homosexuality”), plus claims that administrators do little or even perpetuate the problem (e.g., bullying ignored, victims arrested). Circle reviews lack these high-severity safety/crime reports and do not describe the same scale of administrative non-response.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket groups descriptions of named, high‑level academic offerings and results appearing in square reviews — AP/IB/dual-credit programs, New Technology/MSE, concrete diploma/college placements and alumni success stories (e.g., “the only IB school…higher proportion earning their IB diploma,” “student accepted at Stanford,” “many AP/IB/dual enrollment options”), whereas circle reviews typically lack such specific advanced-program catalogs and measurable postsecondary outcome claims.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more staff and lea: This bucket covers reports of managerial and personnel problems in square reviews — nepotism and favoritism in hiring/opportunities, punitive or image-driven admin practices, inconsistent/dishonest grading, chronic staffing gaps and long‑term substitutes, low paraprofessional morale, and teacher morale/turnover problems (e.g., “nepotism is now the new norm,” “awful counselor...ignored parents,” “many classes unstaffed, relying on long-term subs,” “awful… grades based on popularity”), while circle reviews do not present the same concentrated pattern of institutional favoritism and systemic staffing/grading dysfunction.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize richer, higher‑: This bucket groups square reports of strong, high‑visibility arts and athletics programs, booster support, travel/competition accomplishments, and facility/expansion projects (e.g., outstanding marching band, music department travels internationally, “Center for Advanced Studies addition slated for 2020,” strong booster support), along with complaints that resources are sometimes diverted (e.g., athletics favored over arts). Circle reviews rarely name or document the same scale of extracurricular prestige, booster engagement, or concrete capital projects.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete, mi: This bucket captures square reviews' frequent, specific claims about special-education programs (both strong and failing), guidance/counselor responsiveness, tutoring/ACE/college-prep services, and logistics/facility issues — e.g. explicit IEP failures or praised Life Skills programs, ‘guidance staff ill equipped’ or ‘full time school nurse,’ problems transferring records or Edline navigation, overcrowded lunches, parking/locker hassles, bus/meal programs — while circle reviews rarely supply as many concrete statements about special‑ed services, counselor systems, or the same operational details.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially st: These reviews report concrete programmatic rigor and results (many AP/IB/dual-credit offerings, dedicated academies, robust college counseling and recruiter outreach) and cite measurable outcomes (Ivy/MIT/Cornell acceptances, graduates earning college credits or Associate degrees, high graduation rates); circle reviews by contrast mainly describe routine homework, basic preparation, or lack comparable AP/IB/college-placement evidence (examples: Square: “12 AP classes… admitted to MIT,” “Many graduates earn enough college credits to become sophomores”; Circle: “they get homework everyday… no college placement info”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many square reviews recount physical assaults, repeated bullying (including of students with disabilities), drugs/vaping on campus, and claims that staff or leaders fail to act or apply enforcement unevenly (reports of ignored referrals, cover-ups, or regular fights), whereas circle reviews generally lack systemic violence/drug allegations or describe fewer/unresolved social tensions (examples: Square: “bullied, attacked and seriously injured,” "kids smoking…doing drugs…administration does nothing"); Circle typically notes competitiveness or isolated drama but not repeated violent incidents or administrative concealment).
candidate_defs.square entries highlight broader and hig: Square reviews repeatedly list extensive clubs, competitive athletics, award‑winning band/arts, JROTC/STEM teams, strong school spirit, active PTAs and community events—often naming programs and claiming regional/national success—while circle reviews rarely enumerate comparable extracurricular breadth or community mobilization (examples: Square: “Lots of extracurricular activities and fantastic sports programs… nationally ranked,” “PTA and Band Association… Fall Festival” ; Circle: no comparable program catalog).
candidate_defs.square entries document greater variabil: Square reviews contain polarized accounts—highly praised award‑winning teachers and outstanding counselors alongside accusations of widespread poor teaching, tenure‑driven complacency, language comprehension problems, frequent administration turnover, or punitive/prickly principals—implying inconsistent day‑to‑day staffing and leadership; circle reviews are more uniformly consistent about teacher quality or report different staffing problems (examples: Square: “Some teachers’ English was so bad…”, “Four different principals…”, and “a handful…5 REALLY good teachers” vs. many others accused of poor practice).
candidate_defs.square entries report more tangible faci: Reviewers of square schools describe both recent capital/facility investments and up‑to‑date tech and also list overcrowded halls, pest/cleanliness issues, budget shortfalls or course cuts, problematic tech rollouts, credit‑recovery/lowered‑standards or alleged gaming of placements to improve metrics—features largely absent or not emphasized in circle reviews (examples: Square: “approved over $80 million in renovations,” “smart boards in nearly every classroom,” but also “rats in art class,” “Budget Crisis… cuts to extracurriculars,” and “credit recovery… handing out diplomas to failing students”).
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student: This bucket covers concrete accounts of an unsafe student climate in square: frequent fights and assaults (“fights weekly,” “fights daily in the hallways,” a student ‘‘was pushed against the locker and knocked to the ground’’), pervasive drug/alcohol use (“students smoking pot in the parking‑lot,” “Kids are constantly doing drugs in the bathroom”), race‑based harassment and suicides, and retaliation/poor incident handling after complaints (“if you try to bring [bullying] to the school’s attention, you become even more of a target,” delayed parent notification after a concussion). Circle reviews lack comparable claims of ongoing violence, substance epidemics, or retaliatory escalation.
candidate_defs.square entries document substantially ri: This bucket groups concrete programmatic evidence in square about IB/AP/STEM/dual‑enrollment/magnet tracks and measurable outcomes: named IB and STEM academies, ‘‘AP classes,’’ dual enrollment and transcripted college credits, and booster examples of high AP/college matriculation (e.g., “IB Program (which is EXCEPTIONAL)”, “transcripted college courses…many RH students graduate with over a semester”). Circle contains few or no examples of such sustained advanced coursework, magnets, or large dual‑enrollment outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This bucket captures physical and material conditions in square: overcrowding and large class sizes (“overcrowded,” “couldn't get one on one time”), severe maintenance and sanitation failures (mice, roaches, mold, asbestos, sewage smells, broken bathrooms), parking/traffic and campus scale problems (“drop‑off is a nightmare,” ‘‘80 acres and a maze’’), plus CTE equipment disrepair and budget shortfalls that shift costs to parents. Circle reviews do not describe comparable chronic facility decay, vermin, or major overcrowding/traffic burdens.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater staff/lead: This bucket groups personnel and governance issues appearing in square: high teacher turnover and shortages (“good ones are leaving,” “high turnover rate”), extreme variability in instructional quality (“half the teachers act like they're teaching college and the other half act like they're working a day care”), counselor/front‑office dysfunction and overwork, and allegations of inequitable/unprofessional staff behavior and policy inconsistency (rudeness, favoritism, administrators protecting powerful families). Circle reviews, by contrast, more often portray stable, caring teachers and fewer systemic governance faults.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader and str: This bucket captures square’s repeated, concrete claims about abundant co‑curricular life and athletic prominence: top marching band/orchestra/theatre programs and many clubs, strong sports teams and facility investment, booster/donor fundraising and scholarships (VIP Boosters), and explicit athletic favoritism in resources/selection (‘‘Unless your child plays football, expect no help’’). Circle mentions fewer or narrower extracurriculars and does not present the same breadth, booster backing, or athletics‑first institutional emphasis.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews report concrete, school‑level academic capacity—many AP/IB offerings, national merit finalists, dual‑credit/college credit pathways, diploma tracks and explicit college‑readiness metrics—claims that Circle reviews generally omit or contradict (examples: “Plenty of AP and Honors classes,” “adding an IB program,” “18 college credits transferred,” vs Circle’s lack of AP/IB/dual‑credit evidence and complaints about weak college preparation).
candidate_defs.square entries report far broader extrac: Square reviews repeatedly list wide club/arts/sports breadth and high extracurricular achievement (50+ clubs, award‑winning band/theatre, state championships, ‘Go Comets!’ spirit), and also document visible resource/prioritization bias toward athletics (concession revenue disputes, turf/athletic spending cited as crowding out academics); Circle reviews rarely cite comparable arts/club depth and do not describe the same athletics‑first funding culture.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviewers detail repeated, serious safety incidents and weak or inconsistent responses—ongoing bullying, gang/drug use, fights and injuries, harassment by security, bathroom smoking, and parents threatening legal action or reporting expulsions—whereas Circle reviews lack this pattern or describe isolated, less severe discipline issues.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: Square content contains numerous concrete allegations about personnel and governance problems (principals described as ‘dictatorial’ or negligent; athletic director suspensions; transcripts withheld over fees; counselors ‘too busy’; IEPs ignored or requiring parental/legal fight; teacher favoritism or abusive behavior), while Circle reviews generally do not report the same scale of administrative malpractice or systemic staff misconduct.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete fac: Square reviewers give specific, tangible facility and resourcing details (trailers/overcrowding and bus shortages, ceilings/broken fixtures, mold/expired food, nurse shortages, pools needing refurbishing, or major remodel/performing arts investments and planned replacements), whereas Circle reviews rarely present this level of facility/capacity detail or mixed evidence of both deterioration and capital works.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: These entries name concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes (IB/AP/Honors, dual enrollment/college credit, CTE pathways, algebra acceleration), teacher availability for extra help, and alumni college placements—while circle entries largely lack those catalogs and often report low outcomes or credit/access barriers (e.g., cancelled credits, poor regents performance). Examples: explicit IB/AP/dual‑credit and CTE listings, teachers staying before/after school, and reported college scholarships versus circle’s complaints about weak credit recognition and poor post‑graduation support.
candidate_defs.square entries report substantially broa: These entries document many clubs, competitive athletics and award‑winning arts (marching band, theater, state titles), booster groups and passing levies that fund teams/programs, and explicit resource allocation to extracurriculars; circle entries more often describe limited after‑school activities or no comparable parent booster infrastructure. Examples: multiple clubs/teams, 'state championships' and active band/booster involvement contrasted with circle’s 'very limited to non‑existing after school activities.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These entries recount lockdowns, frequent fights, drug/vaping problems, ganglike behavior, cybercrimes and police interventions or SRO presence, together with claims that administration either ignores problems or applies inconsistent/punitive discipline; circle entries generally report fewer or isolated bullying incidents and a safer climate. Examples include weekly lockdowns, students 'beaten up,' Juul pods/drug references, metal detectors, and allegations that complaints were dismissed or mishandled.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: These entries provide concrete operational breakdowns: mixed/contradictory parent notifications, chronic schedule errors, lost/mishandled transcripts, punitive attendance/legal threats, administrators covering up misconduct or retaliating, and explicit IEP/504 enforcement failures; circle entries rarely make such detailed operational or special‑education complaints and more often cite accessible leadership. Examples: schedule mix‑ups, 'sent you court papers for days missed,' 'changed the notes from the IEP meeting,' and principal/board unresponsiveness or retaliation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: These entries detail physical and capacity constraints (overcrowded classrooms, locked bathrooms, leaking ceilings, asbestos/mold, cold/dirty rooms, damaged new construction) and sometimes contrast cosmetic exterior renovations with poor interior conditions; circle entries seldom describe such severe facility or environmental hazards. Examples: asbestos hanging from ceilings, bathrooms locked after vandalism, overcrowded classes and reports that 'for that beautiful renovated school outside it is very rotten on the inside.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete safety harms and peer-on-peer threats: gangs, frequent fights, vandalism/thefts, pervasive drug/vape use, sexualized harassment, teen suicides, and repeated bullying—often paired with claims that school responses were ineffective or slow (e.g., 'Gang activity… constant fights', 'Drugs are everywhere… teachers either have blinders on', 'highest suicide rate… assemblies/club started'). Circle entries lack or downplay these incidents, so membership means reviews emphasize recurring threats to student physical and mental safety and documented attempts (or failures) to address them.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: This bucket captures reviews that report explicit AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, honors expansion, college‑credit accumulation, active college counseling, and high‑profile matriculations (e.g., 'vast variety of A.P. and honors classes', 'left with 33 college credits', 'accepted at Ivy League schools', 'IB Diploma… dual enrolling'), whereas circle reviews do not present comparable breadth or demonstrated college outcomes; inclusion means the school is portrayed as delivering organized, measurable advanced academics and college pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize wide extracurri: This groups evidence that the school offers many clubs, arts, and leadership roles while simultaneously privileging sports—reports of pay‑to‑play, booster reliance, coaches' misconduct, and selective access tied to parental/local connections (e.g., 'hundreds of clubs', 'too revolved around sports', 'kids who stink at sports but have rich parents make everything', 'booster club expectations'). Circle entries rarely name this mix of broad offerings plus sport‑centered favoritism, so membership indicates both rich extracurricular opportunity and documented inequities or resource skew toward athletics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups concrete complaints about unreturned communications, resistant counselors, inconsistent/biased discipline, nepotism in athletics/opportunities, grade inflation or mis‑handled transcripts, failures to implement 504s, and high substitute/turnover use (e.g., 'left messages… counselor ignored', 'grades are inflated', 'you only pass if you’re a teacher’s pet', 'school had not dropped the classes — forced me to pay'). candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures concrete safety incidents and day-to-day supervision breakdowns (student fights, gang activity, sexual harassment/assault, drug use, theft, unlocked doors, recurring bus/commons fights) described far more often in square reviews (e.g., “sexual harassment and sexual assault,” “fights nearly daily,” “gang violence,” “doors left unlocked,” “drugs in children's bags”) than in circle reviews, which rarely list such operational safety failures. candidate_defs.square entries show more pronounced staf: This bucket groups reviews that juxtapose committed, effective classroom teachers with poor leadership, inconsistent or punitive discipline, counseling failures, favoritism/nepotism, and problematic HR/turnover (e.g., “great teachers but the principal is horrific,” “guidance counselors refuse to help,” “administration honors favors instead of hiring better teachers,” and reports of staff mistreatment of students). In short, square reviews more often report a split between competent instruction and failing/antagonistic administration, whereas circle reviews present fewer such teacher–admin contradictions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe facili: This bucket covers concrete, repeated operational failures and facility hazards: overcrowding and extreme enrollment pressures (e.g., 2,300+ students, closed bathrooms with only 2 stalls for 500 girls), maintenance and health hazards (mold, roaches, asbestos), broken services (nonexistent nurse, bus route chaos), scheduling/registration errors and transcript/records mishandling, and pandemic‑era disruption examples. Circle reviews seldom document these kinds of chronic physical, capacity, or operations failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, more ac: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize a wide range of out‑of‑class programs and community ties — strong performing arts and state‑of‑the‑art arts centers, competitive athletics and marching band, many clubs and volunteer/service options, chapel/faith programming, active alumni networks and parental fundraising/support (e.g., “performing arts center like Juilliard,” “many clubs…JNROTC,” “strong alumni network,” “chapel 3 times a week”). Circle entries typically do not list comparable program breadth, elite extracurricular outcomes, or sustained community/alumni engagement.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger/broader: These reviews describe concrete curricular breadth and college-prep infrastructure in square schools (AP/IB availability, '6 Academies', explicit CTE tracks, a robust College & Career Center, students accepted to Ivies/Stanford and earned '12 hrs of college credit') that circle reviews do not document; examples include explicit AP/IB lists, named academies, 'medical apprentice' and 'Excel Tecc' programs, and repeated claims of measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Many square reviews allege recurring peer-safety incidents (bullying, 'quite a few fights a week', 'drugs are a huge problem') and either weak enforcement or biased enforcement (favoritism toward athletes, unequal discipline, mishandled sexual assault), while circle reviews generally lack systemic safety allegations or describe more effective handling of individual incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more facility, c: Square reviews repeatedly cite physical-plant deficits and crowding—aging buildings, poor cleanliness and pests ('cockroaches', 'smelled disgusting'), lack of AC, overcrowded/oversized classes and bus/seat shortages—often alongside notes of recent renovations or tech rollouts (iPads, one-to-one laptops); circle reviews rarely document these concrete facility/capacity/resource narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These entries contain specific operational complaints (registration/onboarding breakdowns, receptionist/office staff rudeness, onerous residency verification, retention of private documents), governance criticisms ('mishandling of funding', 'administration is clueless', problematic Summit implementation), and poor communication/accountability claims that circle reviews do not make or make far less often.
