candidate_defs.square entries show greater variation in: Square reviewers provide many concrete teacher-level examples—proactive tutoring and mentors ('teachers make room to tutor...'), exceptional named teachers, but also unprofessional conduct, favoritism, credential/competence problems and highly uneven classroom management—whereas circle reviews contain fewer concrete instructional anecdotes and less of this wide within-school variability.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups reviews that attribute concrete academic rigor and college-readiness to Square — e.g., listings of many AP/Honors/IB courses, AP credit accumulation ('30+ hours of credit'), SAT/ACT/high graduation metrics, college counselors and SAT prep, and national rankings ('US News Silver Medal') — contrasted with Circle reviews that do not cite comparable AP/IB breadth or measurable college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive saf: This bucket captures reviews describing frequent fights, drug use, sexual harassment, corporal punishment, student assaults, suicides or self‑harm risk, chronic bullying and students skipping school, plus repeated claims that administration/staff fail to remediate or enforce discipline — e.g., 'fights every day', 'drugs in children's bags', 'bullying is HORRIBLE' and 'admin fails to take action' — whereas Circle contains few or no parallel accounts of pervasive safety failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and high: This bucket includes reviews that enumerate many named clubs, performing‑arts ensembles, award‑winning choirs/bands, extensive sports teams, and competitive achievements (theater, academic decathlon, state awards) — e.g., 'award winning choirs', 'band program is especially good', 'over 20 APs and DECA/ROTC/competitive teams' — while Circle reviews rarely list comparable arts breadth or program accolades.
candidate_defs.square entries report pronounced adminis: This bucket groups reviews that point to leadership turnover, hiring problems, named unresponsive principals, governance scandals and fiscal/legal issues (e.g., superintendent on leave, business manager indicted, frequent principal exits), poor district‑level communication, or active silencing of critics — contrasted with Circle, whose reviews lack comparable reports of district scandals or high‑level instability.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater social str: This bucket covers reviews describing socio‑economic hierarchies, favoritism toward athletes/honors students, tracking or selective attention, reliance on outside AP prep, parents moving in/out or withdrawing kids, long commutes for school choice, and community political involvement — e.g., 'administrators don't care unless you're on the football team', 'parents move here for the school', and 'students who take summer AP prep get the As' — whereas Circle reviews emphasize a smaller, less stratified local community and do not describe the same patterns of selective support or market‑driven enrollment.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, broader,: These reviews describe concrete program breadth and outcomes (AP/IB/IB/ACIE, many AP/Honors/dual‑credit courses, vocational/CNA/welding/ROTC pathways, documented college matriculation and scholarship counts) that circle reviews generally do not (circle lacks program breadth or only gives anecdotal college prep). Examples: multiple square reviewers list IB/AP/dual credit, Engineering/Medical/IT pathways and cite college acceptances and AP score growth, whereas circle provides no comparable schoolwide metrics or specialized tracks.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Square reviews repeatedly allege serious safety problems (drugs, frequent fights, hazing, sexual incidents in bathrooms, bomb/shooting scares, weapons, routine police involvement) and describe recurring threats or searches; circle reviews rarely report these kinds of criminalized incidents and focus instead on isolated bullying or procedural issues. Example evidence: square contains claims of 'drug use and property theft rampant,' 'bomb threats every other week,' 'students had guns on campus' and daily law‑enforcement presence, which do not appear in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater variabil: Square reviews contain many concrete reports of uneven teacher competence, staff misconduct or disrespect, micromanaging or unresponsive administration, counselor reductions, and operational chaos (rude front desk, unanswered parent calls, teacher turnover), while circle reviews more often describe consistent, approachable teachers and active principal‑led improvements. Illustrative raw items: 'teachers with poor English comprehension,' 'administration never returns calls,' 'front office staff rude,' and 'fresh-out-of-college teachers replacing seasoned staff' appear in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete and: Many square reviews name explicit facilities outcomes (new building additions, one‑to‑one device programs, renovated cafeterias and award‑winning facilities) alongside equally explicit problems (mold, broken escalators, flooded fields, bathrooms filthy, buildings over capacity, 40‑student classes), whereas circle reviews seldom provide comparable facility detail. Examples: square cites both '$20M capital improvements' and 'building over 50 years old, twice capacity,' demonstrating that square entries more often report specific facility/capacity realities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic favo: Square reviewers frequently allege preferential treatment tied to athletes/affluent families/favored students, clique cultures, racial profiling, gaming of placements/grades, and both failures and mixed reports regarding special‑education supports; circle reviews either report inclusivity/approachable staff or do not raise these equity/favoritism issues. Representative evidence: square contains claims like 'unless you're involved in football you don't get looked out for,' 'racially profiled by staff,' 'students sent to LD classes to game metrics,' and warnings to 'stay on top of your child's IEP,' none of which appear in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers reports that students face ongoing physical and emotional harm and that staff/administration fail to stop or properly investigate it (e.g., “fights every day between classes,” frequent on‑campus drug use, racial harassment, even sexual‑assault allegations) and descriptions of victims being punished or ignored. Representative evidence: claims of daily fights, gangs/targeting, smell of marijuana, victims not notified or helped, and reviewers saying administration 'did nothing' or 'supports bullying.'
candidate_defs.square entries document more robust adva: This bucket groups concrete curricular strength and pathways: many AP/IB/dual‑credit classes, specialized tracks (STEM, vocational academies), electives (Robotics, Culinary, CAD/Cam), and cited college placements/metrics (high AP counts, National Merit, strong college matriculation). Representative evidence includes explicit counts and programs (“nearly 30 AP classes,” “IB/AVID/AP/dual‑credit,” “accepted to Stanford/UCs”) and claims that these offerings and outcomes are stronger or more numerous than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a broader, highe: This bucket captures descriptions of many and sometimes elite extracurriculars—large award‑winning bands/choirs, debate to Harvard, state‑champion teams, travel teams and D1 athlete pipelines—and also recurring claims that athletics receive prioritized funding/resources (e.g., new bleachers, many varsity coaches) sometimes at the expense of other programs. Representative evidence: '140+ member award‑winning marching band,' 'wrestling and football teams are some of the best in the state,' and accusations that 'funding is skewed towards the football team.'
candidate_defs.square entries show more administrative: This bucket groups operational and leadership failures distinct from incident response: poor parent/school communication, lost transcripts/records, overloaded or ineffective counselors, controversial spending choices, nepotism/favoritism, and a disconnected school board. Representative evidence: reports like 'they threw away my submission,' 'counselors are too busy to be effective,' criticism of spending on flat screens/heated floors, and claims that 'rules do not apply to those with influential parents.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more facilities, c: This bucket covers physical‑plant and everyday operations problems that affect student flow and comfort—historic/disrepair issues, crowded hallways/classrooms, closed bathrooms, poor parking/bussing, and schedule constraints that force students to carry belongings or miss lockers. Representative evidence: 'old buildings... looks like juvenile hall,' 'most bathrooms are closed,' 'crowded hallways… no time to go to lockers,' and 'parking—insanely hard to leave/get into.'
candidate_defs.Square entries show stronger formal adva: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete academic infrastructure and results (AP/IB/magnet/dual‑enrollment, honors tracks, high graduation/college‑placement stats, test‑score emphasis and heavy homework). Examples: 'robust AP program and dual enrolled students with 60+ credits,' '98% graduation rate' and 'students going to Ivy League/Top‑20 schools' vs Circle’s lack of school‑level metrics and limited AP/honors offerings.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more severe bullyi: This groups safety-and‑climate evidence about student violence, harassment, and how the school enforces (or fails to enforce) rules — including SRO/policing concerns, ISS/OSS that removes instruction, harsh attendance suspensions, favoritism toward athletes, and reports of ignored bullying. Examples: 'Fights are every other day,' 'bomb scares,' 'sent to ISS for no belt,' and 'school resource officers strip civil liberties' contrasted with Circle’s relative silence or milder, localized safety complaints.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader, higher‑: This bucket collects descriptions of wide, high‑capacity extracurricular ecosystems and visible community backing — large marching bands and award‑winning arts/athletics, many clubs, vocational certifications and strong fundraising/PTSA activity. Examples: '214‑member marching band,' 'health care academy with CNA/EMT certificates,' '50+ clubs,' and 'Spirit Week raised $228,000' versus Circle’s sparse or absent extracurricular listings.
candidate_defs.Square entries allege more administrativ: This groups reports about leadership and staff behavior (chronic teacher absenteeism/burnout, favoritism/nepotism, cover‑ups, record‑withholding, retire‑rehire or financial scandals, and high leadership churn) rather than instructional program quality. Examples: 'retire‑rehire scandals / missing funds,' 'principal covered up teacher misconduct,' 'teachers chronically absent' and 'lots of turnover' contrasted with Circle’s more consistent praise for helpful, communicative staff and stable leadership.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more overcrowding,: This bucket covers physical‑capacity and operational constraints: overcrowded classes/portables, broken facilities and health hazards, parking/traffic problems, block‑scheduling conflicts that prevent multi‑activity participation, construction disruption, and uneven funding between academies. Examples: '40+ portables, kids get soaked when it rains,' 'block schedule makes it impossible to do band and JROTC,' 'broken shop equipment left 3 years' and 'engineering academy underfunded' versus Circle’s lack of such large‑scale facility or crowding complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a wider, higher‑: This groups comments about breadth and prominence of nonacademic programs: square reviews list many clubs, competitive music/band and performing‑arts wins, robotics, large marching bands and broad CTE/trade offerings (e.g., 'national award winning robotics', 'band invited to play in Normandy', 'largest marching band... almost 800 members'), and also note a strong sports culture; circle reviews rarely enumerate such variety and emphasize a narrower extracurricular picture.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety incide: This bucket covers concrete student‑safety and wellbeing issues and the school's handling of them: square reviews contain frequent accounts of fights, drugs, self‑harm/suicide concerns, bullying and security breaches as well as any school responses (e.g., 'students buying and selling drugs', 'girls cut themselves... suicide assemblies and SOS club', 'fights every day'), whereas circle reviews contain far fewer or no comparable reports of pervasive safety or self‑harm crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report more adult‑staffin: This groups reports about how adults and leaders behave or manage the school: square reviews repeatedly cite uneven/polarized teacher quality, slow or missing communication, counselor unavailability, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, alleged bribery/overpaid executives and punitive or inconsistent discipline (e.g., 'teachers routinely don't return emails', 'family income dictates grades', 'forced into retirement by bribery', 'counselor never available'), while circle reviews rarely allege this cluster of leadership/fairness failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, sch: This bucket captures concrete material and logistical constraints: square reviews document overcrowded hallways and classes, leaking roofs and unsanitary bathrooms, poor cafeteria food, complicated/broken schedules, missing language/technical teachers, and budget‑driven cuts or capital campaigns (e.g., 'roof leaks... school falling apart', 'Pick up/drop off needs improvement', 'Course catalog... outdated', 'cut 6 teachers due to the budget'), whereas circle reviews provide far fewer examples of persistent facility or operational resource failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete curriculum breadth and college/career pipelines in square schools—AP/IB/honors lists, abundant AP courses, dual‑enrollment/CCP, STEM/biomed/magnet academies, internships, vocational shops, and specific alumni college matriculation—contrasted with circle reviews that lack named advanced tracks or report declining college readiness (examples: square mentions dual enrollment/Associates degrees, 25+ AP courses, STEM internships and strong alumni placement; circle cites weak AP pass rates and insufficient college prep).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, higher‑a: This bucket captures reviews noting award‑winning bands, top performing‑arts programs, wide club/participation access, no‑cut teams and many non‑sport electives in square schools versus circle reviews that describe lost or collapsing arts, narrower athletics praise (often only one sport), or fewer named extracurriculars (examples: square cites Normandy trips, state championships, outstanding journalism/music programs and many clubs; circle reports band/chorus decline and mostly basketball praise).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This groups accounts of fights, gang/drug activity, overdoses, sexual assault allegations, pervasive bullying, bathroom smoking/drug use and parents/students saying administration turned a blind eye or acted ineffectively—whereas many circle reviews offer no comparable safety incidents or describe lower/semi‑addressed bullying (examples: square reports weekly fights, OD deaths, unaddressed sexual assaults and ignored bullying; circle usually lacks these claims or reports isolated, manageable bullying).
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical fac: This bucket collects concrete infrastructure and health complaints about mold, asbestos, lack of air conditioning, flooding, pest infestations, rusty water fountains, filthy bathrooms and moldy/contaminated school lunches in square schools versus circle reviews that describe upgraded or clean facilities and classroom technology (examples: square names asbestos in ceilings, mold making students sick, roaches and slimy/contaminated milk; circle highlights renovated buildings and classroom touchscreens).
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket groups reviews that describe both positives (organized PTO, weekly admin communication, online gradebooks, teachers who go above and beyond, strong college counseling in some cases) and governance/personnel problems (front‑office rudeness, staff harassment, favoritism toward athletes/families, punitive attendance/discipline contracts, grade‑manipulation/protection of staff, overloaded or missing counselors) contrasted with circle reviews that more consistently report either steady teacher care or limited program support but fewer of these extreme internal contradictions (examples: square cites PTO/online monitoring alongside allegations of being followed to cars by admin, nepotism, transcript errors and counselor understaffing; circle lacks comparable claims of nepotism or such extreme administrative punishment).
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews report concrete curricular offerings, outcomes, and structural tracking (IB/AP/AVID/dual enrollment, honors/ivy‑track, transcripted credit, freshman 'tracks', measurable AP/SAT/college matriculation) and note both positive preparation and the AP/IB-driven stratification that leaves non-honors students behind (e.g., “offers the IB Diploma Programme and many AP classes… prepared students for college” and “If you are not in AP courses… the other 4/5 of the school provides a very low education”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These items document fights, bomb/shooting threats, on-campus drug/alcohol use and searches, gang presence, routine bullying (often severe), and either visible security measures or staff inaction—frequently with reports that counseling/administration failed to stop harms (e.g., “6 bomb threats… students have openly sold drugs,” “bullying forced students to be homeschooled,” “infested with gangs… school does nothing”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff/leaders: Reviews emphasize nepotism and status-based favoritism (athletes/wealthy/teacher-children get opportunities), staff cliques, alleged staff misconduct or abusive behavior, and wide variability in teacher competence and awards (e.g., “nepotism… opportunities go to students of school employees,” “teachers belittle students,” and conflicting claims of award-winning vs. many ‘terrible’ teachers).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more operational: These comments point to chronic inaccessibility, lost/excused‑absence errors, mishandled records, ignored or inconsistently executed IEP/504 plans, overloaded guidance counselors, and pandemic/policy communication failures (e.g., “guidance counselor 300+ students, had to call/email a month before they finally started his IEP,” “office is not reachable… attendance staff forgot to excuse DMV appointment”).
candidate_defs.square entries document richer and more: Many square reviews enumerate strong music/theater programs, vocational labs, athletics facilities, 1:1 tech, special magnet tracks and major capital projects (pools, tracks), while also debating budget choices (athletics vs. academics) (e.g., “outstanding music program,” “BioHealth Magnet… pottery/woodworking/automotive,” “brand new Olympic sized pool” and critiques that money prioritizes turf over classroom supplies).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, formal a: These reviews describe concrete, school-level academic assets (AP/IB/dual-enrollment, magnet/Governor’s School, AP Capstone, high AP/SAT/ACT performance, documented Ivy/elite college matriculations and graduates earning college credit) that are repeatedly named in square but absent or unsubstantiated in circle (e.g., “AP Capstone courses...dual enrollment,” “outstanding IB, AP, and arts programs,” “many graduates earn enough college credits”).
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher-pr: Square reviews list wide, named co‑curricular offerings and high‑visibility successes—marching band ranked nationally, state championships, extensive theater/choir/orchestra, career-technical clubs and competitions—whereas circle reviews seldom provide comparable program depth or documented awards (examples: “band is top notch...third best high school band in the US,” “girls basketball program won state 3 years in a row,” many named vocational pathways).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviewers recount concrete incidents and patterns—fights, stabbings, guns, drugs/vaping, bullying, students assaulted, unlocked doors and lockdowns—and describe uneven enforcement and athlete-favoritism that lets some students evade consequences, while circle contains far fewer or no reports of such high-severity safety problems (examples: “trash can fire...a stabbing, and a gun problem,” “kids smoke/vape in the bathrooms,” “If you are an athlete in season you can get away with weapons”).
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: These items document systemic leadership and operational failures in square schools—principal criticism/forced removals, mass staff exoduses, transcript/grade errors, refusal of accommodations/transfers, slow or non-existent responses to parents, cover-ups and authoritarian policies—whereas circle reviews typically do not recount comparable administrative breakdowns (examples: “mass exodus,” “they screwed up my daughter's transcript,” “took EXACTLY four months for a reply,” “administration is afraid of the sports coaching staff”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete, vis: Square reviews contain many specific, operational resource facts—building renovations and new construction alongside chronic shortfalls (cut arts funding, lack of supplies), volunteer-run programs, mandatory device costs, frequent referendums, and either overcrowding or underpopulation affecting class access—whereas circle reviews rarely present this same level of facility/funding detail (examples: “brand new main building...”, “resource teachers are severely underfunded,” “Seniors are required to have laptops,” “buses are always late and/or double loaded,” “classes are small and plenty of openings”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe and fr: This bucket captures reviews describing violence, gangs, weapons, drug use, arson/fires, repeated fights/lockdowns, sexual assault allegations, pervasive bullying, second‑hand smoke and other acute safety hazards, plus examples of poor or delayed emergency/mental‑health responses (e.g., “a student was stabbed in the hallway,” “one kid set a fire,” “lockdowns nearly weekly,” “drug infested,” “my freshman year a kid passed away and the school didn’t even care,” dropped phone calls during emergencies). Many square reviews also recount administrators and staff failing to stop or satisfactorily investigate incidents, whereas circle reviews lack this pattern of sustained, severe safety incidents and crisis‑response failure.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a broader, deepe: This bucket groups reviews that list numerous, competitive, award‑winning co‑curricular programs and their tangible outcomes — music/marching band conservatory, debate/forensics, robotics (MATE, FLL), STEM academies, strong athletics with playoff records, vocational/CTE and culinary excellence, and documented college or certification outcomes (e.g., “award winning marching band,” “STEM Academy…top scores,” “Robotics won First Place in Design,” “students placed into Ivy League/top conservatories”). Circle entries generally do not enumerate comparable program breadth, high‑level awards, or repeated college/career placement anecdotes.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete, co: This bucket covers reviews that detail IEP/504 practice, life‑skills classrooms, ELL inclusion, guidance‑counselor behavior, coordinated multi‑role interventions, or explicit noncompliance/shaming (examples: “doesn’t follow the law when it comes to special needs,” “Life Skills teachers were very attentive,” “Guidance counselor said ‘I don’t know…maybe you could get in?’,” “become defensive if called out for not following IEPs”). Square reviews more often supply these operational specifics and legal/process complaints or praise; circle reviews rarely address special‑education or counseling at this level of detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit admi: This bucket captures critiques about how leadership and district policy shape the school: principal/district schedule/curriculum overrides (e.g., eliminating AP Biology), nepotistic hires or athletic favoritism, superintendent resignations/scandals, punitive or inconsistent discipline rules, rights violations (searches, graduation exclusions), and bureaucratic impediments (e.g., refusal to release a child without emailed permission). These are concrete governance‑level problems and policy‑driven obstacles that square reviews document far more frequently than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: This bucket groups curricular and instructional evidence: advanced/AP/IB/STEM course presence, specialized academies, lab/tech resource notes, tutoring availability and teacher‑accessibility (positive: “teachers available before and after school,” “many AP classes,” “IB school”); it also includes operational academic problems like uneven teacher quality, grade‑inflation or lenient make‑up policies, poor lab access, and conflicting reports of rigor (examples: “many AP courses…we have top scores,” vs. “many teachers promote poor study skills by providing make‑ups”). Square reviews more often include concrete statements about course portfolios, resource gaps, measurable test/college outcomes, and variability in teaching than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries present stronger advanced: These reviews repeatedly name formal advanced tracks (AP, IB, AVID, AICE), dual‑enrollment/College‑in‑High‑School and vocational/certification pathways and cite concrete college placements and test-prep help (Ivy admits, 90% college matriculation, AP/IB successes), whereas circle reviews rarely list such program inventories or verifiable post‑secondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent/seve: Square reviewers document guns/violent incidents, gang activity, pervasive bullying (including race‑based harassment), drug/vape use and even suicides, often paired with claims that staff/administration failed to stop or properly discipline offenders; equivalent, concrete safety or unresolved‑bullying accounts are absent from circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square reviews name elite band/performing‑arts, state/national championships, extensive club/CTE offerings, strong athletic facilities and active booster/parent investment (parents moving districts, affluent funding), while circle reviews rarely catalogue comparable program breadth, competitive success or organized community boosters.
candidate_defs.square entries document pronounced admin: Square reviewers allege favoritism (athletes, legacy families, coaches’ relatives), selective enforcement, administrators protecting staff, pay‑to‑play or PR‑driven priorities and calls to remove principals or boards; circle reviews do not report the same pattern of biased discipline or governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: Square reviews report wide teacher quality swings and turnover, outdated textbooks/labs, counselor scheduling failures, IEP/special‑education neglect and rigid course‑scheduling limits, whereas circle reviews offer fewer examples of these systemic instructional/resource failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student: This bucket captures accounts that describe pervasive peer harm and campus danger (bullying, daily fights, gang activity, on‑campus drug/alcohol use, sexual harassment/assault, shooting/arson incidents, social‑media harassment) and ineffective response by staff—e.g., “Bullying is rampant…drugs, sex and alcohol are rampant,” “shooting incident,” “Someone set fire to the bathrooms,” and “staff doesn’t take action.” These items focus on student conduct and immediate safety climate rather than facilities or curricula, and are consistently reported more in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader and bett: This bucket groups statements that list concrete program breadth and college‑prep outcomes—AP/IB offerings, STEM/academies, CTE pathways, dual‑credit, strong music/theatre programs, extensive clubs and leadership opportunities, and alumni college placements—e.g., “full IB diploma,” “AP, Honors and Governor's School,” “Information Technology Systems program,” “band traveled to China,” and alumni admitted to Ivy League schools. These are programmatic/opportunity descriptions and outcome evidence (scholarships, college readiness) that square reviewers cite far more than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more administrativ: This bucket covers claims about governance and personnel practices: poor communication and ignored parent contacts, arbitrary or punitive discipline and misuse of suspension, favoritism (teacher/athlete/alumni hires), special‑education failures and IEP noncompliance/misclassification, chronic teacher absenteeism or unqualified substitutes, and credential concerns—e.g., “On my IEP… they don’t plan on following it,” “they arbitrarily enforce ed codes,” “most teachers… do not have state certification,” and “they will suspend an assaulted victim.” These are operational and equity failures within staff and leadership reported more often in square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, inf: This bucket groups concrete, physical and resourcing problems: decaying buildings, cockroaches/mold, cracked ceilings, locked/disgusting bathrooms, overcrowded classrooms/closed campus, lack of textbooks/supplies, and explicit budget mismanagement or fee‑extraction—e.g., “buildings are decaying… one caved in from the cockroaches,” “library closed due to mold,” “bathrooms are disgusting,” and “not enough textbooks for MANY classes.” These material and fiscal shortcomings are repeatedly attributed to square schools more than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, deeper ad: These reviews describe concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment, magnets, STEM/STEAM tracks, named centers like CCT, AVID/GearUP, internships) and cite measurable results (high SAT/ACT averages, scholarships, college acceptances) that square entries mention much more often than circle entries (examples: “abundant AP offerings,” “IB/CECA but poor delivery,” “Mrs. Woodland provided GearUp college resources,” “30 on his ACT,” contrasted with circle’s lack of AP/IB detail or college‑prep metrics).
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize stronger, highe: Square reviews repeatedly name robust extracurricular ecosystems — varsity sports and athletic prestige (football champs, district champs), nationally recognized band and theatre programs, numerous clubs and student governance bodies — while circle reviews rarely list that breadth (examples: “half the student body in band and/or choir,” “new band director brought us to state,” “plethora of after‑school activities,” versus circle’s sparse or negative comments about extracurricular options).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews recount daily or repeated safety incidents and substance use, explicit racial harassment or sexual harassment, and examples of administration/counselors failing to stop threats (examples: “fights EVERY day,” “high rate of fights, gang activity and lots of drugs,” “racial slurs… brought to the school's attention and nothing has been done,” and life‑threatening bullying ignored), whereas circle reviews typically do not report such sustained, severe safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviewers frequently note principal/assistant‑principal turnover, high teacher/coach churn, poor recordkeeping, unresponsive or authoritarian administrators, teacher/coach misconduct or favoritism, and uneven or punitive discipline policies (examples: “assistant principals have come and gone every year,” “teachers that are also coaches pay more attention to sports,” “they lost her transcripts,” “bathroom denial and harsh cell‑phone punishments”), problems only sporadically raised or absent in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more detailed, mi: Square reviews both praise concrete investments (1:1 netbook programs, new pool/track, science buildings) and call out serious maintenance, overcrowding, or budget impacts (moldy bathrooms, closed libraries, elective cuts), and they more often describe formal support services (special ed inclusion, credit recovery, scheduled tutoring, counselors) — a level of operational detail and contrast rarely present in circle entries (examples: “technology program… every student loaned a netbook,” “one bathroom shut for a year,” “FMHS offers credit recovery,” versus circle’s lack of facility/support program detail).
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more pervasive st: This bucket groups reviews that describe tangible safety failures inside the building and ineffective responses — e.g., reports of gangs, sexual activity in bathrooms, repeated fights that hospitalized students, pervasive bullying and racist/homophobic harassment, widespread vaping/drug use, and repeated claims that staff/administration do nothing (e.g., 'Bullying is prevalent and no one does anything', 'vaping epidemic', 'multiple kids were beaten up so badly they were hospitalized'). These items are about concrete student‑safety and behavior breakdowns and the school’s failure to prevent or remediate them (distinct from administrative tone or curricular issues).
candidate_defs.square entries show concentrated pockets: This bucket captures reviews describing a polarized academic landscape: selective magnet/IB/AP pockets with clear college/athletic outcomes (IB/AP success, Ivy/Ivy‑adjacent admits, state championships, dual‑enrollment credits) alongside broad complaints that most students face watered‑down instruction, restricted access to advanced courses, and remedial outcomes (e.g., 'magnet program are excellent…', 'one student going to Yale' vs. 'Most of my assignments are fill‑in‑the‑blank', 'sorting hat leaves many students out in the cold', 'dumbing down' and need for summer school). The theme is structural inequality in academic opportunity and outcomes rather than general program breadth or extracurricular emphasis.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: This bucket groups concrete logistical and facility problems described by reviewers — overcrowded schools and classes ('3000 students', 'class sizes nearing 1,000 per grade'), lunch rooms running out of food and long lines, unsafe/unreliable busing and parking shortages, chaotic large‑event organization ('900 kids in a room…open house fiasco'), pest sightings and filthy facilities, and confusing multi‑platform digital systems. These are operational/capital and scheduling failures distinct from pedagogy, staff professionalism, or curricular strengths.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket collects reviews that allege front‑office and instructional staff failures in responsiveness, professionalism, governance and equitable enforcement — e.g., unanswered emails and boilerplate replies, principals dismissing medically affected students, accusations of cover‑ups ('don’t want the public to know…'), favoritism toward athletes/high scorers, rude office staff, and selective or punitive discipline practices. These items are about staff/admin behavior, communication, decision‑making, and governance rather than curricular content or physical capacity.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: This bucket captures the many concrete listings of extracurricular and vocational offerings and their measurable results found in square reviews — band, theater, robotics, cosmetology, STEM academies, JROTC, culinary arts, numerous clubs, state athletic championships, one‑to‑one tech programs, and published scholarship/college outcomes — and paired concerns that athletics sometimes receive priority over arts. These items describe program variety, participation, and visible program outcomes distinct from academic curriculum quality or administrative responsiveness.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer parental ac: This bucket captures schools where reviewers describe restricted parental access and low administrative responsiveness — e.g., “Parents are not allowed in the classroom… We can only go to the cafeteria,” and accounts of office staff being “unhelpful and often rude” or principals not communicating visitors’ plans. Falling into this bucket means reviews document concrete policies/practices or staff behaviors that hinder parent engagement and show administrative unresponsiveness relative to circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger formal: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize school-level credentials and outcomes such as being “the only IB school in [city],” higher IB diploma rates than state average, and alumni winning “full ride scholarships at top notch out of state colleges.” A review fits here when it highlights formal program offerings (IB/AP) or concrete outcome metrics (diploma rates, college scholarships) at square schools more than at circle schools.
candidate_defs.square entries report inconsistent class: This bucket covers critiques of day-to-day teaching quality — for example, reports like “Most AP courses are not taught appropriately… some are REALLY good… some others have no control over their classes or don't teach well at all.” Reviews in this category point to variable teacher effectiveness and weak delivery of advanced coursework at square schools relative to circle schools.
candidate_defs.square entries report widespread student: This bucket includes accounts of pervasive student mental-health and engagement problems such as “Most students are depressed and wanting to run away… I have never before seen or heard so many students who truly HATE high school.” Reviews here document broad patterns of student disengagement and poor wellbeing at square schools not present in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more bullying inci: This bucket captures reviews that focus principally on bullying and safety issues (the comparison notes Circle reviews “focus solely on bullying”), meaning circle schools’ reviews emphasize incidents of bullying or safety concerns more often than square reviews, which lack such reports.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pervasive s: This bucket captures reviews that report concrete student-harm incidents (fights, assaults, racial slurs, sexual harassment/Title IX complaints, pervasive bullying, vaping/drug epidemics, suicidal or trauma outcomes, threats) and either no effective response or very slow/ineffective remediation (administration ‘turns a blind eye’, no anti-bullying system, Title IX inaction). Examples: reports of assaults left unpunished, bathroom slurs on display for months, widespread vaping/drug use, and students hospitalized for mental-health crises that staff discouraged treating.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, more nume: This bucket groups evidence of explicit advanced academic pathways (AP/Pre-AP/IB, dual‑enrollment, CIS/magnet/STEM programs), plentiful vocational/CTE options, thriving arts and extracurriculars, and concrete postsecondary metrics (large scholarship totals, elite college matriculation, internship/research experiences). Examples: numerous AP/dual-credit mentions, Science & Technology magnet internships, award‑winning arts programs, and reports of students winning millions in scholarships or attending top universities.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize clear operation: This bucket includes concrete, day-to-day physical and logistic conditions — budget shortfalls, outdated or missing instructional materials, overcrowded classes, sanitation/maintenance failures, scheduling/locker logistics, and district-level capacity/rezoning issues — as well as explicit tech programs (both positive and negative). Examples: complaints about outdated computers and bathrooms without supplies, overcrowded classrooms and shared lockers, complex schedules and freshmen registration failures, and also mentions of 1:1 Chromebooks or modernized labs.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent ad: This bucket centers on leadership/management problems and staff-level misconduct: mis-scheduled classes, erroneous guidance advice, overloaded counselors, punitive complaint-handling, alleged coverups/nepotism, tenure-protected poor performers, and frequent staff/leadership turnover or forced retirements. Examples: guidance counselors giving wrong graduation info multiple times, school protecting bad teachers, schools ‘very good at coverup,’ and repeated principal/staff instability.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight community compo: This bucket captures reviews that attribute school dynamics to parent/ community factors — affluent or activist parent bodies moving into districts, foundation funding directed to elites, multi‑generational local ties, selective admissions/entrance exams, parental advocacy or manipulation, and a disconnected or politicized board — showing how community makeup and resource control affect access and climate. Examples: parents moving into the district for the school, claims that 'money talks' or foundation funds go to the top 10%, and allegations that popular/connected families receive preferential treatment.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete program breadth and outcomes (IB/AVID/AP/dual‑credit, specialized academies, many AP classes, doubled AP enrollment, AP credits that skip college semesters, alumni at Harvard/Vanderbilt/Georgia Tech) that circle reviews do not document; examples include claims of ‘18 AP classes,’ ‘IB program is exploding,’ and rising API/college‑readiness rates versus Circle’s lack of AP/IB/dual-credit evidence and repeated notes of poor standardized scores.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many square reviews recount explicit safety incidents—fights, drug busts, guns/assaults, sexual harassment, racial slurs—and persistent verbal/cyberbullying with administrators or officers not adequately responding, e.g. ‘gang fights…a kid had a gun,’ ‘drug busts every week,’ and ‘bullied day in and day out…nothing ever gets done,’ whereas Circle reviews rarely report such concrete safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: Square reviews frequently list large extracurricular breadth and high‑level achievements (award‑winning band, national cheer/dance placements, many clubs, strong sports, aviation/STEM magnets) and note capital work (new high school, new gym, $20M improvements), but they also report space problems tied to scale (overcrowded hallways, parking congestion, 40+ class sizes), a mix of substantial facility investment and enrollment/space strain that Circle does not detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater polarizati: Square reviewers repeatedly describe a split—very committed Honors/AP teachers versus disengaged regular teachers—and also allege favoritism for athletes/wealthy students, teacher bullying/proselytizing, nepotism, and discriminatory staff actions (e.g. ‘teachers bully you…favorites,’ ‘nepotism is rampant,’ ‘don’t teach evolution’), while Circle reviews tend to portray staff as more uniformly caring and less politically/ethically problematic.
candidate_defs.square entries document more operational: Concrete operational complaints appear throughout square reviews—misfiled transcripts/VOEs, counselors not available or giving wrong advice, disorganized LMS/Canvas, robot calls, restrictive scheduling and bussing gaps, and failure to follow up on thefts—examples include ‘counselor forgot course wasn’t UC approved,’ ‘did not prepare my granddaughters VOE,’ and ‘Canvas is disorganized,’ problems that Circle reviews seldom describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety failures at square schools—frequent fights, assaults, vaping/drug use, gangs, pervasive bullying (including ethnic slurs), and administrators or on-site police who fail to intervene—whereas circle reviews consistently describe a safer, better‑supervised environment; examples include reports of weekly fights, students high in class, bullying met with ‘lip service’, and police/staff indifference at square versus circle’s claims of a ‘safe, small town setting’ and effective handling of incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: Square reviews list concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes—AP/Pre‑AP, IB, AVID, dual‑enrollment/concurrent‑credit, early‑college pathways, AP Capstone, honors tracks, higher test/ranking citations and documented college matriculations—while circle reviews rarely name these programs and focus less on advanced-course breadth; examples include square’s IB/AVID/dual-enrollment claims, AP classes and college scholarships versus circle’s lack of specific advanced-program detail.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater variabili: Square reviews repeatedly report a wide spread—from highly engaged mentors, individualized teacher support, and named standout instructors to passive/video‑based teaching, outright teacher bullying, refusals to accommodate special‑needs students, and poor classroom management—whereas circle reviews tend to present staff quality more uniformly (either generally caring or uniformly problematic); evidence includes square statements like 'some great teachers but some bad ones,' alongside examples of strong mentorship and claims of teachers who 'make fun of' students or 'sit in front of a video.'
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: Square reviews frequently enumerate extensive clubs, award‑winning band/choir/athletics, JROTC/robotics/UIL and cite new auditoriums, remodels, pools and technology upgrades—yet also note pay‑to‑play fees, cafeteria concerns, overcrowding and some facility complaints—whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable extracurricular breadth or capital projects; examples include square’s many named programs and new construction alongside complaints about ‘pay to play’ and cafeteria quality.
candidate_defs.square entries report systemic access, t: These reviews document structural inequities at square schools—formal tracking that segregates students by race/ability, favoritism toward high‑GPA students and athletes, selective extracurricular role assignment, opaque grading/placement policies, and failures to support students with disabilities—while circle reviews do not present the same pattern; examples include claims of ‘Pre‑AP classes filled with white students,’ ‘if you’re not a jock you have no chance,’ denied 504 accommodations, and inconsistent grading/RC room practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report substantially stro: These reviews describe concrete curricular assets (IB/AP/Honors, STEM academies, AVID, dual‑enrollment/CTE partnerships, ability to earn college credit) and documented alumni/placement outcomes (scholarships, Ivy/college matriculation) in square entries, whereas circle reviews lack named advanced programs and measurable post‑secondary outcomes; examples include repeated mentions of IB/AP offerings, STEM/CTE academies, dual enrollment credits, and graduates going on to conservatory/college success versus circle’s absence of comparable offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, deeper, a: Square reviews repeatedly name and praise extensive extracurriculars (award‑winning band/theater, robotics, travel clubs, national competitions, internships, marquee sports programs and recognitions), while circle reviews contain little or no comparable programmatic detail; illustrative items include travel trips to China/Russia/Egypt, award‑winning music and theater departments, Engineering/STEM clubs, and state/national competition placements described for square but not for circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain numerous, specific incident‑level claims—daily fights, gang and drug activity, pervasive bullying, high suicide/attempt rates, tolerated racist displays and homophobia—and repeatedly note inadequate counseling or inconsistent discipline, whereas circle reviews do not document this scale or severity of safety/crisis problems; examples include 'fights EVERY day,' 'kids doing drugs in the bathroom,' 'suicide rate seems very high,' and administration allowing confederate flags versus circle’s lack of comparable reports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers describe concrete organizational failures (lost transcripts/papers, registration 'nightmare,' schedule/dismissal mismanagement, counselors holding transfers hostage, repeated unreturned phone calls), while circle reviews do not present the same pattern of recordkeeping and day‑to‑day operational breakdowns; representative evidence includes 'they lost her transcripts,' 'Every year registration has been a nightmare,' and parents waiting months for callbacks in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: Square reviews repeatedly cite physical plant and resource problems (overcrowded campuses, no gym, leaking toilets, roaches, old computers, funding cuts and diverted funds, pay‑to‑play for sports/band), whereas circle reviews rarely describe these material constraints; examples include 'ridiculously small…no gym,' 'old macs and windows 98,' 'Programs are suffering due to funding cuts,' and 'Sports and marching band are pay to play.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, deeper: These reviews report concrete curricular and opportunity advantages in square schools—more AP/IB/Honors options, dual‑enrollment and college matriculation evidence, extensive CTE/pathways and specialized STEM labs, plus richer arts, music, clubs, and athletic programs (examples: “IB program is excellent,” “18 AP and numerous PreAP courses,” “new biotechnology lab,” “band/choir/outstanding music program,” and many named clubs)—whereas circle reviews rarely mention comparable named advanced courses, career pathways, or programmatic breadth.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Square reviews include repeated accounts of violence, fights, gang activity, drug/vape epidemics, lockdowns, bus/transport safety problems and even police arrests of students (examples: “lock‑down almost every day,” “many gang fights,” “Vape Epidemic,” and police called on bullied special‑needs students”), often paired with uneven security responses (either active SRO/security presence or administrative inaction), while circle entries largely lack these kinds of chronic safety/criminality reports.
candidate_defs.square entries document more polarized a: Square reviews supply specific, actionable claims about adult actors—both strong teacher commitment and responsiveness (e.g., ‘teachers stay countless hours, very helpful’) and systematic failures (overloaded/unsupportive counselors, unresponsive front office, favoritism toward athletes, punitive/incorrect disciplinary actions, IEP/504 noncompliance, and alleged administrative hostility or misconduct)—whereas circle entries do not present this same intensity or the same range of concrete personnel practices.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extreme and: Square schools are described at both ends of the spectrum—major recent capital investments, 1:1 device programs and new labs/performing arts centers on one hand, and aging buildings, overcrowding, sanitation/pest problems, textbook/ supply shortages and budget cuts on the other (examples: “large bond… Brighton Center,” “1:1 Apple laptop program,” vs. “terrible insect problems,” “old, small and crammed,” and ‘funds are cut every year’), plus explicit parent‑funded inequities and booster involvement skewing resources; circle reviews rarely show that same range or those funding‑allocation complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries depict a more exclusionar: Square reviews emphasize peer dynamics and community culture that exclude or marginalize students—athletics‑centric hierarchies, cliques and class/wealth divides, racial/religious/sexuality hostility, and conservative legacy norms (examples: ‘if you are not in sports you are invisible,’ ‘very cliquey,’ ‘homophobic…if you’re not Christian/Republican’), while circle entries are far less likely to describe such pervasive social exclusion or ideological homogeneity.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more extensive a: These reviews name concrete college‑prep pathways, AP/IB/Cambridge/AICE offerings, dual‑enrollment and vocational credential programs (e.g., Project Lead the Way, ROP, welding/CNA certificates), measurable college placements and scholarship totals (Stanford, UCs, Ivy acceptances, millions in scholarships), which Circle reviews largely do not enumerate or document with outcomes.
candidate_defs.Square entries report worse student safe: Many Square reviews recount frequent fights, gang/drug presence, sexual‑assault allegations, retaliation after reporting bullying, bus and security‑staff misconduct, and administrators who fail to enforce discipline—patterns and severe incidents that Circle reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.Square entries show more administrative: Square reviewers repeatedly cite absent or hostile principals, unresponsive front offices, erased credits/graduation‑blocking errors, favoritism toward athletes or insiders, mismanaged fees/fundraising, high turnover and questionable budget/prioritization decisions—concrete governance and operational failures largely absent from Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader, higher‑pr: Square reviews list extensive clubs, award‑winning music/theater, competitive sports with college scouting, longstanding alumni pride and families moving into the district, and active parent fundraising/donations—features and community investment that Circle reviews rarely describe.
candidate_defs.Square entries provide more explicit ind: Numerous Square reviews name one‑on‑one guidance counselors, SAT/college‑prep tutoring, targeted supports for struggling learners and life‑saving counselor interventions (though implementation is sometimes uneven), whereas Circle reviews offer little or no comparable, concrete evidence of these individualized supports.
candidate_defs.square entries show stronger advanced ac: These reviews describe concrete academic breadth and outcomes in square schools—AP/IB/honors access, dual‑enrollment and CTE pathways, high test scores and cited selective college matriculation—whereas circle reviews lack or question such offerings (examples: multiple square notes of AP/Honors, dual enrollment and students attending Duke/MIT/Harvard; circle reports limited AP or remedial gaps). Falling into this bucket means the text documents institutionally supported advanced coursework, college credit programs, or clear alumni college success stories that circle entries do not.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive saf: Square reviews frequently recount fights, guns/drugs, recurring bullying, staff‑linked sexual misconduct, police involvement, and harsh/exclusionary punishments (suspensions, isolating ISS practices), while circle reviews largely omit these systemic safety failures. A review belongs here if it contains repeated concrete safety incidents or descriptions of ineffective or punitive disciplinary responses (e.g., daily fights, drug/gang reports, alleged staff sexual abuse, humiliating breathalyzer/photograph episodes).
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square texts enumerate many extracurriculars (award‑winning band, theater, 30+ sports, marching band tours, strong arts and career academies) and frequently note booster funding or resource skew toward athletics and athlete favoritism; circle entries generally offer fewer program details or report program decline. Include a review in this bucket when it lists diverse/large arts, CTE or sports offerings or documents athletics being privileged (new stadiums, coaches' favoritism, boosters funding uniforms) relative to other activities.
candidate_defs.square entries document more and more sp: Square reviews contain concrete facility narratives—either recent rebuilds and high‑tech labs or severe crowding, broken AC, filthy bathrooms, parking shortages and textbook/equipment shortages—while circle reviews mostly omit such detailed facility/capacity evidence. A text fits this bucket if it names physical‑plant status or capacity problems (new building openings, overpopulation at lunch, class size ratios, vandalism, or lack of textbooks) that materially affect schooling.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews frequently accuse leadership of nepotism, arbitrary or unaccountable discipline, bureaucratic unresponsiveness, broken scheduling/coordination, high teacher turnover, state corrective action or lawsuits; circle reviews contain far fewer of these governance‑level critiques. Put a review here if it details systemic management failures or contested leadership practices—examples include claims of family‑name favoritism, buried racism scandals, slow refunds/scheduling failures, corrective‑action status, or repeated calls for new administrators.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program offerings (IB, AP, dual‑enrollment, Honors Academies), college‑matriculation and scholarship evidence, and explicit college‑prep supports (college fairs, counselor outreach), whereas circle reviews lack program detail and portray weaker college readiness; examples: 'amazing International Baccalaureate (IB) program', 'AP and dual-enrollment classes', and 'impressive scholarships to the best universities' in square versus no comparable outcomes in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: Square reviews contain detailed accounts of fights, assaults, drug/vaping culture, monthly lockdowns, and victims being suspended or ignored by administration, while circle reviews rarely describe such extreme incidents; illustrative items include 'There is some kind of lock down almost every month,' 'a freshman was beat with a metal marching band baton,' and 'The drugs and violence happening freely in the middle of the school day.'
candidate_defs.square entries document greater variabil: Many square reviews describe a mix of excellent, dedicated teachers and widely reported apathy, unfair grading, staff bullying, athlete favoritism, and explicit claims that unions impede accountability—contrast with circle’s more consistent praise of caring teachers; examples: 'a few teachers that are very good… some that shouldn’t be teachers,' 'teachers grade based on character not work,' and 'no accountability due to the union.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square reviews catalogue extensive club lists, award‑winning band/arts programs, strong sports/ROTC traditions, and school-run community outreach (college fairs, rallies, festivals), whereas circle reviews rarely enumerate such breadth; examples include 'hundreds of sport and extracurricular activities,' 'award winning marching band,' '3 orchestras… more than 4 choirs,' and 'college & career fair every year.'
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete ope: Square reviews frequently mention explicit policies and operational facts—tardy/substance policy changes, renovations, lost paperwork, phone‑blast systems, overcrowding or modern facilities, and mass staff exits—while circle offers fewer concrete governance logistics; supporting evidence: 'new tardy policy is really making a difference,' 'turned in something… they had thrown it away,' 'the building and facilities are beautiful,' and 'mass exodus' of staff.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, stronge: These reviews highlight that Square schools more often report extensive AP/IB curricula, dual‑enrollment and CTE pathways, industry certifications, and measurable college admissions/test outcomes (examples: IB/MSA/Project Lead The Way, many APs, dual enrollment producing 18 college credits, CNA/EMT certification, ACT scores of 34–36 and top‑tier college placements), whereas Circle reviews do not list comparable program breadth or consistent high‑end matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report a sports‑centric c: Square reviews repeatedly describe dominant athletic programs, top sports facilities and visible investment in athletics (e.g., new turf, stadiums, top‑notch complexes), plus claims that money, staff time, and preferential treatment are skewed toward athletes (grade/resource favoritism, politicized team selection), while Circle reviews do not make comparable claims of athletics-first resourcing.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: Square reviewers document pervasive student conduct and safety crises — fights, gang activity, stabbings, visible drug/alcohol use, chronic bullying, social‑media harassment and punitive or biased security responses — often coupled with ineffective preventive discipline; Circle reviews lack or explicitly deny the same breadth/severity of safety and bullying incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater chronic admi: Square reviews more often allege leadership failures (principals not returning calls, deleted reviews, ignored safety complaints), governance scandals or secrecy, active community appeals/escalations to district/state authorities, and administrators who discourage parental involvement, whereas Circle reviews contain far fewer or no such governance/unresponsiveness claims.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit larger operationa: Square schools are more likely to be described as having teacher shortages or coverage failures, highly variable teacher quality, weak or delayed special‑education and counseling services, mandatory after‑school interventions that conflict with students' lives, overcrowded classes, aging/unsanitary facilities, problematic scheduling (cohort lunches, early start times), poor emergency drills and ineffective tech rollouts — while Circle reviews generally do not document this same cluster of staffing, space, and logistics breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: These reviews describe concrete, school-level college-prep strength in square texts — plentiful AP/Honors/IB offerings, dual‑enrollment and college‑credit pathways, established STEM/advanced‑math tracks, and named outcomes (top‑college admits, D‑1 college success, scholarships) — details largely absent from circle. Examples: repeated mentions of IB programs, ‘plenty of AP and Honors classes,’ paid AP exams/dual credit, and measurable alumni outcomes (Fulbrights, Ivy admits) support this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Square reviews repeatedly document higher incidence and severity of misconduct — fights, weapons/AR‑15 threats, gangs, drug overdoses, tasing, frequent lockdowns, pervasive bullying and vaping — and numerous accounts that the school’s responses are inadequate or inconsistent. Examples include daily fights with police involvement, students tazed, drug‑related deaths, chronic bullying that ‘got to the point of attempting suicide,’ and repeated notes that administration/counseling failed to protect victims.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more systemic ad: These texts emphasize leadership problems and accountability breakdowns at scale: unresponsive counselors/front offices, cover‑ups and unequal discipline, hiring/nepotism complaints, recordkeeping and scheduling chaos, and even staff‑led harassment of community members. Illustrative items: allegations of administrators ‘covering up’ complaints, counselors being ‘completely uninterested,’ retention/quota incentives for seniors, staff stalking/harassment, and chaotic registration or month‑long grade fixes.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical inf: Square reviews contain concrete facility and resourcing failures: severe overcrowding and heavy portable use, broken/old desks and HVAC, infestations and dirty restrooms, inedible or moldy food, missing textbooks, and chronic budget shortfalls. Representative evidence: ‘primarily portables (102 to be exact),’ cockroaches in bathrooms, freezing classrooms, no math/spanish books, and ‘ran out of money…couldn’t even buy paper.’
candidate_defs.square entries document broader extracur: Square texts list many structured non‑academic pathways and high‑visibility programs (JROTC/Junior ROTC, band/theater with state awards, vocational shops, aviation academy, career‑center partnerships) and often note athletic/booster prioritization, pay‑to‑play fees, or selection favoritism that shapes student experience. Examples: ‘award‑winning band,’ state championships, JROTC leading to elite placements, aviation academy development, booster funding expectations, and repeated claims that athletics/boosters receive outsized attention or resources.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket captures reports of physical violence, threats, sexual harassment, persistent bullying, drug/party culture, stabbings/arsons, and reviewers describing staff/administration failing to stop or adequately respond (e.g., 'fights constantly in the halls', 'student was stabbed', 'bullying for 3 years… nothing has been done', 'Thizzin Thursdays' drug references, and Title IX/IEP complaints left unresolved). Items belong here when the review documents concrete unsafe incidents and reviewer claims that school leadership or staff did not protect students or enforce discipline.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, stronger,: This bucket groups mentions of formal advanced programs and measurable postsecondary results such as AP/IB offerings, dual-enrollment/college-credit partnerships, honors/academy tracks, college scholarships and elite acceptances (e.g., 'IB and AP courses', 'dual enrollment with community college', 'full athletic and academic scholarships', 'students accepted to Ivy League and top universities'). Include reviews that list concrete program breadth or cite verifiable outcomes (SAT/SAT ranking, scholarship, matriculation) distinguishing program availability and college-readiness evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff and lea: This bucket covers concrete governance and personnel problems—hostile or demeaning principals, nepotistic hiring, teacher misconduct or bullying, chronic counselor unresponsiveness, high turnover, cover-ups, strikes and board failures (e.g., 'principal constantly talks bad about teachers…every year there are new teachers', 'Teachers bully students and nothing is ever done', 'hired friends and family', 'no accountability=who cares'). Use this when reviewers describe operational leadership failures, staff abuse or protectionism, or systemic lack of follow‑through that undermines school functioning.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket contains concrete, day-to-day physical and logistical deficits: overcrowded classrooms/hallways, unsanitary buildings and pest infestations, outdated or missing textbooks, unreliable wifi/devices, dangerous bus stops and pickup/dropoff failures, and scheduling/cafeteria/locker logistics (examples: 'class sizes were huge…no seat', 'roaches everywhere', 'textbooks are largely outdated', 'dangerous bus stops assigned to our children', 'wifi is extremely unreliable'). Include reviews that describe material conditions or system logistics that materially impede students' experience.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and more-vari: This bucket groups reviewer evidence about breadth and culture of extracurricular life—wide offerings in arts, band, music, robotics, many clubs and sports, strong traditions and school pride (e.g., 'many extracurricular activities…Go S‑P‑A‑R‑T‑A‑N‑S!', 'incredible band', 'performing arts center')—and also notes when access is uneven (small‑school inclusivity or, conversely, favoritism toward athletes). Use this for reviews that emphasize program variety, participation, and spirit or that describe extracurricular access dynamics (inclusive small‑school participation vs. athlete privilege).
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent, serious student-safety problems and inadequate responses (e.g., “Bullying is HORRIBLE,” repeated fights, drug dealing ‘right next to the in house police officers,’ Nazi graffiti, students beaten and suicidal, and staff failing to intervene), whereas circle reviews rarely document systemic violence, drugs, or racially-targeted assaults and instead describe isolated meanness or acceptance.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more n: This groups reviews that list concrete advanced-program infrastructure and outcomes (AP/IB/magnet tracks, Running Start/dual‑enrollment, CTE certifications, career academies, scholarship and university matriculation data—e.g., ‘Science Magnet… AP courses… alumni at Brown/MIT,’ or ‘CTE certifications (CNA, EMT, IT)’) that circle reviews do not document or support with comparable evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Includes complaints about opaque communication, ignored parental concerns, counselors who won’t help, leaders who silence critics, unequal enforcement or protection for athletes/alumni, and nepotistic hiring or alumni favoritism (e.g., ‘they tell you they will do something but never do… parents who post get called in,’ ‘nepotism reigns supreme,’ and ‘athletes get grade inflation’), while circle reviews either praise responsiveness or do not raise systemic favoritism/accountability failures.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, more co: Covers reviews that itemize many organized clubs/teams/arts majors, specialized arts time commitments, career/technical shops, and named facilities or investments (e.g., ‘band and chorus, ceramics, Science Research, 2–3 hours per day in your artistic major,’ modern tech labs, stadium spending, robotics/aviation/PTECH), whereas circle reviews generally lack similarly detailed listings of programs or dedicated physical student facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries describe weaker everyday: This bucket groups reviews that point to low classroom rigor or poor subject preparation—‘teachers teach to the state test, memorization, no essay training, poor AP passing rates, math and English unpreparedness’ and students denied remedial help—while circle reviews more often describe engaged teachers, AP/IB rigor, or at least do not report pervasive instructional failure.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete programmatic strengths—AP/IB/magnet/dual‑credit/CTE offerings, measurable test/graduation outcomes, elite college placements, and well‑developed arts/athletics (e.g., “AP program is amazing,” “IB student…rigorous courses,” “dual enrollment…quarter of students,” ‘top music/band,’ ‘engineering magnet…now at UF,’ and lists of Ivy/USC/UCLA acceptances’). Falling here means the review emphasizes formal advanced curricula, verified college‑credit pathways, or named extracurricular departments as central, which square reviewers do far more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reviews reporting concrete safety failures or widespread student misconduct—fights, drug use/sales, gang/weapon incidents, lockdowns, and claims the school ignored or inadequately responded (e.g., “Drugs are a big problem,” “3 gun lock downs so far this year,” “They also ignore instead of addressing bullying,” ‘student thrown over rotunda,’ ‘cameras don’t work’). A review belongs here if it details incidents or systemic failure of safety protocols; those complaints appear far more frequently in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This bucket groups evidence of problematic leadership or operations: biased or nepotistic staffing, favoritism for athletes/parents, inconsistent or lenient discipline, punitive fees/fines blocking graduation, transcript/record errors, and unresponsive/rude administrators (examples: “nepotism is now the new norm,” “fees over 300... without paying them my brother would not be able to graduate,” “they are constantly messing up students transcripts,” and “administration is extremely incompetent”). Reviews here focus on how school governance or office practices create unfair outcomes, a pattern attributed to square more than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries discuss facilities, fundi: This bucket covers concrete physical‑plant and resource statements: chronic underfunding, unsanitary or dilapidated conditions, recent renovations or new buildings, overcrowded classrooms and stalled expansions, or uneven capital spending (e.g., “generally dirty and falling into disrepair,” “brand new --- built about 10 years ago,” “soooo over crowded,” “won’t build second high school despite bonds,” and ‘renovated just a few years ago’). A review falls here if it centers on building condition, space/capacity, or explicit funding/bond outcomes—topics emphasized in square entries relative to circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more detailed sp: This bucket groups reviews that provide concrete accounts of special‑education practice, counseling capacity/outreach, IEP implementation or exits, and explicit equity problems (racial bias, homophobia, religious/intolerance incidents) — for example, reports like “Teachers think IEPs are meaningless,” success stories of IEP removal and regents gains, “overworked, understaffed counseling department,” and allegations such as “They are extremely homophobic,” or “lower expectations for African American students.” Reviews here focus on how the school serves (or fails to serve) vulnerable students and underrepresented groups, a set of issues square reviewers raise far more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries describe far stronger and: This bucket captures references to concrete curricular assets and measurable outcomes: square reviews repeatedly name AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/magnet programs, 30+ AP courses, 5.0 GPA options, college credit transfer and alumni admitted to selective universities (e.g., “30+ AP courses”, “dual enrollment…saved us thousands”, “both my children went to University of Pennsylvania”), while circle reviews lack these programmatic details or report barely any AP/college-prep offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher-: Square reviewers enumerate and celebrate flagship activities and competitive success—marching band/state championships, NJROTC, numerous clubs, high-attendance sporting culture and community fundraisers (e.g., “marching band has been 1st in state…”, “The athletics department is AWESOME!”, “parents provided over $4 million”)—whereas circle reviews seldom list sustained, high-level programs or community sports success.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket groups concrete safety/crisis evidence: square reviews cite police calls, shelter‑in‑place events, weapons/fights, pervasive drug/gang activity, sexual activity in bathrooms, and bystander/administrative inaction (e.g., “many…involved with drugs and gangs”, “shelter in place every 2 weeks”, “kids bring brass knuckles or knives”), while circle reviews rarely document such high‑severity incidents and instead emphasize lower levels of bullying or improving discipline.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical inf: Square reviewers repeatedly describe building disrepair and capacity problems—mold, asbestos, broken escalators, no air conditioning, overflowing commons, overcrowded classes and missing supplies—and operational breakdowns like device/schedule distribution and unreliable transport (e.g., “mold in the air vents”, “3000+ students…overcrowding”, “no account to log in to school computers…locker two weeks in”), whereas circle reviews rarely report comparable facility or logistical crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This bucket covers governance and personnel problems: square reviews document unstable leadership (multiple principals in a few years), nepotism/coach favoritism, punitive or inconsistent policies, unresponsive or overloaded guidance, and concrete special‑education failures (e.g., “3 principals in 7 years”, “coach blames one child…if you’re not his favorite you will not play”, “IEP supports removed”, “guidance counselors 200+ students”), while circle reviews more often describe caring teachers, improving leadership, or lack these systemic governance complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries present broader advanced: This bucket groups reviews where square schools emphasize concrete curricular depth and credential pathways (many AP/IB courses, dual‑enrollment, specialty academies, structured diploma tracks, CTE credentials) and cite measurable post‑secondary outcomes (scholarships, elite college matriculation, AP credit hours) — e.g., “tons of AP class options,” “ended up with 30+ hours of credit from AP,” “IB program…can't be beat,” and named alumni admissions — while circle reviews lack comparable advanced-course breadth, dual‑credit evidence, or numeric outcome claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe and va: This bucket captures reviews describing frequent, concrete student-safety and conduct problems (regular fights, drug sales/use, sexual misconduct, arson/threats, pervasive bullying, racial harassment, outsiders breaching campus) and hostile peer cultures; examples include “We get threats every single week,” “bullying is rampant,” “drug deals are made in the hallways,” and allegations of sexual misconduct — patterns that circle reviews do not report or report far less often.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: This bucket covers reviews that describe systemic managerial problems and broken processes (part‑time or hostile principals, district mismanagement, mass teacher turnover/targeted layoffs, scheduling/registration/onboarding errors, counselor unavailability) — e.g., “Administration…is lost,” “superintendent eliminated all supervisory positions,” “couldn't access the computer system,” and “guidance counselors refuse to help” — a set of organizational failures that circle reviews rarely allege.
