candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive a: This bucket groups reviews that cite concrete physical‑plant and resource realities — both positive capital projects and acute deficits — including gym rebuilds and new buildings as well as overcrowded cafeterias, bad lunches/food‑safety incidents, HVAC/bathroom problems, parking issues, and added security gates/K‑9 searches; example texts: “reconstructing the large gym,” “lunch lines…kids are eating nothing,” “building was torn down and a new one built,” and “added steel security gates…turned the school into a prison,” which circle reviews do not similarly report.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize smaller, close‑: This bucket captures reviews where circle schools are presented as smaller or more intimate, with cohesive parental engagement, clearer/consistent enforcement or efforts to 'regain local control,' and community/spiritual cohesion — e.g., “this being a small school…they truly care,” “Administration enforces rules that are the same for everybody…on its way to regaining local control,” and praise for warm staff/faith formation — themes that contrast with square reviews' frequent descriptions of scale, fragmentation, or administrative chaos.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more e: These reviews report that square schools more often list concrete AP/IB/dual‑credit offerings, structured college-credit pathways, and high test/college‑matriculation evidence (e.g., “offers nearly every AP class,” “IB Diploma (1 year college credit)”, students entering UGA/Harvard, “state’s highest AP/SAT scores”), whereas circle reviews lack named advanced-program breadth or measurable outcome claims and focus on general instruction rather than formal college‑prep structures.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: Square reviews repeatedly enumerate many clubs, competitive sports, marching band and arts programs, booster fundraising and high-cost athletic facilities (e.g., “100+ team championships,” large stadium with turf, elite music/performance center), and also allege resource bias and preferential treatment for athletes, while circle reviews mention far fewer organized extracurriculars and do not document the same funding/priority or championship-level participation.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more frequent an: Square reviewers provide vivid, repeated accounts of violent fights, bus bullying, vaping/drug use, suicides, life‑threatening bullying incidents and both exploitative or punitive discipline (e.g., police tickets, O.S.S., random searches) as well as staff complacency or variable enforcement, whereas circle reviews rarely report comparable safety crises and generally emphasize kinder student behavior or administrative handling of bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: Square reviews more often allege politicized district/board dynamics, favoritism/nepotism, grade‑tampering, admissions and counseling failures, hostile public meetings, and unresponsive or threatening leadership (e.g., ‘cesspool of politics,’ ‘VP changing teachers’ grades,’ ‘principal threatened juvenile hall’), while circle reviews contain few such governance‑level misconduct claims and instead focus on classroom/program issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete oper: These reviews repeatedly mention tangible campus and service realities at square schools — overcrowded classes and trailers, counselor overloads (hundreds per counselor), facility disrepair or new construction, outdated/1:1 technology programs, pay‑to‑participate fees, and explicit special‑education outcomes ranging from inclusive support to push‑out practices — while circle reviews rarely enumerate this level of operational detail or mixed programmatic support.
candidate_defs.Square entries exhibit stronger, more ex: These reviews repeatedly name AP/IB/honors pathways, specialized academies, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit programs, high AP/ACT scores and elite college placements (e.g., Ivy acceptances, AP score growth), and link instructional rigor and teacher support to college readiness; examples include "huge pile of AP and Honors courses," "AP Biology scores among the highest in the country," and alumni reporting easy transitions to top universities. This bucket captures claims about curricular breadth, teacher‑led rigor, AP/IB/STEM signatures, and concrete academic outcomes that square reviewers emphasize more than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain multiple concrete incidents and patterns — chronic bullying, weekly fights, gang/assault episodes, drug/vaping epidemics, teen suicides, death threats, and claims that anti‑bullying policies are not enforced — e.g. "lots of bullying which is tolerated by faculty," "students are dropping unconscious in class," and "OFFICER WALKER... slamming a highschool girl's head on the concrete." This bucket groups all evidence about student misconduct, physical safety, substance use, and ineffective disciplinary enforcement that distinguish square from circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe greater administ: Square reviewers more often accuse leadership and the district of favoritism, politics, corruption, misallocated budgets (flashy tech/athletics over basics), punitive or unnecessary police interventions, top‑heavy administration, and prioritizing reputation over student wellbeing — e.g. "UNLESS YOU HAVE MONEY... THEY WILL NOT ACKNOWLEDGE YOU," "administrative budget increased while test scores drop," and "football team...doesn't even get to retain the concession sales!!!" This bucket covers structural governance, funding choices, board/superintendent critiques, and administrative policy behavior that set square apart.
candidate_defs.Square entries document stronger, more v: Square reviews frequently cite state/national championships, award‑winning bands/choirs, extensive clubs and competitive teams, and sustained post‑graduation pride — examples include "state championships for boys swimming/diving and soccer," "nationally recognized Show Choir," and "I can't hide my #warriorpride." This bucket groups claims about extracurricular breadth, competitive achievement, coach support, and prominent school spirit that appear more in square than circle.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more consistent,: Circle reviewers more often report an inclusive environment and reliable supports — statements like "leadership fosters an environment where everyone belongs," positive counselor/teacher responsiveness, and accommodation anecdotes — while many square reviews allege IEP noncompliance, poor counseling access, or intensive parental advocacy (e.g., "special needs kids fall through the cracks" vs. Circle's reports of belonging). This bucket captures differences in how well special‑education implementation, guidance counseling, mental‑health support, and day‑to‑day inclusion are described across the two groups.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: This bucket groups reviews where square schools report explicit, institution-level advanced academics and measurable postsecondary outcomes—IB/Cambridge, many AP/dual-credit courses, guaranteed college credit or vocational credentials, and concrete college acceptances/scholarships (e.g., IB transfers of 15 college credits, AP/Dual Credit programs, students admitted to UT‑Austin/USC/MIT). Circle entries lack those programmatic claims or report limited/declining preparation instead, so content that documents named advanced programs and documented college/career outcomes belongs here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures accounts of frequent fights, gang activity, drug use, sustained/clique-based bullying, sexual misconduct, threats/assaults, and reviewers describing long‑term psychological harm or students leaving because of danger (e.g., 'drug and gang activity...not a safe environment', ' bullied to death ', 'girl had her face slammed into a table', 'student under psychological treatment'). Circle reviews generally do not document this level of violence or pervasive peer-cruelty, so items describing those concrete safety/behavior harms map here.
candidate_defs.square entries foreground facility and c: This bucket covers comments about building capacity and physical plant: chronic overcrowding and large enrollments, unsanitary conditions, toxic mold/asbestos/roaches, HVAC/heat problems, long attendance waits, or conversely explicit major renovations and new facility investments (e.g., 'overcrowded, building is filthy', 'toxic mold...seizure‑like symptoms', and '8 Million Dollars worth of great changes', 'incredible new athletic additions'). Circle entries rarely emphasize those concrete facility/capacity or major renovation issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher-pr: This bucket groups reviews that describe large, award‑winning extracurricular ecosystems and formal career/technical pathways—extensive band/choir/orchestra, national debate/speech championships, robotics, manufacturing/automotive/engineering academies, JROTC, and guaranteed career certifications—as well as commentary that athletics receive outsized attention or funding (e.g., 'number one speech and debate team', 'Manufacturing Academy', 'multi‑million dollar locker room' and also 'sports get priority over learning'). Circle entries do not provide comparable evidence of broad, high‑profile extracurricular or vocational programming.
candidate_defs.square entries document more personnel,: This bucket collects concrete staffing and governance issues: frequent teacher absenteeism and reliance on unqualified subs, tenure‑protected low‑effort teachers, lost counseling records, mishandled transcripts, punitive or inconsistent discipline, alleged bribery/favoritism toward athletes, rude security/staff, and weak special‑education supports (e.g., 'unqualified subs', 'counselors keep 0 track', 'teachers protected by tenure', 'favoritism for star athletes', 'phone unlawfully seized and read'). Circle reviews rarely allege that range of administrative/ personnel mismanagement or show such pronounced variability, so those governance/support-system failures belong here.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, stronger,: This bucket groups reviews that describe explicit programmatic depth—AP/IB/academy offerings, niche advanced courses, dual‑enrollment/college partnerships, robotics/magnet programs, award-winning arts and athletics, internships, and concrete college matriculation statistics—claims which appear much more often in square than circle (e.g., “tons of AP classes… IB program… partnered with Southwest Technical College,” robotics, state championships, students winning scholarships or full rides).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This captures reviews describing ongoing fights, bomb/gun threats, drug overdoses, pervasive bullying and racial harassment, sexual misconduct, and suicides or NAACP involvement—systemic safety/climate harms that square reviewers repeatedly allege but circle reviewers rarely do (examples: “1-2 fights a week,” “two kids OD… and died,” “bullying is not dealt with,” “racial slurs… NAACP had to get involved”).
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This includes allegations about opaque discipline, selective enforcement, favoritism (by wealth, religion, athletes), administrative retaliation/coverups, mismanaged records/IEPs, pressure to pass students for state ratings, and budgeting/resource misallocation—concrete governance failures emphasized in square (e.g., “students involved in bloody fights do not get reported…”, “administration gives pay raises to their friends,” “they keep things quiet,” and “big push to reduce number of kids with disabilities”).
candidate_defs.square entries contain more explicit fac: This groups descriptions of physical and tech infrastructure—new wings, fab labs, 1:1 laptop/LMS programs, renovated science centers as well as mold/pest complaints, filthy bathrooms, portables/overcrowding, and broken HVAC—features square reviewers specify far more often than circle (examples: “fab lab… distance learning lab… 1:1 laptop PowerLearning,” vs. “moldy smell,” “too many students in classes… portables,” and “the majority of the computers are frustratingly slow”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more p: This bucket captures concrete human supports: proactive teachers who 'go above and beyond,' named counselors who help with FAFSA/college planning, tutoring/mentoring programs, tight small‑school personalization, and multigenerational alumni/community backing—specific relational supports frequently reported in square but less often in circle (examples: “His counselor, Ms. Sax, was wonderful,” “teachers helped before and after school,” “smaller class sizes offer more one on one,” and local families moving to the district).
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, named: These reviews report concrete programmatic rigor (AP, IB, dual‑enrollment, SAT/college‑credit offerings) and numeric outcomes (proficiency rates, scholarship/college acceptances) — e.g., “23 dual credit courses and 18 AP courses,” “63% of Juniors take at least 1 IB class,” and named admits to Notre Dame/Clemson/Virginia Tech — whereas circle reviews lack comparable program names, scores, or documented college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: Many square reviews catalog extensive clubs, band/choral/performing‑arts strengths and booster/alumni engagement (jazz band, All‑State orchestra, big marching band, FFA, robotics) and also repeatedly allege funding/prioritization captured by athletics (football funding/favors, fundraising to sustain non‑sport programs); circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth and focus less evidence on funding capture.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute safety,: Square reviewers cite drugs, gangs, fights, sexual harassment, metal detectors, multiple lockdowns and administrators who 'brush it under the rug' or fail to report incidents (e.g. 'notified but nothing to police', 'metal detectors held kids...'), while circle reviews contain far fewer or less severe safety/discipline allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Square accounts contain persistent accusations of favoritism, protected or underperforming teachers, politicized board/health‑policy decisions, rigged student governance, tracking that pushes minorities into lower classes, expulsions/selection to preserve image, and leadership instability (principals changing or vice‑principal running the school), whereas circle reviews provide fewer or opposite claims of managerial politicization or systemic favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: Squares contain detailed operational complaints and facts about building condition, enrollment and logistics — overcrowded classrooms/hallways, attendance/office mismanagement, scheduling and dismissal problems, mold/cracked ceilings or lack of AC — alongside repeated mentions of major capital actions (large bonds, $100–192M remodels); circle reviews lack this same mixture of intense facility, capacity and operational detail.
candidate_defs.Square entries exhibit stronger, broader: These reviews highlight concrete programmatic rigor at the school (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment, Syracuse/college‑sponsored courses) and named college placements (Yale, MIT, elite colleges) or expanded AP counts—e.g., “Top 5 AP School in AZ,” “full IB program,” “number of AP classes doubled,” and alumni college matriculation—features Circle reviews do not provide or explicitly contrast with weaker AP outcomes or reliance on alternatives (Running Start).
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive, be: Reviewers list many named non‑academic offerings and capital resources—band/choir/theater/magnet arts, NJROTC, sports with state championships, international trips, internships, $52.4M facility, 1:1 Chromebooks/Apple laptops—evidence of broad extracurricular breadth and facility/tech investment that Circle reviews generally lack or criticize as underfunded.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more frequent an: Multiple Square reviews report near‑daily fights, gang/drug activity, police presence, severe bullying (legal/therapy outcomes), sexual‑misconduct incidents, medical‑response failures and weapon incidents—often paired with ineffective or inconsistent school responses—whereas Circle reviews do not report this level of chronic, high‑severity safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.Square entries show greater variability: Square reviews frequently contain polarized accounts—'some teachers are excellent, some are awful,' chronic teacher absenteeism/cancelled classes, mixed guidance/counseling reports, and contradictory special‑education experiences (from 'great focus' to 'awful for invisible disabilities'), indicating wide unevenness in day‑to‑day instruction and individualized supports that Circle reviews present far more consistently.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: These items describe district/school leadership problems and policy/operational barriers—frequent principal turnover, opaque/defensive administration, spending priorities criticized as misallocated (marquees/TVs/landscaping/football over textbooks or female sports), punitive/overused alternative placements, scheduling/transfer/transportation failures, and secrecy or resistance to criticism—issues that Circle reviews seldom allege or that Circle frames as responsive leadership instead.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger and broa: This bucket groups reviews where square schools describe extensive AP/Honors/magnet/dual‑enrollment/CTE offerings and formal academic supports (AVID, HPA, many APs, Project Lead The Way, college concurrent credit), plus structured college‑prep help (dedicated counselors, after‑school homework/ACT prep). Example evidence: “over 20 APs…three magnets…entering college with over 60 credit hours,” “wonderful after school homework class four days a week,” and “faculty guided me through applications and scholarships.”
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater extracurr: This bucket captures reviews reporting many and well‑funded extracurriculars, championship athletics, standout music/theater programs, and capital investments (performing arts center, pools, tech wings), often with resource priority toward athletes. Example evidence: “well over 30 clubs…bands rank at the very top nationally,” “huge weight room…they find money for the huge football program,” and “new Olympic size pool under construction.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive saf: This bucket groups accounts of routine and severe student safety problems (daily fights, stabbings, guns, drug use, gang presence), chronic bullying/harassment, and school responses that are absent, inconsistent or punitive. Example evidence: “trash can fire…a stabbing, and a gun problem,” “bullying goes unchecked…they do nothing,” and “dogs are sent in monthly to check for drugs.”
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This bucket covers reviews documenting unstable or smothering leadership, high faculty turnover, unresponsive front offices, punitive attendance/discipline policies, lack of transparency about spending, and district‑level reform/turnover struggles. Example evidence: “70% faculty turnover…administration is smothering,” “they don’t return calls or email,” “they fight AGAINST parent involvement,” and “money is being used for other things not educating our children.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe smaller‑scale, m: This bucket groups reviews where circle schools are portrayed as small‑school or pod‑structured, with committed/qualified teachers and counselors, more effective bullying reduction, and stronger parent/staff collaboration that yields safer, more nurturing experiences. Example evidence: “the way the classes are organized by floors…has really eased the transition,” “highly qualified committed staff,” and “bullying has been fixed tremendously compared to last year.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews repeatedly document ongoing safety incidents and student‑on‑student harm—daily fights, bomb threats, on‑campus drug use/vaping, suicides/attempts and chronic bullying—with reviewers saying staff/administration often fail to protect students. Examples include "fights every day between classes," "drug use galore," "at least two suicides due to bullying," and reports that administration 'did nothing' or 'told parents they can't do anything about it'; Circle reviews, by contrast, rarely report such persistent violent or crisis behavior.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater staff and: Square reviews repeatedly allege unhelpful or rude counselors and office staff, arbitrary or biased discipline (athlete/wealth favoritism, nepotism), misuse of suspension to avoid accountability, and repeated 504/IEP noncompliance or case‑management breakdowns. Representative claims: 'counsellors do not care... refuse requests to move a bullied child,' 'they will choose a student if say their parent is in the school system,' and '504 Education plans are not consistently followed'; Circle reviews do not describe these systemic responsiveness, favoritism, or special‑education enforcement failures.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: Square reviews contain both reports of recent, modern investments (smart boards, 1:1 laptop rollouts, new buildings) and sharp counterexamples of severe resource shortfalls—budget cuts, filthy bathrooms, overcrowded classrooms, or understaffing—indicating larger swings in physical and operational conditions. Evidence: claims range from 'Smart boards in every room' and 'Every student gets their own laptop' to 'horrible bathrooms... rarely clean,' 'way over crowded,' and 'bus system is terrible'; Circle reviews generally lack this same degree of facility/resource extremes.
candidate_defs.square entries report a wider, more conc: Square reviews enumerate many named non‑core programs—marching band with international travel, LISA/Cirque, AFJROTC, technical shop, biomedical/engineering pathways, strong music/theatre, many clubs and athletics—while also flagging access issues or resource allocation conflicts (arts cut in favor of football, favoritism in team selection). Examples: 'the only public Cirque high school program in the country,' 'Information Technology Systems program,' 'music department travels internationally,' and simultaneous complaints like 'football is taking $ away from the art department'—Circle reviews rarely list comparable programmatic breadth or unique specialized offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews describe specific, established academic pathways and outcomes (many AP/IB/honors classes, Calc III, dual‑enrollment/college credit, vocational academies, stated graduation and SAT/ACT figures) that reviewers tie to college matriculation and scholarships—for example: “They teach over 30 AP classes,” “enough college credits to nearly complete freshman year,” and reported high graduation/college‑placement rates—whereas circle entries lack comparable concrete program names, metrics, or sustained outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, better‑fu: Square reviewers repeatedly list and praise many named clubs, travel programs, strong band/choral/athletic achievements, inclusive participation claims and long‑running continuity (e.g., ‘over 100 student clubs,’ Model UN travel to major cities, ‘Best band in Tennessee!!’, repeated playoff seasons), while circle reviews rarely enumerate such high‑quality, high‑participation extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews allege drug use, frequent fights, sexual harassment/assault reports, weapons/illegal searches, bomb threats or lockdowns and administrators who fail to enforce consequences (examples: ‘High drug use including heroine,’ ‘fight or incident nearly every day,’ ‘illegal search’), while circle reviews generally do not contain the same level of criminalized behavior or systemwide safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Square reviewers cite unresponsive/rude office staff, high teacher turnover and out‑of‑state recruitment, staff misconduct or investigations, protected favoritism toward athletes/insiders, and mishandling or neglect of special‑education/IEP needs (examples: ‘teachers quit before the end of semester,’ ‘counselor involved in child abuse,’ ‘preferential treatment for athletes,’ ‘had to fight tooth and nail for proper education’), whereas circle reviews more often describe stable, caring staff and fewer systemic personnel failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse facilities,: Square reviews frequently document concrete infrastructure and resourcing issues—overcapacity and trailers, aging HVAC and poor cafeteria/food, outdated computers and equipment, budget‑driven large classes, and program cuts or monetization of activities (e.g., ‘building over 50 years old and handling twice capacity,’ ‘teachers have big class sizes due to the budget constraints,’ ‘computers are very old’), while circle reviews contain far fewer of these concrete facility/funding complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: These reviews repeatedly describe fights, on-campus drug/tobacco use, bullying, assaults and even fatalities plus administration/staff failing to stop or adequately discipline offenders (e.g., “a fight every week,” “Drugs are a HUGE problem,” “reported threats…they did nothing,” and cameras/officers that ‘failed to act’), while circle reviews contain few or no comparable accounts of violence, pervasive bullying, or tolerated substance use.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger advance: Many square reviews name concrete offerings and outcomes — multiple AP/IB courses, concurrent dual-enrollment partnerships with community colleges, students earning large transferable credit totals and full tuition scholarships, and explicit elite-college placements — whereas circle reviews typically note limited or improving honors/AP options and provide fewer program- or outcome-level specifics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews frequently cite leadership instability, micromanagement, biased enforcement (athlete favoritism or racialized discipline), lost/withheld records, registrar/enrollment failures and unreturned calls that directly harmed students (e.g., missed DMV excuse, withheld nurse records, repeated principal turnover), while circle reviews emphasize staff friendliness or single-administrator complaints rather than pervasive operational malpractice.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater breadth: Square reviewers repeatedly list extensive clubs, championship athletics and band programs, award-winning vocational shops, one-to-one devices and funded international trips or new buildings (e.g., ‘Every student has an IPAD,’ ‘award winning culinary arts,’ ‘brand new campus’), whereas circle reviews focus on limited clubs, funding constraints, or note only modest extracurricular access.
candidate_defs.square entries report more structured in: Square reviews name concrete support mechanisms — before/after-school tutoring, Writing Center/Eagle Time, proactive IEP implementation and successful special-education cases, counselor-driven college planning and targeted improvement tracking — while circle reviews rarely describe such consistent, programmatic remediation, counseling or special‑education evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and bro: This bucket groups reviews where square schools list concrete advanced coursework and pathways (AP, IB, honors, specialized academies, dual‑credit), documented awards/DOE/US News recognition, and named elite college matriculations or alumni success—e.g., 'many AP offerings,' 'IB program is one of the best,' and 'placements were Harvard, MIT, Stanford'—while circle entries lack comparable program breadth or elite outcome claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: Includes reviews describing assaults, near‑daily fights, drug/alcohol availability, theft, sexual harassment/assault, gang activity, and supervisors or staff failing to intervene or protect students (e.g., 'female students deal with sexual harassment,' 'fights on a weekly basis,' 'no supervision around'), whereas circle entries do not describe this level of recurrent, serious safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: Covers reviews that enumerate many clubs, award‑winning arts programs, AFJROTC, competitive speech/drama, marching band, extensive spirit traditions and high student participation (e.g., 'tons of extracurricular options,' 'AFJROTC...the one and only thing that deserves 5 stars!,' 'homecoming...fireworks'), while circle entries generally omit or report far fewer and less prominent extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries document more facility, m: Groups reports of sewage/mold/pest contamination, dirty restrooms, ceiling/roof failures, trailers and overcrowded halls, shortages of books/technology, and complaints that funds are prioritized for sports over academics (e.g., 'sewer smell,' 'no books!!!', 'overcrowded, 30 per teacher', 'quit spending money on football fields'), whereas circle entries provide fewer or no persistent facility/resource complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Captures reviews that allege frequent principal/board turnover or scandal, unresponsive or absent counselors (even blocking graduation), arbitrary or biased rule enforcement favoring athletes/wealthy families, secrecy or tenure‑protected poor teachers, and parents being ignored or obstructed (e.g., 'Ms. Schecter was NEVER available,' 'rules change based on WHO the student is,' 'superintendent resigned amid scandal'), while circle entries contain far fewer such systemic governance or accessibility complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more acute stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent fights, weekly lockdowns, students bringing weapons or drugs, gang activity, teen pregnancy, recurrent bullying, and formal security sweeps — often paired with administrators or staff who ignore or inconsistently handle incidents (examples: 'bomb squad search', 'kids pass liquor while dean drove by', 'fights almost every week', 'rapists attend and admins did nothing'). These items jointly measure school climate and safety breakdowns (incidence + adult response) and are distinct from curricular, staffing, or facilities complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, broade: This bucket groups claims about institutional program breadth and demonstrated outcomes — e.g., numerous AP/IB courses, dual‑enrollment and transcripted college credits, vocational certifications (automotive, nursing, aviation), documented scholarship totals and college placements ('graduating class received $4 million in scholarships', 'students enter college with 16–32 credits'). These are programmatic offerings and outcome evidence (not teacher tone or facility condition) and contrast with Circle's more generic/limited curriculum descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced st: This bucket covers reviewer claims of hostile or bullying teachers, coach/athletic favoritism, political discipline systems, rude front‑office staff, substitute‑teacher noncooperation, lost paperwork, and IEP/504 coordinator absences or procedural breakdowns ('IEP not worth the paper', 'teachers bully students', 'administration rude', 'favoritism in extracurricular selection'). These are operational and equity failures tied to personnel and processes (distinct from curriculum quality or facility state).
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete, de: This bucket groups resource- and infrastructure-related evidence: smartboards, campus Wi‑Fi and rebuilt 'private‑school' facilities, bond-funded renovations, but also chronic overcrowding, broken HVAC, mold, roaches, asbestos, poor food quality, and district funding shortfalls ('building falling apart...no AC', 'Smartboards in every classroom', 'mold causing health problems'). It captures physical capacity, maintenance, health hazards, and explicit funding/policy tradeoffs (separate from academic program or staff behavior).
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, more dive: This bucket groups accounts of large extracurricular menus, strong band/choir/theater, championship sports, active booster/PTA support, internship/industry partnerships, and multi‑generational alumni ties ('marching band sold out shows', 'state/national ranked sports', 'strong alumni association', 'PTSA is strong'). These items describe organized out‑of‑class opportunities and external community support distinct from in‑class academics, safety, staff professionalism, or facility condition.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger formal: These reviews report that square schools more often offer structured advanced programs (AP/IB/Honors, magnet curricula, engineering/medical/ROTC pathways), documented college supports (Naviance, UT OnRamp) and concrete post‑secondary outcomes (Ivy/elite acceptances, National Merit) — e.g., “offers the IB Diploma Programme,” “wide range of AP classes,” and students accepted to Ivy League schools — while circle reviews lack comparable, school‑level AP/IB/magnet evidence or outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries portray broader, higher-p: Square reviews repeatedly describe large, award-winning extracurricular portfolios and capital investments (theatre magnet touring/Edinburgh Fringe, Telly‑award TV production, state‑champion sports, new gyms/pools/weight rooms), e.g. “Dr. Phillips Theatre Magnet…traveled to Scotland,” “girls basketball won state 3 years in a row,” and “brand new Olympic sized pool,” whereas circle reviews mention only limited or smaller-scale arts/sports offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report larger-school scal: Many square reviews document systemic space/scale problems — schoolwide overcrowding, classes of 30–40+, mall‑style hallways that prevent locker access, construction disrupting learning and stretches of understaffing — e.g. “over flowing with students…over 1500,” “class sizes in the high 30s,” and “mall like design makes changing classes extremely crowded,” while circle reviews tend to describe smaller cohorts, small class sizes or expanding but not overcrowded facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more frequent st: Square reviews contain numerous accounts of campus safety incidents and mixed responses — daily fights, widespread drug/alcohol exposure, tolerated bullying or ignored assaults, K‑9 searches and sheriff involvement, and both overly punitive and negligent enforcement — e.g. “fights almost every day,” “85% of the school is involved in drugs,” and “teachers turned their heads,” whereas circle reviews include far fewer or no comparable safety/criminality incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: These reviews report patterns of favoritism/cronyism (preferential treatment for wealthy/influential families), cover‑ups or poor parent communication, leadership instability or careerist hires, and district/budget mismanagement (textbook shortages, questionable spending), e.g. “based on who you know and how much money you have,” “the school system seems to try and cover things rather than call parents,” and “budget cuts…not enough textbooks,” while circle reviews contain fewer or different governance complaints and less evidence of systemic cronyism.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews repeatedly list concrete advanced offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, dual enrollment, PSEO/college credits, STEM academies, high AP pass rates, Ivy/competitive college matriculation and scholarship counts) whereas Circle reviews lack comparable program breadth or college‑placement evidence (examples: 'numerous upper level, PSEO and college‑credit classes', 'IB diploma', 'I graduated and went to a top US university').
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many Square reviews describe daily bullying, fights, drug/alcohol incidents, even arson and police/metal detectors, and administrators who either ignore incidents or respond with harsh/punitive measures for minor infractions (e.g., 'they do nothing about bullying', 'VIOLENCE and the BULLYING is OUTRAGEOUS!!', 'detentions for standing up to the teacher', 'dogs and police in the school'), while Circle contains far fewer or no comparable safety/bullying reports.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Square reviewers frequently accuse leadership of favoritism (athletes/wealthy/band), nepotism, gaming placements for metrics, rude front‑office behavior, slow or contradictory communication, and scheduling/case‑management errors (examples: 'favoritism toward football players', 'rude receptionist', 'took EXACTLY four months for a reply', 'sending below average students to LD classes to boost scores'), complaints that Circle reviews do not substantively mirror.
candidate_defs.square entries document more overcrowdin: Square reviews cite severe space and maintenance issues (dangerously undersized halls, no lockers, locked bathrooms, rodent/cockroach infestations), failing/old tech and broken furnishings, and explicit tradeoffs like stadium spending instead of air conditioning or course cuts (e.g., 'packed into classes like sardines', 'infested with bugs and rats', 'spent millions to build a football stadium instead of removing asbestos'), while Circle reviews rarely contain this cluster of infrastructure strain.
candidate_defs.square entries show more polarized instr: Square reviews often pair praise for high‑quality AP/IB teachers, award‑winning music/sports and abundant clubs with separate reports that regular classes, math instruction, and special‑education supports are poor or legally noncompliant and that families must pay for outside tutors (examples: 'majority of the best teachers teach the honors/AP track', 'math field is extremely weak', 'School doesn't follow the law when it comes to special needs', 'Had to pay Sylvan $3,000'), a pattern not evident in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete, frequent safety incidents and failed protections at square schools—e.g., “2–3 fights a week,” rampant vaping/drugs, students sexually harassing peers, and bullying that “never gets punished”—while circle reviews rarely report comparable fights, drug use, or systemic failure to protect students.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers repeatedly cite leadership and policy problems—principals who ignore parents, shifting/executed policies, counselors who miss scholarship deadlines, and claims that administrators protect staff or favor popular students—whereas circle reviews focus less on broad governance breakdown and more on isolated staff or resource critiques.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ac: Square reviews enumerate named programs and measured outcomes—SAS/IB/AG programs, AP/dual-credit transfers, vocational classes, strong IEP advocacy, and private tutoring markets—and also describe subject‑specific strengths/weaknesses (e.g., math dept problems), while circle reviews provide fewer concrete program names or explicit college-credit outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Many square reviews give specific infrastructure or logistics complaints—severe overcrowding and trailers, no AC/cockroach problems, parking shortages and bad entry design, or lack of public transit to campus—conditions that circle reviews seldom raise.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: Square reviewers frequently list rich extracurricular breadth and competitive success (state/national awards for band, robotics, mock trial; feeder athletics programs) plus active parental fundraising and paid tutors, whereas circle reviews rarely document this level of award-winning programs or intense parental/alumni financial intervention.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe frequent fights, rampant bullying, drug use/odor, sexualized harassment, self‑harm signals and routine threats to student safety — together with staff/administration that tolerate or mishandle these incidents (e.g., “fights almost every week,” “the whole school smells like pot,” “girls cutting wrists…,” and “Administration is horrible in dealing with bullying”) — a pattern repeatedly described in square but absent or explicitly denied in circle (which reports a safe environment and effective handling of disruptive students).
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: This bucket covers concrete program and outcome strength reported in square: AP/IB offerings, specialized academies, dual‑enrollment and college credits, prestigious recognitions and scholarship/college placements (examples: IB/engineering magnets, dozens of APs, students entering UNC/Ivies, National Merit semifinalists, large AP/college‑credit totals), a set of named advanced programs and measurable outcomes that circle reviews do not similarly document.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal more administrativ: This bucket captures critiques in square about leadership problems, inconsistent enforcement, nepotism/favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, monetized fees and procedural harms (wrong class placements, denied credit or graduation, unexpected fees for clubs/classes), and district/board corruption or turnover (examples: “they gave me the wrong classes,” “students must pay $1200 for IB fees,” “administration gives athletes many chances”), patterns far more prevalent in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more severe and: This bucket groups facility and resource evidence in square that ranges from severe maintenance/pest and cafeteria breakdowns and overcrowded classrooms (“no central heating or a/c,” “rat fell out of a ceiling,” “lunch lines so long they run out of food,” classes of 35–40 or 3,000 students) to explicit references to bond campaigns or large capital investments (new PAC, stadium, STEAM center), a mixed-but-concrete facilities story not echoed by circle’s generally well‑maintained/new facility descriptions.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent,: This bucket collects circle evidence of steady adult support and systems that help students (examples: AVID and college trips, counselors described as ‘extremely supportive,’ accessible principals/teachers, organized communication and improved supervision) and a safer, more inclusive social climate — contrasts that appear repeatedly in circle reviews and stand opposite many of square’s reports of counseling failures, staff apathy, and exclusionary culture.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety incide: This bucket captures substantive reports of student safety and conduct problems (frequent fights, weapons, bomb threats, vaping/drug epidemics, student pregnancy, hate‑crime incidents) coupled with allegations that staff/administration fail to protect or appropriately discipline (lockdowns without parent notice, bullying allowed or favored, police‑level incidents). Examples: “constant fights,” “a gun found…in a student backpack,” “rampid drug/drinking problem,” and “bullying of disabled kids was not only allowed but encouraged.”
candidate_defs.square entries report worse facility con: This bucket groups concrete, on‑the‑ground infrastructure and logistics problems: dilapidated buildings, pests/rodents, filthy bathrooms and lunches, tiny detention rooms, broken elevators, 20‑minute lunches, bus no‑shows, and chronic lack of textbooks or supplies. Examples: “you can sometimes hear rats running in the ceiling,” “WAY TOO OVERCROWDED…2715 students,” “If your kids miss school you will hear about it three weeks later via snail mail,” and “no textbooks…they don't follow the curriculum.”
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger/more nume: This bucket covers tangible programmatic strength: multiple AP/IB/dual‑credit/Early College/ROP/CTE pathways, named academies and competitive academic teams, and concrete alumni/college placement claims (Ivies, top‑20, associate degrees at graduation). Examples: “numerous AP classes,” “Early College…Dual Credit and AP classes,” “24 AP and Honors courses…alumni to MIT, Yale, Harvard,” and “Cambridge Academy program is of the highest quality.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures governance and personnel practices: authoritarian exclusion of parents, nepotism and bias (favoring athletes/wealthy families), punitive or inconsistent discipline, poor record transfers, IEP failures, and hostile/unresponsive front office or admin behavior. Examples: “The administration runs roughshod over parents,” “If you don't have a reputation and are very rich, you are treated like dirt,” “gave our son's new school a hard time when they requested his school records,” and “Complete failure with special needs. If your kid needs an IEP get a lawyer.”
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and higher: This bucket groups concrete descriptions of many and often nationally successful extracurriculars (marching band to Carnegie Hall, award‑winning robotics, vocational shops, no‑cut teams, successful sports), stronger parent fundraising/volunteer support, plus reported tradeoffs — athletics or elite programs prioritized over general academics and program‑based social elitism (IB vs general). Examples: “band invited to China…Grammy,” “H‑Hall…best vocational programs,” “parents come out in droves to fundraise,” and “IB Program is an elitist program that breeds…hate traditional program students.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, better‑: This bucket groups reviews where square schools enumerate concrete program breadth and outcomes (IB/AP counts, CTE/health/robotics/arts magnets, academies, college credit/dual‑enrollment, scholarship totals and alumni acceptances), e.g. 'IB program… prepares for college,' 'nearly 30 AP classes,' 'tremendous amount of opportunity through CTE,' and reported alumni at Ivy/Columbia; circle reviews typically do not list comparable programs, AP/IB volume, or measurable postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize an athletics/co: This bucket captures reviews describing a staff culture centered on sports, coaches holding outsized influence, budget prioritization for athletics, and athlete privilege or nepotism (e.g. 'Every teacher there is a coach…sports are emphasized over teaching,' 'budget for some classes is very low because it is being used on sports,' and 'athletes are treated as gods'), whereas circle reviews lack sustained claims that athletics crowd out other priorities.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer physical fa: Includes concrete operational/facility grievances tied to building condition and scale—decaying buildings, pests and unsanitary bathrooms, lack of AC, overcrowded classrooms, broken/old tech, long lunch lines and construction impacts (e.g. 'buildings are decaying…one caved in from the cockroaches,' 'classes of 44,' 'very old netbooks…printers barely work'), while circle reviews rarely raise these facility/capacity failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket groups reviews describing pervasive misconduct and safety threats plus failures of investigation/discipline—examples include 'bullying is rampant and ignored,' 'fights every 2 days,' 'drug problems…we were on lockdown for hours,' and accounts that administrators 'failed to view the video' or 'swept things under the rug'; circle reviews do not document this scale or investigative failure.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more variable an: This bucket covers reports about teacher absenteeism/ incompetence, uncertified instructors, high turnover, poor or defensive administrative behavior, dysfunctional guidance/counseling, record‑keeping errors, nepotism, and staffing instability (e.g. 'not engaging kids…not even showing up,' 'teachers without state certification,' 'third principal in three years,' 'guidance is nonexistent' and 'transcript errors'), while circle reviews more often describe consistent, responsive teachers and stable leadership.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student: These reviews describe concrete safety failures in square schools (frequent fights, gang/drug activity, bomb/shooting threats, corporal punishment, teacher-on-student physical harm, suicidal-risk from bullying and ineffective anti-bullying response) that are absent or far less frequent in circle reviews (which rarely report systemic violence). Examples: '20–25 fights', 'bomb threats and shooting threats', 'drugs run rampant', 'my son came home crying... the school did nothing'.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, more ex: Square reviews often list concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes—IB/AP breadth, dual‑enrollment, strong vocational academies, competitive honors tracks, and explicit college matriculation claims—whereas circle reviews seldom detail such formal pathways. Examples: 'entire IB Programme', 'wide array of AP classes', 'dual enrollment at AIMS', 'students accepted to Johns Hopkins / Ivies / large scholarship totals'.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic facil: Many square reviews specify overcrowded campuses, broken/restroom/food-service problems, asbestos/mold and pest concerns, late/dangerous buses, poorly designed new buildings, and resource shortages; circle reviews generally do not report these systemic infrastructure or transportation hazards. Examples: 'extremely overcrowded and lunch time is crazy', 'asbestos hanging from ceilings', 'buses are late or dangerous', 'building in horrible disrepair'.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater polarizat: Square reviews frequently contradict one another—some describe highly caring, dedicated teachers, strong tutoring/counseling and targeted supports, while others report teacher negligence, favoritism, staff bullying, and counselor shortages—producing a wide within‑school variability not seen in circle reviews. Examples: 'teachers are dedicated... amazing administration' versus 'teachers are downright pathetic', 'tons of after-school tutoring' versus '3 counselors for ~3000 students'.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer extracurric: Square reviews more often enumerate extensive clubs, championship athletics, strong music/arts programs, alumni pride and active parental/community support, but they also report community-level cultural tensions, racial hostility, mascot fights, and administrative favoritism toward athletes; circle reviews seldom show the same breadth or the same public cultural conflicts. Examples: 'over 80 different activities', 'five time golf state champions', 'community involvement was exceptional' alongside 'racism is prevalent... adults in the community fight over the mascot' and 'administration favors athletes'.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reviews that describe ongoing safety incidents (e.g., gang violence and multiple weekly fights, widespread drug/alcohol use, explicit sexual‑assault allegations, students self‑harming, transfer/withdrawal for safety reasons) together with claims that responses are ineffective or inconsistent; Circle reviews contain little or no comparable safety evidence and often say the school felt safe. Examples: 'Gang violence... one through three fights weekly,' 'school has a r*pist,' 'an unusually high number of girls cut themselves,' contrasted with Circle's lack of safety incidents or statements like 'We didn't have to worry about the safety of our child.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket groups claims about concrete college‑prep infrastructure and outcomes — expanded AP/IB curricula, formal dual‑enrollment partnerships, targeted ACT prep, unusually high AP pass rates and elite college admissions — which Circle reviews do not document. Examples: 'IB program… one of the most rigorous,' 'SLU 1818 program and AP program,' 'brought my ACT from an 18 to a 25,' and students admitted to MIT/Harvard, contrasted with Circle's lack of dual‑enrollment/IB detail and more limited AP mentions.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pr: This bucket covers reviews that list many named extracurriculars, high‑performing arts/forensics/band programs, vocational tracks and nationally recognized teams (theatre, marching band invited to Normandy, debate state wins, robotics, agricultural centers), whereas Circle largely mentions a narrow set of athletics or few electives. Examples: 'the band is truly outstanding... invited to play in Normandy,' 'Theater, Robotics, Visual Arts, Science, Health Science, Communications,' versus Circle's focus on 'Cross Country, Track, and Basketball' or sparse elective offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: This bucket captures specific, actionable facility and operations evidence — overcrowded hallways and lunches, leaking roofs/mold/rodents, closed bathrooms, failed science‑lab funding, security breaches/locked‑entry changes, and also named capital projects (new performing arts center, aquatics center) — while Circle rarely cites these operational specifics. Examples: 'hallways are extremely crowded,' 'couldn't get a bond passed to expand the Science dept.,' 'special doors installed — must buzz in,' and contrasting mentions of no comparable facility or logistical complaints in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse staff/admini: This bucket groups critiques of personnel and governance: unresponsive guidance/administration, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, high teacher turnover and substitute use, budget choices that prioritize athletics over academics, and parents fighting over IEP/504 services; Circle reviews rarely report systemic favoritism, administrative unresponsiveness, or widespread special‑education failures. Examples: 'Communication is especially the worst,' 'sports are basically everything... cutting courses over sports,' 'I fought with the district on getting him his 504 plan,' and 'revolving door with teachers,' versus Circle's relative absence of such systemic governance claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: These reviews describe concrete, school-level offerings and measurable outcomes that square schools advertise (IB/Cambridge/magnet tracks, AP and dual‑enrollment, engineering/STEM tracks, college credits, National Merit and Ivy/elite matriculation). Example evidence: multiple square reviews cite IB/Cambridge programs, AP/dual‑enrollment credit, ‘graduating with 12 hrs of college credit,’ and alumni attending Harvard/Duke/Stanford—claims that circle reviews do not make or mention only sparsely.
candidate_defs.square entries report more school‑safety: Square content repeatedly documents violent or criminal incidents, frequent fights/drugs/weapons, systemic peer bullying, and staff/administration failing to intervene (students leaving or switching to online school as a result). Illustrative items include reports of a bullet found in a bathroom, students stabbed or arrested, ‘bullying is not addressed,’ ‘staff turn a blind eye,’ and unsupervised classes due to no substitutes—problems largely absent from circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: These reviews point to concrete administrative breakdowns—poor communication, lost or unreviewed student records, oversized counselor caseloads, transcript/grade errors, nepotistic hiring, cost‑cutting policies that restrict classroom resources, and unresponsive principals. Examples: counselors with 500 students, ‘8 months to notify us’ about truancy, centralized printing that charges teachers, and administrators who ‘never responded’ or ‘cover up’ incidents; circle reviews are far less likely to describe these systemic operational failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: Square reviews frequently inventory many clubs/sports/arts, newer facilities and technology programs, and championship teams, while simultaneously reporting selective access, tryouts/auditions, pay‑to‑play, and funding skewed toward athletics. Representative evidence: ‘over 200 clubs,’ new pool/netbooks, state championships, alongside complaints that lead roles are for the elite, ‘many extracurriculars require audition/tryout,’ and ‘they spend all their money on sports,’ contrasts with circle’s lack of comparable extracurricular breadth.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater within‑sch: Square reviews often describe sharp divides (IB/AP/honors vs. regular students), heterogeneous teacher quality, low‑stake grading or grade‑inflation practices, and unequal attention tied to race, socioeconomic status, or athletic/parent clout. Examples: explicit IB/non‑IB segregation, ‘huge difference between Honors and regular classes,’ complaints that B students are neglected, allegations that ‘minority students are not given the same attention,’ and teacher‑level reports of ‘every assignment is only worth 1%’—patterns that circle reviews do not emphasize or characterize as consistently.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reviewer reports of active student‑to‑student harm and unsafe common spaces: frequent fights, gang presence, pervasive bullying (including racial slurs and retaliation against reporters), vaping/drug epidemics, self‑harm reports, bomb/drug arrests, and repeated fire‑alarm evacuations (e.g., “numerous fights every year,” “Kids that vaped turned the schools bathroom into a vaping break place,” “multiple kids were beaten up so badly they were hospitalized”). Circle entries lack comparable accounts of these systematic student‑safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and strong: This bucket groups descriptions of named rigorous pathways and documented outcomes at the school level: AP/IB/dual‑credit offerings, themed institutes/STEM tracks, CTE/dual‑enrollment, AVID/IB programs, and alumni college/scholarship evidence (e.g., “Many AP classes and dual credit classes,” “STEM program…make students ready for college,” and alumni attending Duke/Johns Hopkins/Stanford). Circle reviews generally do not enumerate these structured advanced programs or the same level of measurable college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent,: This bucket covers reviewer claims about leadership and staff governance: selective enforcement and favoritism (athlete/cheerleader privileges), punitive policies that criminalize students or punish victims (e.g., “If your child is attacked…both will be punished,” police arrests at graduation), administrative cover‑ups, heavy-handed security measures (bag checks, drug‑sniffing dogs, armed follow‑outs), refusals to meet parents, and leadership instability or absenteeism (e.g., calls to remove principals). Circle reviews do not describe this same pattern of punitive/favoritism‑driven governance.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic facil: This bucket groups concrete material and operational problems and contested funding choices: underfunded programs and deteriorated equipment (band instruments held together with tape), overcrowding and space/parking shortages, cafeteria/food complaints, unequal spending prioritized to athletics over arts, aging or missing instructional materials, and technology/maintenance problems (e.g., “They put so much money into the football program… the band instruments are held together with tape,” “severely overcrowded,” and “we need new books in almost every class”). Circle reviews more often describe adequate or improved facilities and investment instead.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures or c: This bucket captures reviewer evidence on legal/non‑compliant or exclusionary practices and socioeconomic/racial stratification: denied or punitive treatment of students with IEPs/GIEPs, refusal to evaluate or provide accommodations, discriminatory tracking and segregated honors/AP placement, and pronounced socioeconomic or racial self‑segregation (e.g., “They will not allow to let them go into honor class even though they qualify,” “very economically and racially segregated,” and “RACISM is still strong in this community”). Circle entries do not contain comparable patterns of special‑education noncompliance or systemic segregation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete harmful incidents and recurring safety breakdowns—assaults, sexual assault, suicides, regular fights, bomb/gun/drug incidents (e.g., “a teacher now beaten by the students,” “a student came to school with a loaded handgun and drugs,” “2 suicides in past couple of years”)—and repeatedly say staff/administration failed to stop or properly respond; Circle reviews do not report comparable weapon/drug/serious‑violence or multi‑year safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and stro: Square reviews list many concrete program offerings and outcomes—IB and full‑diploma programs, 25+ AP courses, Early College/AA pathways, dual‑credit/transcripted credit, vocational academies and certifications, robust band/theater/arts with international trips and scholarships (e.g., “Early College program allows you to graduate with an AA,” “My older child got a scholarship to one of the top 3 art schools”)—while Circle reviews rarely document that program breadth or college/dual‑credit infrastructure.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures and: Multiple square reviews document unmet IEPs/504s, lack of follow‑through, segregation of students with behavioral needs, and parents forced into sustained advocacy (e.g., “there is no IEP set in place… emails to the case manager never received any help,” “they are not reading IEPS”); Circle reviews either do not mention special‑education breakdowns or instead occasionally praise effective special‑needs support, so systemic SpEd implementation problems are concentrated in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical fac: Square reviewers provide specific facility/health evidence—mold making someone sick, roaches/rats, burst sewage pipes, 51 health violations, peeling walls, portable trailers and 30–35 student class sizes, overcrowded lunches and traffic—whereas Circle reviews are largely silent about such severe maintenance, hygiene, or capacity/health hazards.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger instruct: This bucket captures content where square schools are described as offering AP/IB/early-college/STEM tracks, measurable college outcomes, formal tutoring/support periods, and teacher/counselor actions that produce college readiness (examples: ‘many AP, IB classes,’ ‘early college Academy,’ ‘MCAS prep sessions,’ ‘great scores, great for college readiness,’ and schedule/tutoring structures like study halls or smart‑lunch). It also covers reviewer statements about teacher availability/quality as it affects instruction (both high-performing named teachers and variability across staff) and math/subject-specific instructional failures when contrasted with the presence of advanced options in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reports of on-campus harm and hostile social climates—repeated bullying, large fights, vaping/drug use, bomb threats, racial/LGBTQ discrimination, student depression/withdrawals—and reviewers’ claims that school responses are ineffective or punitive (examples: ‘bully other students and basically get away with everything,’ ‘kids vaping and getting high in the bathroom,’ ‘Racism and homophobia rings in the hallways,’ and ‘I had to pull him out… he was suicidal’). It intentionally bundles incident frequency with reviewers’ evidence that discipline, reporting, or counseling systems are inadequate or inconsistent.
candidate_defs.square entries show broader and higher-p: This bucket covers accounts that square schools have wide, high-quality extracurricular offerings (championship athletics, top band/orchestra, thriving theatre, JROTC, career-certification programs) while simultaneously describing preferential support for athletes or marquee programs and budget sacrifices for fine arts (examples: ‘best band program in the state,’ ‘tripled music program,’ ‘offers CNA/EMT certification,’ and complaints like ‘all the income goes to football’ or ‘take money away from the fine arts program’). It therefore groups both program strength/breadth and the documented inequities or prioritization inside extracurricular budgets.
candidate_defs.square entries document worse facilities: This bucket groups concrete, physical‑infrastructure complaints about square schools—collapsed ceilings, rodent/mold infestations, overflowing sewers/smells, unsanitary food/bathrooms, lack of handicap access, extreme overcrowding/cafeteria seating shortages, and site traffic/entrance problems (examples: ‘rats, cockroaches, mold,’ ‘ceilings have already fallen,’ ‘not accessible nor safe,’ ‘2,300+ kids… too small for the amount of kids,’ and ‘over 2000 students pass through one intersection’). It captures both chronic maintenance/sanitation failings and capacity/design constraints that harm daily operations.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal more pronounced ad: This bucket groups reviewer evidence that square schools show strong and active parental/booster involvement and community wealth effects (boosters, scholarships, alumni prestige), alongside recurring claims of problematic governance—nepotistic hiring, favoritism for staff/kids, punitive fee collection/transcript withholding, billing/enrollment enforcement, district-level mismanagement, and lost paperwork (examples: ‘active PTA and sports booster,’ ‘offers scholarships and CHOICE program,’ ‘staff especially admin are completely catered to,’ ‘they will hold your transcripts if you don’t pay,’ and ‘lost the school… paperwork’). It intentionally bundles community resource effects with concrete administrative/financial practices and policy failures distinct from classroom instruction or facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more severe st: This bucket captures reports of routine bullying, frequent fights, drug/alcohol use and overdoses, teen pregnancy, weapons searches, emergency-protocol breakdowns and chaotic incident response at square schools (examples: “5 freshman overdosed together,” “weekly fights, drug use,” failed fire/bomb responses, students wandering off campus), whereas circle reviews either describe safer, controlled environments or only delayed/limited disciplinary problems.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This groups concrete curricular and outcome claims (IB/AP offerings, high AP/IB test scores, valedictorians, elite college matriculation, robust CTE/college-credit options) that reviewers attribute to square schools (examples: “IB curriculum,” “Wide selection of AP courses,” “students to MIT/Caltech/Yale”), while circle reviews generally lack such program-level evidence and give fewer measurable college/career outcome indicators.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket covers institutional-level problems at square schools—grade-changing scandals, public misconduct, favoritism toward athletes/donors, opaque leadership/financial mismanagement, and broken commitments that require district escalation (examples: “public grade-changing trial,” “principal favors athletes/donors,” missing millage funds), whereas circle reviews contain far fewer or none of these governance/misconduct allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more organized, fo: This groups structured in‑school supports square reviewers describe—credit recovery/E2020, built‑in support blocks, free after‑school tutoring, inclusion teachers, strong counseling in some cases—alongside frequent notes that teacher quality is inconsistent (some excellent, some ineffective) (examples: “Smart Block...teachers plan to meet,” “credit recovery courses,” and “teachers are hit and miss”); circle reviews, by contrast, more often describe insufficient counseling and lack of consistent academic support.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater physical: This bucket captures square schools’ repeated claims of major facility investments (new PACs, bond-funded wings, remodeled campuses), broad extracurricular programs and competitive successes (marching band, JROTC, top athletic teams), and also operational constraints tied to size or maintenance (overcrowding, locked/unsanitary bathrooms, transportation gaps) (examples: “PAC addition...renowned music/drama,” “3500+ students,” “many bathrooms locked”), whereas circle reviews generally do not report comparable facility upgrades, program breadth, or the same scale‑related infrastructure problems.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more div: These reviews describe concrete programmatic breadth and outcomes (AP/IB/GATE/Running Start, STEM magnets, career/technical tracks, dual‑enrollment, robotics, national merit finalists and quantified college‑acceptance/ scholarship rates) that square reviewers cite as evidence of college readiness and higher rigor—examples: “IB/AP student,” “25 AP courses,” “over 90% of graduates going to college,” “students accepted to Harvard/Columbia/Georgia Tech”). Circle reviews lack comparable program detail or measurable outcomes and instead give only general or limited advanced‑course mentions.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more accessible,: Square reviews frequently name standout educators and describe teacher accessibility, emotional support, in‑school special‑education counseling, and higher credentials (National Boards, AP/G/T training)—e.g., “Mrs. Silvernail…a miracle worker,” “teachers answer emails in the evening,” and “counselors right in school that help them.” Circle reviews, by contrast, more often report teacher unresponsiveness or give only generic praise without concrete examples of individualized, high‑qualification staff support.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: Square reviewers recount concrete safety incidents (daily physical fights, gang activity, drug use, racial harassment, sexual assault), describe staff/administration failing to intervene or even punishing victims, and mention intensive policing/searches and frequent lockdowns—examples: “physically assaulted…punished for reporting,” “bullying happens all the time…staff does NOTHING,” and “school goes on lockdown very frequently.” Circle reviews do not document comparable levels of violence or systemic safety failures and more often emphasize a safer, caring climate.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight administrative: Square reviews cite withheld incident documentation, inconsistent/enforced policies, nepotism/favoritism, budget mismanagement or athletic spending over academics, leadership turnover, and broken parent communication (e.g., “they will NOT provide documentation,” “spend IDEA money on football buses,” “no accountability…trickles down to the classroom”), while Circle reviews more often describe stable or responsive administration and do not report those governance abuses.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize scale, faciliti: Many square reviews point to tangible capacity and operational issues—very large enrollments (1,200–3,000+), overcrowded classes/halls, inadequate spaces (small auditorium, parking), rigid schedules/tardy policies, heavy activity fees, and high‑profile construction or renovations that disrupt school life—often coupled with complaints that resources are prioritized for athletics over academics (new football fields vs. books). Circle reviews rarely report these large‑scale capacity or operational constraints.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more n: These entries repeatedly name AP/IB/dual‑enrollment pathways, specialty curricula, and quantified postsecondary outcomes (e.g., "many AP classes…students start college with 20+ credits," "full rides," "Top 20 in California," "20 National Merit Scholars")—claims and program lists that Circle reviews mostly lack or only mention generically. Examples: specific AP/IB/dual‑credit counts, pathway descriptions (medical, media, CTE tracks), and documented alumni college success appear in Square but are absent or minimal in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews contain repeated concrete safety incidents and climate complaints—frequent fights, gang presence, on‑campus drug use/vaping, sexual harassment, thefts and lockdown/notification failures (e.g., "multiple fights a day," "over half the kids vape," "student got stabbed with a pencil," "no notifications for 2 lockdowns"); Circle reviews do not provide comparable accounts of pervasive violence or drug problems. This bucket groups behavioral risk, supervision failures, and security/incident‑handling breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pronounced: Square reviewers enumerate campus size, aging vs. newly renovated buildings, specific facility problems or investments (leaks, remodeling, new turf/bleachers, stadiums, 1:1 laptop programs), plus a wide roster of clubs/arts and high‑visibility athletic spending and scholarships—material claims Circle rarely makes. This covers physical plant condition, technology rollouts, cafeteria/transport logistics, breadth of extracurriculars, and explicit resource/prioritization choices (e.g., sports capital projects vs. arts funding).
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviews frequently accuse leadership/district of punitive policies (truancy lawsuits, exclusionary discipline), favoritism to wealthy/athletic families, retaliatory behavior toward complainants, budget mismanagement, and failures in basic communication (misplaced records, schedule errors, ignored complaints), while Circle tends to lack such systemic governance allegations. This bucket captures managerial actions, accountability, fairness, and procedural transparency problems.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: Square contains multiple concrete reports of counselor overload, ineffective college advising, IEP/special‑education noncompliance, scheduling misplacements, and unmet mental‑health accommodations (e.g., "guidance is SWAMPED," "IEP goals not completed," "counselor is terrible," refused accommodations), whereas Circle reviews rarely raise comparable special‑education or counseling failures. This groups operational student‑support systems and their fidelity to student needs.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student-: This bucket captures concrete accounts of unsafe student behavior and ineffective supervision described more often in square reviews — e.g., repeated fights, gangs, weapons, filmed assaults, on-campus drug/alcohol incidents, sexual misconduct, pervasive bullying, homophobic/racist harassment, and claims that staff ignore or unevenly enforce rules (even when anonymous hotlines exist). Content belongs here when reviewers describe frequent physical/sexual harm, substance use, harassment, or gang activity and link it to inadequate prevention or resolution — distinctions that Circle reviews generally do not contain.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: This bucket groups references to explicit academic offerings and outcomes more often named in square reviews — AP/IB/Honors courses, dual-enrollment, magnet/STEM/arts/CTE tracks (cosmetology, auto, engineering), college scholarships and higher matriculation rates, and formal freshman/college guidance programs. Include square content that enumerates program breadth, advanced coursework, dual enrollment or CTE pathways and cites college placement, test-score or scholarship evidence; Circle reviews more often lack or criticize these programmatic offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report chronic facilities: This bucket covers physical-plant and resourcing issues emphasized in square reviews — deteriorating buildings, vermin/asbestos, broken bathrooms, overcrowded classes/hallways, short lunch windows or poor food, staffing shortages and late/locked classrooms, plus specific budget choices (stadiums/turf/iPads over basic supplies) and fee shifts to families. Use this bucket for concrete, repeated evidence of infrastructure decay, service failures, overcrowding, and contested or misaligned spending priorities that Circle reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries portray persistent admini: This bucket groups recurring administrative- and counseling-level failures found in square reviews — unresponsive principals/counselors, ignored parent emails or court-ordered access, mishandled IEP/504/504 refusals, inconsistent or punitive discipline, searches/rights violations, and slow or politicized complaint resolution. Include items where reviewers report systemic noncompliance, lack of meaningful counselor support, denied accommodations, or leadership that privileges insiders; Circle reviews generally lack these systemic administrative-legal complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal more uneven teache: This bucket captures the mixed, teacher-level evidence in square reviews — stark splits where some teachers are highly supportive, provide long-term mentoring, extra‑help, innovative pedagogy, or award-winning instruction while others are inexperienced, uncaring, over-reliant on substitutes, assign excessive busywork, or unevenly apply grading/homework/test policies. Include square content that documents variability in classroom teaching, individualized interventions, homework/test burden, or pronounced differences between regular and AP/IB teacher quality; these classroom-level patterns are more heterogeneous in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: These reviews describe tangible safety failures (gangs, weapons brought to campus, repeated lockdowns, sexual assaults, frequent fights, pervasive drug/vaping use) and explicit administrative failure to protect or discipline; e.g., reports of multiple on‑site lockdowns for guns, students hospitalized after beatings, and administrators who “turn a blind eye” appear in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more formal adva: Square reviews repeatedly name AP/IB/STEM pathways, magnet academies, National Merit and college‑placement outcomes, award‑winning sports/band programs and championship teams, and also note stratification (strong honors/AP tracks vs weak standard classes); circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth, outcomes, or track‑based elitism.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete rep: Square reviewers cite on‑site supports (full‑time nurse, guidance departments, ACE/ACT tutoring, before/after school tutoring, college fairs) and also document IEP/504 non‑implementation or problematic 504/IEP handling, while circle reviews lack this level of programmatic/special‑education detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square reviews frequently note overcrowding and capacity strain (very large enrollment, 50+ students/room), physical‑plant conditions or renovations (cockroaches/mice, mildew, outdated textbooks, lack of AC, parking/busing mismanagement) or recent upgrades, none of which are central in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger pattern: Square reviewers recount systematic favoritism (athletes given privileges, parents/old families getting preferential treatment), cliquishness and socioeconomic or racial exclusion, and discriminatory discipline practices or religiously‑biased enforcement; circle reviews do not make comparable claims about entrenched favoritism or institutionalized social ostracism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more serious safet: This bucket captures concrete reports of violence, sexual acts, assaults, and repeated theft present in square reviews but absent in circle reviews (e.g., “Not a safe school… reported violent, even sexual acts,” “cellphone… stolen twice,” “He has also been assaulted… scar for life”), indicating a harsher safety/discipline climate in square schools relative to circle schools.
candidate_defs.square entries describe weaker academic/: This groups contrasts where square reviewers explicitly call out a poor curriculum or academic program weakness (e.g., “poor curriculum”), while circle reviewers describe supportive school practices and systems that give students a better chance of success (e.g., descriptions of practices that “give the best chance for success for all involved”).
candidate_defs.square entries indicate leadership that: This bucket covers reviewer claims that school or district leadership over-emphasizes sports at the expense of academics or other priorities (e.g., warnings that the superintendent “cares about more than just football and basketball”), a criticism present in square reviews but not in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staffing inst: This groups concrete operational problems in square reviews such as classes without teachers or frequent coverage gaps (e.g., “At one point she didn't have a teacher…”), contrasting with circle reviews that describe consistent, present teachers and instructional stability.
candidate_defs.square entries report heavier student ho: This bucket captures descriptions in square reviews of excessive homework or workload that prevents students from joining activities or completing chores (e.g., “She gets so much homework… she doesnt have time for basketball practice or chores”), whereas circle reviews describe balanced workloads and accessible extracurricular offerings.
